formulations.name: Wolfram's formal statement of Problem 1 (2019), corrected
formulations.statement: Wolfram writes NotExists[{p, i}, ForAll[t, t > i, c[t + p] == c[t]]]. Intended reading, with c(t) the t-th center value: there are no integers p >= 1 and i >= 0 with c(t+p) = c(t) for all t > i. With T = i+1 this is not EP(c), where EP(f) := exists T P, 0 < P and for all t >= T, f(t+P) = f(t). Bookkeeping variants that are also equivalent: any shift t -> c(t+k); and 'no nonempty word w and T with c(T+n) = w[n mod |w|] for all n'.
formulations.proof_of_relation: An index shift (t > i iff t >= i+1). Caveat, my own reading of the post: as printed, p is not restricted to p >= 1, and c[t_] := CellularAutomaton[30, {{1},0}, {t, {{0}}}] is the list of the first t+1 values. With p = 0 the inner ForAll holds, so the literal NotExists is false. With lists, c[t+p] == c[t] is False for every p != 0, so the p >= 1 part is vacuously true. The intended statement needs p >= 1 and the t-th value; Wolfram's own Problem 3 uses Last[c[n]] for the n-th value. Our Lean Problem1 has 0 < P, so it matches the intended reading.
formulations.lean: Project, core Lean without Mathlib: Ruliology.CellularAutomata.Rule30Prize.Problem1 := not EventuallyPeriodic center, with Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic f := exists T P, 0 < P and for all t, T <= t -> f (t+P) = f t. Rule30StripCertificates.problem1_iff_no_word already proves the word form. The t > i and shifted variants are omega-level lemmas. Mathlib has no eventually-periodic predicate: grep for EventuallyPeriodic, preperiodic and 'eventually periodic' found nothing. The nearest notions are Function.Periodic (Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Periodic.lean) and Function.IsPeriodicPt (Mathlib/Dynamics/PeriodicPts/Defs.lean).
formulations.known_results: The project README says Problem1 matches formal-conjectures' Rule30.centerColumn_not_eventually_periodic. The prize site states the problems for 'the infinite sequence of center-cell values ... generated by rule 30 evolving from a single nonzero cell'.

formulations.name: The rule 30 constant is irrational (the user's example)
formulations.statement: x := sum_{t>=0} c(t) 2^{-(t+1)} = 0.11011100110001011001...(base 2) = 0.86238978394738404864080024608675112810853... (OEIS A365254). Equivalently x = lim_n A092539(n)/2^{n+1}, where A092539(n) is the first n+1 center bits read as a binary integer. Problem 1 iff x is irrational.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Source: Wolfram 2019, section 'The Digits of Pi'. He converts the column to a number with N[FromDigits[{Flatten[CellularAutomaton[30, {{1}, 0}, {500, {0}}]], 0}, 2], 85] and recalls that 'the only numbers whose digits repeat are rational numbers'. Proof, needing no named theorem: (<=) if c has period P from T, then x = N/2^T + 2^{-T} B/(2^P - 1) for integers N and B, by the geometric series. (=>) if x = a/q, the tails y_n := 2^n x - floor-part lie in [0,1] and satisfy q y_n in Z intersect [0,q]. Pigeonhole gives y_n = y_m with n < m. If y_n is not dyadic, its binary expansion is unique, so the tails at n and m coincide and c has period m-n from n. If y_n is dyadic, both of its expansions end in 0^inf or 1^inf, so c is eventually constant, hence eventually periodic anyway.
formulations.lean: Mathlib/Analysis/Real/OfDigits.lean has Real.ofDigits {b} (digits : N -> Fin b) : R = sum d_i/b^(i+1), Real.ofDigitsTerm, Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits (prefix plus scaled tail), Real.abs_ofDigits_sub_ofDigits_le, Real.ofDigits_nonneg, Real.ofDigits_le_one, Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one, Real.digits, Real.ofDigits_digits and Real.continuous_ofDigits. Mathlib/NumberTheory/Real/Irrational.lean has Irrational, irrational_iff_ne_rational and exists_rat_of_not_irrational. Missing: the lemma 'Real.ofDigits d is rational iff d is eventually periodic'. Statement: Problem1 <-> Irrational (Real.ofDigits (fun t => if center t then (1 : Fin 2) else 0)). The project's Lean snapshot is core-only, so this needs a separate Mathlib-based Lake project.
formulations.known_results: My script reproduces A365254 to 40 digits. My own corollary of the project theorem Rule30FactorWindow.transient_add_period_ge (T + P >= 16359): write x = a/(2^s m) in lowest terms with m odd. Its expansion has preperiod s and period ord_m(2) <= m - 1, so s + m >= 16360 and the denominator is at least 16,361. The case m = 1 (x dyadic) is already excluded by center_not_eventually_period_one.

formulations.name: Irrationality in any base b >= 2
formulations.statement: For each fixed integer b >= 2, x_b := sum_{t>=0} c(t) b^{-(t+1)} is irrational. This reads the 0/1 column as base-b digits; for example 0.1101110011... read in base 10. Problem 1 iff Irrational x_b.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The same argument as for the binary constant: a number is rational iff its base-b expansion is eventually periodic. For b >= 3 the digits never equal b-1, so the expansion is unique and the dyadic-type exception disappears. This generalization of Wolfram's base-2 and base-10 remarks is my own.

formulations.name: The 2-adic center number is irrational
formulations.statement: X := sum_{t>=0} c(t) 2^t, a 2-adic integer, is not rational. That is, X is not a/b with integers a, b and b odd.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A p-adic number is rational iff its digit sequence is eventually periodic. This is standard; see F. Q. Gouvea, p-adic Numbers, 2nd ed., Springer 1997. (<=) uses the 2-adic geometric series 1/(1 - 2^P). (=>) uses pigeonhole on the tails. The formulation is natural in Wolfram's integer form, where rows are integers and c(t) is bit t of row t. The equivalence is my own addition.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has PadicInt (Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/PadicIntegers.lean) and Padic. It has no digit expansion of Z_p and no rationality criterion.
formulations.known_results: The denominator bound for the binary constant adapts (my own reasoning).

formulations.name: The generating function is not rational, over GF(2) or Q
formulations.statement: C(X) := sum_t c(t) X^t is not rational in either of two senses. (a) In GF(2)[[X]] there is no nonzero Q in GF(2)[X] with Q*C in GF(2)[X]. (b) In Q[[X]] there is no nonzero Q in Q[X] with Q*C in Q[X].
formulations.proof_of_relation: (<=) If c has period P from T, then (1 - X^P) C(X) is a polynomial of degree < T+P. (=>) If Q C = R with Q != 0, then from some index c satisfies a fixed linear recurrence of order d = deg Q. The window (c(t),...,c(t+d-1)) takes finitely many values, since entries are 0/1, and it determines the next value, so pigeonhole gives eventual periodicity. Wolfram contrasts rule 30 with linear feedback shift registers and the linear rule 60, whose sequences have rational generating functions (1986 paper, sections 9-11; NKS note on p. 975). The equivalence itself is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has PowerSeries, Polynomial, RatFunc and LaurentSeries (coercion via RatFunc.coeAlgHom in Mathlib/RingTheory/LaurentSeries.lean), ZMod 2, and LinearRecurrence with LinearRecurrence.IsSolution, mkSol and charPoly (Mathlib/Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean). Missing: 'a power series with finitely many coefficient values is rational iff its coefficients are eventually periodic'.

formulations.name: Natural boundary of the center-column power series (Szego)
formulations.statement: f(z) := sum_t c(t) z^t on |z| < 1 has the unit circle as its natural boundary. Equivalently, f is not a rational function, and f has no analytic continuation across any arc of |z| = 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: 'Rational iff EP' is part (b) of the generating-function form. Szego (1922): a power series with finitely many distinct coefficients is either rational, with eventually periodic coefficients, or has |z| = 1 as natural boundary. Carlson (1921) proves the Polya-Carlson theorem: integer coefficients and radius 1 give the same dichotomy. This analytic form is not from Wolfram; it is my addition.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has no Szego theorem, no Polya-Carlson theorem and no natural-boundary notion; the grep for 'Fatou' found only the measure-theoretic lemma. The rational-function core is the generating-function form.
formulations.known_results: None specific to rule 30.

formulations.name: Unbounded linear complexity over GF(2)
formulations.statement: Let L(n) be the length of the shortest linear feedback shift register over GF(2) that generates c(0..n-1); the connection polynomial may be singular, which allows a transient. This is the Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity. Problem 1 iff L(n) -> infinity, equivalently L is unbounded.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c has period P from T, then c(t+T+P) = c(t+T) is a register of length T+P, so L <= T+P. Conversely, suppose L(n) <= L for all n. There are finitely many connection polynomials of degree <= L. By prefix-closure and pigeonhole, one recurrence holds on all of c. Its L-bit window then evolves deterministically, so c is eventually periodic. The algorithm is Massey (1969). Wolfram compares rule 30 with registers in the 1986 paper, sections 9-11, and in the NKS note on p. 975. The equivalence is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: LinearRecurrence (Mathlib/Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean) gives recurrences over a commutative semiring. Mathlib has no Berlekamp-Massey and no linear-complexity profile.
formulations.known_results: Project round 1, the 'algebraic' agent in research/results/round1.json: the Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity of c stays within 9.5 of n/2, the profile of a random sequence.

formulations.name: Factor complexity: blocks of the center column (Morse-Hedlund)
formulations.statement: Let p_c(n) be the number of distinct length-n words that occur in c. Problem 1 iff p_c(n) >= n+1 for all n >= 1, iff p_c is unbounded.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Morse-Hedlund (1938): a one-sided sequence is eventually periodic iff p(n) <= n for some n. Easy direction: period P from T gives p_c(n) <= T+P. Converse: if p_c is bounded, then p_c(n) = p_c(n+1) for some n. Every length-n factor then has a unique right extension, so the length-n window follows a function on a finite set, and c is eventually periodic. Wolfram (2019) asks the related question 'whether all the blocks even ever occur'.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has no factor complexity and no Morse-Hedlund theorem (grep). Mathlib/Dynamics/SymbolicDynamics/Basic.lean has Pattern, Pattern.occursInAt and LanguageOn for configurations G -> A, which could host the definition. The project already counts factors: Rule30FactorWindow.transient_add_period_ge.

formulations.name: Infinite shift orbit: c is not a preperiodic point of the shift
formulations.statement: Let sigma be the left shift on Bool sequences, sigma f = fun t => f (t+1). Then there are no m and n with 0 < n and sigma^[m+n] c = sigma^[m] c. Equivalently, the forward orbit {sigma^[n] c} is infinite, and so is the orbit closure of c in {0,1}^N.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Unfold the definitions: sigma^[m+n] c = sigma^[m] c iff c(t+n) = c(t) for all t >= m. An infinite orbit means not preperiodic, by pigeonhole. A finite orbit is closed, so the orbit closure is finite iff the orbit is. This is standard; the formulation is my own.

Mathlib has no ready lemma 'finite forward orbit implies preperiodic'; it has only Function.exists_iterate_apply_eq_of_mem_periodicPts.

formulations.name: Positions of black cells are not Presburger-definable
formulations.statement: S := {t in N : c(t) = 1} (OEIS A327984) is not definable in Presburger arithmetic (N; 0, 1, +), even with parameters. Equivalently, S is not semilinear: it is not a finite union of arithmetic progressions up to a finite set.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Ginsburg-Spanier (1966): Presburger-definable sets are exactly the semilinear sets, and in dimension 1 semilinear means ultimately periodic. For Bool-valued c, 'S is ultimately periodic', i.e. exists k, exists p > 0, for all x >= k, x in S iff x+p in S, is exactly EP(c). This is not from Wolfram. I include it because Mathlib already proves the theorem it needs.
formulations.lean: Mathlib: FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic : A.Definable₁ presburger s <-> exists k, exists p > 0, for all x >= k, (x in s <-> x + p in s) (Mathlib/ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/Definability.lean). Also FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable_iff_isSemilinearSet, and Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic in .../Presburger/Semilinear/Defs.lean. Then Problem1 <-> for all A, not A.Definable₁ presburger {t | center t = true} is a short corollary that needs only Bool/Set bookkeeping. This is the cheapest Mathlib-backed equivalence.

formulations.name: Integer form: NKS bitwise recurrence for the rows
formulations.statement: Let a(0) = 1 and a(t+1) = a(t) XOR (2 a(t) OR 4 a(t)). The values are OEIS A110240: 1, 7, 25, 111, 401, 1783, ...; one step is OEIS A269160, n -> n XOR (2n OR 4n). Then cell(t,p) = bit (t-p) of a(t) for |p| <= t, so c(t) = floor(a(t)/2^t) mod 2. Problem 1 iff t -> testBit(a(t), t) is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: NKS p. 871 note: 'The first n elements can be found efficiently using Module[{a = 1}, Table[First[IntegerDigits[a, a = BitXor[a, BitOr[2a, 4a]]; 2, i]], {i, n}]]'. The 2019 post uses BitGet[a, ...; i - 1] with the same update. Bit k of a(t+1) is bit k of a(t) XOR (bit k-1 OR bit k-2), which is rule 30 with bit index k at position t-k. Proof by induction on t. I checked cell(t,p) = bit(t-p) for t < 200 and c(t) for t < 1500.
formulations.lean: Core Lean 4.30 suffices: Nat.testBit_xor, Nat.testBit_or, Nat.testBit_shiftLeft, Nat.testBit_mul_two_pow and Nat.testBit_two_pow_mul (Init/Data/Nat/Bitwise/Lemmas.lean in the v4.30.0 toolchain). It fits the project's core-only snapshot.

formulations.name: Inverse (sideways realization) form
formulations.statement: For a column s : N -> Bool, let L(s) be the unique initial row that is white at all positions >= 1 and whose column-0 evolution is s. Problem 1 iff, for every eventually periodic s, L(s) is not the single black cell: either s(0) = 0 or L(s) has a black cell at some position -m with m >= 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Rule 30 is linear in its left cell, so a column together with the right half determines everything to the left, and every column sequence arises from some initial condition (Wolfram 1986, sections 3-4 and 7; NKS p. 1087 note: 'all 2^t possible single columns of t cells can be generated from some initial condition'). The single seed realizes c, so by uniqueness c is eventually periodic iff some eventually periodic s has L(s) = seed.
formulations.lean: Project, core Lean: Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique (R : Int -> Bool) (c : Nat -> Bool) gives a unique configuration with right half R whose column 0 is c. Its left columns are lc R c m t. Rule30Realization.seed_perturbation is also there. The period-2 reduction Q01 (Rule30PeriodTwo, Rule30ZeroBoundary) is this statement for s of period 2. Not in Mathlib.
formulations.known_results: Q01, the period-2 case, holds for every start of width <= 52 in the catalog and <= 56 in research/. Seed-perturbation barrier: for each n, some configuration agrees with the seed at all positions >= -n, and its column 0 equals c up to time n and is white afterwards.

formulations.name: Mirror and complement rules 86, 135, 149
formulations.statement: Problem 1 is equivalent to each of: (a) the center column of rule 86 from a single black cell is not eventually periodic (it equals c); (b) the center column of rule 135 from a single white cell on a black background is not eventually periodic (it equals NOT c); (c) the same for rule 149 from a single white cell on black (it equals NOT c).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Rule 86 is the mirror image of rule 30, and the single seed is mirror-symmetric. Rule 135 is the black/white complement, so complementing the seed's whole spacetime pattern gives rule 135 from the complemented seed. Rule 149 is the mirror complement. Complementing preserves eventual periodicity. MathWorld: 'Rule 30 is the mirror image, complement, and mirror complement of rules 86, 135, and 149'. Wolfram 1986: rule 30 is 'equivalent to rule 86 under reflection'. OEIS A051023: it is also the middle column of rule 86. I checked all three for t < 1500. Rule 135 from the usual single black cell on white is a different problem, the rule-30 white seed.
formulations.lean: Needs a generic elementary-CA evolution plus reflection and complement conjugacy lemmas, about 50-100 lines of core Lean. Project: Rule30WhiteSeed.problem1_black_or_white and problem1_30_or_135. Mathlib has no cellular automata.
formulations.known_results: Proved in the project: Problem 1 or its white-seed analogue holds.

formulations.name: Simple transforms: differences, running parity, complement, run lengths
formulations.statement: Problem 1 iff each of the following is not eventually periodic: (a) the first differences dc(t) = c(t) XOR c(t+1) (OEIS A327974); (b) the running parity s(t) = c(0) XOR ... XOR c(t); (c) the complement NOT c (OEIS A226474); (d) the run-length sequence of c (OEIS A327983).
formulations.proof_of_relation: (a) If c is eventually periodic, so is dc. If dc has period P from T, then c(t+P) = c(t) XOR sigma, where sigma is the parity of one period of dc, so c has period 2P. (b) s is the prefix XOR of c and its differences are c shifted, so the same argument applies. (c) is immediate. (d) needs c not eventually constant, which is proved (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant); then c is eventually periodic iff its run lengths are. My own; the sequences come from OEIS cross-references.
formulations.lean: Core Lean; no Mathlib needed. Run lengths need a list-of-runs definition and are the only fiddly part.
formulations.known_results: Period 1 is excluded (proved).

formulations.name: Decimations
formulations.statement: For each fixed k >= 1: Problem 1 iff some residue r < k has t -> c(k t + r) not eventually periodic. In particular, Problem 1 iff c at even times or c at odd times is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c has period P, every decimation has period P. Conversely, if all k decimations are eventually periodic with periods P_r from T_r, then c has period k lcm(P_r) from k max T_r + k. My own.

formulations.name: Finite-state unpredictability
formulations.statement: No finite-state predictor is eventually always right on c. That is, there is no finite set Sigma, start state s0, transition delta : Sigma x {0,1} -> Sigma and guess g : Sigma -> {0,1} such that, with s_{t+1} = delta(s_t, c(t)), g(s_t) = c(t) for all large t.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c has period P from T, a predictor with T+P states tracks the phase. Conversely, once g(s_t) = c(t) for t >= T0, the update s_{t+1} = delta(s_t, g(s_t)) is an autonomous map on a finite set, so s_t is eventually periodic and so is c(t) = g(s_t). This matches Wolfram's description (2019) of Problem 3 as asking whether there are 'predictable regularities', and finite-state predictability (Feder-Merhav-Gutman 1992). The equivalence is my own.
formulations.lean: Core Lean, or Mathlib's DFA (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean) extended with an output map; pigeonhole via Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite.
formulations.known_results: Wolfram 2019: statistical tests, compression, cellular-automaton-based tests and neural networks found no predictive regularity.
sources: https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/
M. Feder, N. Merhav, M. Gutman, Universal prediction of individual sequences, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 38 (1992) 1258-1270

formulations.name: Pi-2 arithmetic / Diophantine form
formulations.statement: Problem 1 is the Pi-2 sentence: for all P >= 1 and all T there is t >= T with c(t+P) != c(t). Here c(t) = i is Diophantine: there are integer polynomials D_i with c(t) = i iff D_i(t, x) = 0 for some x in N^k. So Problem 1 iff, for all P, T, there exist t, x, y with P = 0, or t >= T and (D_1(t+P, x) = 0 and D_0(t, y) = 0, or D_0(t+P, x) = 0 and D_1(t, y) = 0).
formulations.proof_of_relation: NKS p. 1160 note ('Universal Diophantine equation', for p. 786): one rule-30 step on integer-coded rows is BitXor[a, 2 BitOr[a, 2a]]. BitAnd, BitOr and BitXor become integer equations via Lucas: Mod[Binomial[x, y], 2] == 1 iff the bits of y are a subset of those of x. Coding the t-step iteration needs Matiyasevich's exponential-Diophantine machinery, or the MRDP theorem. Wolfram (2019) notes a negative answer could be non-constructive ('show that eventually the sequence has to be periodic, but not know even any bound') and raises independence from Peano arithmetic or ZFC. The negation is Sigma-2, so it is not refutable by finite computation alone.
formulations.lean: Mathlib: Dioph, DiophFn, Dioph.pow_dioph (Matiyasevich: exponentiation is Diophantine), Dioph.mod_dioph, Dioph.div_dioph and Dioph.ex_dioph (Mathlib/NumberTheory/Dioph.lean). formulations.name: Not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic (Cobham)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 iff c is not simultaneously 2-automatic and 3-automatic. More generally, iff c is not both k- and l-automatic for some multiplicatively independent k and l.
formulations.proof_of_relation: An eventually periodic sequence is k-automatic for every k >= 2: a finite automaton reads n in base k, computes n mod P and checks n < T. Conversely, Cobham's theorem (1969): a sequence that is k- and l-automatic for multiplicatively independent k, l is eventually periodic. Wolfram (2019) asks whether the column can come from a substitution system. His rule 161 and rule 69540422 (Thue-Morse) examples show automatic columns that are not periodic. The equivalence is my addition.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has DFA, DFA.accepts and Language (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean) and MyhillNerode. It has no automatic sequences and no Cobham or Christol theorem (grep).
formulations.known_results: Project: the 2-kernel of c shows no finiteness; all 2^{K+1}-1 subsequences c(2^k n + r) with k <= 13 are pairwise distinct on n < 64. Nersissian (2026): any LSD-first 2-DFAO generating c needs at least 8191 states.

formulations.name: Problem 3 implies Problem 1
formulations.statement: Problem 3, in either form, implies Problem 1. Verbal form: no machine computes c(n) with effort o(n). Wolfram's formal form: NotExists[m, ForAll[n, machine[m][n][[1]] == Last[c[n]]] && MaxLimit[machine[m][n][[2]]/n, n -> Infinity] < Infinity], i.e. no O(n)-effort machine.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Wolfram 2019, 'The Formal Character of Solutions': 'If the answer to Problem 3 is affirmative (as I strongly suspect), then it implies that the answer to Problem 1 must also be affirmative. The contrapositive is also true.' Proof: if c(t+P) = c(t) for t >= T, then c(n) = c(T + (n-T) mod P) plus a finite table, which takes O(log n) steps on binary input (an automaton for n mod P). Caveat, my own reading: the formal form forbids even O(n) algorithms, so it is stronger than the verbal Omega(n) form; both imply Problem 1. Further variants Wolfram lists also imply Problem 1, since eventually periodic sequences are cheap: no O(n^g) algorithm for g < 2; no NC algorithm (NKS p. 1149 note); his remark that the question is 'more like a P vs. LOGTIME question'.
formulations.lean: Mathlib: Turing.TM2ComputableInTime and Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime (Mathlib/Computability/TuringMachine/Computable.lean), with time as a function of input length, so O(n) corresponds to O(2^len) for binary n; Computability.finEncodingNatBool and Computability.encodeNat (Mathlib/Computability/Encoding.lean). Missing: a concrete TM2 machine for an eventually periodic sequence. That is laborious, not deep. A model-free alternative is 'c is not automatic', which already implies Problem 1.
formulations.known_results: Wolfram 2019: deep-learning attempts found no shortcut. Wolfram 1986, section 7: DNF size of the t-step map grows like 4^{0.65t}.

formulations.name: Not automatic, not morphic, or transcendental generating function (Christol)
formulations.statement: Each of these implies Problem 1: (a) c is not 2-automatic, i.e. no finite automaton with output computes c(n) from the base-2 digits of n; (b) c is not morphic, i.e. not a coding of a fixed point of a substitution; (c) C(X) = sum c(t) X^t is transcendental over GF(2)(X).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Eventually periodic sequences are automatic and morphic, and automatic sequences are morphic, so (b) implies (a), which implies Problem 1. Christol (1979; Christol, Kamae, Mendes France and Rauzy 1980): c is 2-automatic iff C(X) is algebraic over GF(2)(X), so (c) iff (a). Also (c) gives 'C not rational' and hence Problem 1 directly. Wolfram 2019: 'Will it turn out that the center column of rule 30 can be generated by a substitution system? Again, I'd be amazed'. Rule 69540422, whose center column is Thue-Morse, shows automatic non-periodic columns exist.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has DFA, PowerSeries and Transcendental (Mathlib/RingTheory/Algebraic/Defs.lean). Missing: automatic and morphic sequences, Christol's theorem, and the automaton for an eventually periodic sequence. (c) implies Problem 1 is easy once the generating-function form exists.

formulations.name: Every block occurs, or normality
formulations.statement: (a) Every finite 0/1 word occurs in c, i.e. c is disjunctive: p_c(n) = 2^n for all n. (b) c is normal: every length-k word has limiting frequency 2^{-k}, equivalently the rule 30 constant is normal in base 2. (b) implies (a), which implies Problem 1; (b) also implies Problem 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c has period P from T, then p_c(n) <= T+P < 2^n for large n, so (a) implies Problem 1. A word with positive frequency occurs, so (b) implies (a). Wolfram 1985 (Twenty Problems, Problem 15): the center site 'contains all possible subsequences with equal frequencies'. Wolfram 2019: 'whether ... the center column of rule 30 will contain any given sequence of length k', and normality is 'a reasonable guess'. NKS note on digit-sequence properties covers normal numbers.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has no normal numbers and no disjunctive sequences (grep). The definitions are short and the implications elementary.
formulations.known_results: Every block of length <= 22 occurs, with first-complete steps as listed in the factor-complexity entry. The 10^9-bit black/white ratio is about 1.0001. Nothing is proved.

formulations.name: Equidistribution of the right-half rows along progressions
formulations.statement: Let y_t := sum_{p>=0} cell(t,p) 2^{-(p+1)}, the right half of row t from the center, read as a binary fraction. Then c(t) = [y_t >= 1/2] exactly, because the right half of a row is finite. Strengthening: for every P >= 1 and r < P, the sequence (y_{Pk+r})_k is equidistributed in [0,1], or merely its first binary digit is not eventually constant. This implies Problem 1, and Problem 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Wolfram 2019 (Problem 2 section) plots y_t ('the sequence of numbers formed by looking at the right-hand side of the rule 30 pattern'). He finds it consistent with equidistribution and compares it with Weyl's theorem and FractionalPart[(3/2)^n]. If c has period P, then [y_{Pk+r} >= 1/2] is constant for large k, which contradicts equidistribution along that progression. Problem 1 itself is equivalent to: for every P >= 1, some r < P has [y_{Pk+r} >= 1/2] not eventually constant. My own reasoning.
formulations.lean: Real.ofDigits can express y_t. Mathlib has no equidistribution API (grep for equidistrib found nothing).

formulations.name: Excluding fixed periods
formulations.statement: For fixed P >= 1, NoPer(P) says there is no T with c(t+P) = c(t) for all t >= T. Problem 1 iff NoPer(P) for all P >= 1. Each NoPer(P), and each finite conjunction of them, is weaker. It suffices to exclude P = k! for all k, or any family cofinal under divisibility, since a period P gives every multiple mP.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Specialization, plus multiples of periods. Wolfram 2019: 'we know the sequence doesn't become periodic in the first billion steps'. That is a statement about prefixes, not a proof of any NoPer(P).

That needs cell(t,i+1) only when cell(t,i) = 0. NKS p. 1087: 'whenever there is a black cell in the left column it is irrelevant what appears in the right column'. That gives (b). perspectives: Randomness criteria. Wolfram (2019): 'Each of the Prize Problems in effect uses a different criterion for randomness.' The known implications: Problem 3 implies Problem 1; normality implies every block occurs, which implies Problem 1; non-automatic implies Problem 1; normality implies Problem 2; Problems 1 and 2 are independent. Wolfram also lists non-compressibility and failing statistical tests.

The digits-of-pi analogy (2019). The center column is the binary expansion of 0.8623897839... (OEIS A365254). Problem 1 is its irrationality, Problem 2 its simple normality, the block version its normality, and Problem 3 corresponds to digit extraction (BBP). Wolfram: for 'naturally constructed' numbers no digit regularity is known and nothing about digit frequencies is proved.

Left-permutivity and sideways evolution. Rule 30 = p XOR (q OR r) = (p+q+r+qr) mod 2 is linear in the left cell (NKS p. 1087 notes; Wolfram 1986, sections 3-4). So the pattern runs sideways: two adjacent columns, or one column plus the neighbor where it is white, determine everything to the left, and every single column occurs for some initial condition. This drives Jen's theorem and the project's reductions. Rules 90, 150 and 210 share it but have periodic centers, so a proof must use the nonlinear qr term; Wolfram notes 'all the complexity of rule 30 comes from ... that one little nonlinear q r term'.

Diagonal structure (NKS p. 871 note; Wolfram 1986, Table 6.1; Rowland 2006). Right diagonals at depth n have period at most 2^n, growing roughly exponentially. Left diagonals double their period only at depths 3, 8, 29, 400, 87,867 and 2,107,985,255 or more, each time a diagonal becomes white and its left neighbor has an odd number of black cells per period. The center column crosses diagonals of ever larger period. The project proved the right-edge orbit closure is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer.

Integer and 2-adic dynamics. The NKS p. 871 integer form makes row t equal f^t(1), where f(n) = n XOR (2n OR 4n) (OEIS A269160). f is a 1-Lipschitz map of the 2-adic integers, its orbit mod 2^k is purely periodic with 2-power period, and c(t) is bit t of f^t(1), so Problem 1 is about a diagonal of an odometer-like system. This reading is my own. Wolfram (2019) contrasts rule 30, which has 'no relation to any standard operations', with powers of 3 in base 6: they form a CA and can be predicted by repeated squaring.

The order/disorder boundary (2019; NKS p. 871 note; about 0.25 in 1986). The periodic left region spreads at about 0.252 cells per step with random-walk fluctuations. Wolfram's heuristic: the center would become periodic only after a huge fluctuation brought order across it. Long transients exist elsewhere (4-color code 150898; Skewes's number), so finite data cannot settle the question.

Computational irreducibility. Problem 3 is the irreducibility of rule 30; Wolfram calls it 'more like a P vs. LOGTIME question'. He suspects no NC algorithm (NKS p. 1149 note), PSPACE-complete cycle questions, and possibly NP-complete inversion. Any lower bound beyond what eventually periodic sequences need (O(log n) time, O(1) memory) implies Problem 1.

Proof theory. Problem 1 is Pi-2 and its negation Sigma-2, so even a 'periodic' answer need not be checkable by finite computation. Wolfram (2019) raises independence from Peano arithmetic or ZFC, and welcomes formal proofs as part of a 'computational contract' for the prize.

Finite-size models. On n-cell rings, periods are about 2^{0.63n}, and empirically the center period equals the global period. Mathematica used such registers (Method 'Rule30CA'). How this relates to the infinite case is unknown (Wolfram 2019).

Rule equivalences. Mirror and complement conjugates (rules 86, 135, 149) give identical or complemented columns. Directional sampling equals a vertical column of the rule composed with a shift (NKS p. 1087). Rule 30 is the square of the 3-color, radius-1/2 rules 11736, 11739 and 11742 (NKS p. 956), so c is the even-time trace of those rules.

The program Wolfram proposes (2019, 'Generalizations and Relations'): survey many rules for long periods and transients; classify center-column sequences and find minimal CAs for given columns (NKS 12.10 note); add long-range 'exceptions' to rule 30; vary initial conditions (finite seeds, defects, substitution-generated, FSM ensembles); study other angles and rows; seek universality or NP-completeness results.

Ensembles and dynamical systems. Rule 30 is a surjective continuous map of the Cantor set. From the uniform ensemble, every block occurs in every column with equal frequency. The Lyapunov exponents are 0.25 on the left and 1 on the right. Wolfram (2019) suggests pushing results for finite-state-machine ensembles toward the single seed.

Inverse and cryptanalytic view (Wolfram 1986, sections 7-8; NKS p. 1087; Meier-Staffelbach 1991). Information-theoretically, about 1.2 temporal sequences fix the seed, but the Boolean expressions explode. Problem 1 asks which eventually periodic columns have the single seed as their realizer.
surveys.notes:
I found 33 formulations: 18 equivalent to Problem 1, 8 stronger, 2 weaker and 5 related. 'difficulty' rates the effort to machine-check the stated relation, not the problem itself. 'open' marks related entries where no relation can be proved and the statement is itself open.

**Sources read.** All under /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/wolfram-writings/: downloads in dl_*/ (untrusted, never executed), text in txt/.
- The full 2019 announcement.
- rule30prize.org and its bibliography.
- MathWorld's Rule 30 page.
- NKS: the complete notes PDF plus note pages for pp. 869-871, 975, 1087, 1149 and 1160.
- Wolfram's papers: Random Sequence Generation (1986), Twenty Problems (1985) and Cryptography with Cellular Automata (1985).
- Wolfram's posts: 2017 'Oh My Gosh', 2024 Code 10, and the 2024-2026 posts listed below.
- OEIS A051023, A365254, A092539, A110240, A269160, A327974.
- The Wolfram Language random-number tutorial.

**Later Wolfram writings.** I checked Can AI Solve Science, Nestedly Recursive Functions, What Is Ruliology, P vs NP, What Ultimately Is There, Theory of Bugs and the September 2026 post on pure math and AI. They mention rule 30 only in passing; none adds a formulation of Problem 1 after 2019. MathWorld cites Rowland's August 2026 video 'The Hidden Structure of Rule 30', which I did not review.

**Caveats** (my own reading):
1. Wolfram's printed formal Problem 1 lacks p >= 1 and uses list-valued c[t], so taken literally it is false (p = 0 satisfies it). Our Lean Problem1 has 0 < P.
2. His formal Problem 3, MaxLimit[effort/n] < Infinity, forbids even O(n) algorithms. That is stronger than the verbal 'less than O(n)'. Both imply Problem 1.
3. Wolfram 1986 says two periodic columns force periodicity of 'all sequences to their right'. For rule 30, reconstruction runs leftward (his Eq. 3.3), so this looks like a slip.
4. The stephenwolfram.com/publications/academic/*.pdf links on the prize bibliography now serve an unrelated PDF (Geometry of Binomial Coefficients). The working copies are at content.wolfram.com/sw-publications/2020/07/.
5. The 1986 table and the NKS p. 1087 numbers are finite-size data, not single-seed data.

**Checks I ran.** scripts/check_forms.py, run with python3 -I, confirms for t < 1500:
- the NKS/OEIS integer form gives cell(t,p) = bit (t-p) of a(t), and therefore c(t);
- rule 86 from a single black cell gives c;
- rules 135 and 149 from a single white cell on black give NOT c;
- the constant equals 0.8623897839473840486408002460867511281085.

**Lean status.**
- Mathlib names were found by grep in /Users/swish/src/mathlib4/Mathlib; core names in the v4.30.0 toolchain's Init/Data/Nat/Bitwise/Lemmas.lean.
- Mathlib has no eventually-periodic predicate, factor complexity, automatic sequences, normal numbers, Cobham, Christol, Szego, equidistribution, cellular automata or DPRM.
- The project's Lean snapshot is core-only, so the Mathlib-based forms (real, 2-adic, power series, linear complexity, shift orbit, Presburger, Diophantine, automaticity, transcendence) need a separate Mathlib project.

**Suggested first batch.**
- Core Lean: the Wolfram-statement variants, the integer recurrence, the 86/135/149 conjugates, the simple transforms, decimations, finite-state predictability and the realization form.
- Mathlib: the Presburger corollary via FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic, and the shift-orbit form.
- Then the user's irrationality example. It needs one general lemma, 'Real.ofDigits d is rational iff d is eventually periodic', which also gives the base-b form and makes the transcendence implication immediate.
- Then Morse-Hedlund.

formulations.name: Binary real number 0.c(0)c(1)c(2)... is irrational (the user's example)
formulations.statement: x₂ := Σ_{t≥0} c(t)·2^{-(t+1)} = 0.c(0)c(1)c(2)…₂ ≈ 0.8623897839473840486408002460867511281085… is irrational. Integer-only form, with no reals: there are no p, q ∈ ℕ with q > 0 such that c(t) = ⌊2^{t+1}p/q⌋ mod 2 for all t. In words, c is not the binary expansion of a rational.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Classical lemma (Hardy–Wright Ch. IX). For any base b ≥ 2 and digits d: ℕ → {0..b−1}, Σ d(t) b^{-t-1} ∈ ℚ ⇔ d is eventually periodic.
(⇐) Geometric series. If d(t+P) = d(t) for t ≥ T, then x = A/b^T + B/(b^T(b^P−1)), where A and B are the integer values of the blocks d[0,T) and d[T,T+P).
(⇒) Suppose x = p/q. The tails x_t = Σ_{s≥0} d(t+s) b^{-s-1} = b^t·x − (an integer) lie in (1/q)ℤ ∩ [0,1], which has q+1 points. If some x_{t+1} = 1, every later digit is b−1. Otherwise x_{t+1} = frac(b·x_t) and d(t) = ⌊b·x_t⌋. That is a deterministic map on a finite set, so d is eventually periodic.
Integer form: put r_t = 2^t·p mod q. Then ⌊2^{t+1}p/q⌋ mod 2 = ⌊2r_t/q⌋ and r_{t+1} = 2r_t mod q. Conversely, an eventually periodic c is the greedy expansion of its value, because c is not eventually 1 (Lean: center_not_eventually_constant).
Exact dictionary: if x₂ = p/q in lowest terms with q = 2^a·q′, q′ odd, then the minimal transient is a and the minimal period is ord_{q′}(2). Any valid pair (T,P) gives q | 2^T(2^P−1).
Only geometric series and pigeonhole are needed.
formulations.known_results:
Kernel-checked consequences, through the dictionary (my derivation):
- Rule30FactorWindow.transient_add_period_ge gives T+P ≥ 16359. The minimal T+P is at most q−1, so x₂ ≠ p/q for every q ≤ 16359.
- Rule30Window.no_small_eventual_period gives x₂ ∉ (2^8192·(2^P−1))^{-1}ℤ for 1 ≤ P ≤ 4096.
Data, not kernel-checked:
- the column is not periodic in the first 10^9 steps (Wolfram 2019);
- per the project brief, every P ≤ 2.5·10^8 has a disagreement c(t) ≠ c(t+P) with t ∈ [5·10^8, 10^9).
The 40 digits above were computed here (nt_data.py).
sources: G. H. Hardy, E. M. Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Ch. IX (decimal and other expansions of rationals)
S. Wolfram, Announcing the Rule 30 Prizes (2019), https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/
OEIS A051023 (center column), https://oeis.org/A051023; OEIS A092539 (its prefixes as binary integers), https://oeis.org/A092539
Mathlib Mathlib/Analysis/Real/OfDigits.lean (V. Nesterov, 2025)

formulations.name: Same digits read in any integer base b ≥ 2
formulations.statement: Fix an integer b ≥ 2. Then x_b := Σ_{t≥0} c(t)·b^{-(t+1)} = 0.c(0)c(1)…_b is irrational. Examples: x₃ ≈ 0.4623450726095034173712…, x₁₀ = 0.1101110011000101100100111010111…. Both 'for some b' and 'for all b' are equivalent to Problem 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Same lemma as for b = 2, with digits {0,1} ⊂ {0,…,b−1}. For b ≥ 3 the map {0,1}^ℕ → ℝ, d ↦ Σ d(t)·b^{-t-1}, is injective (Cantor-set coding), so the double-expansion issue cannot arise. For b = 2 it is handled by c not being eventually constant. Any injective digit encoding {0,1} → {0,…,b−1} works the same way.
Cautions (my remarks): only positional encodings in an integer base give an equivalence.
- Σ c(t)/t! is irrational, and Σ c(t)·2^{-t!} is a Liouville number, for every sequence with infinitely many 1s. Both are true unconditionally and carry no information about Problem 1.
- In base φ (golden ratio) the blocks 100 and 011 have the same value. So 'Σ c(t)φ^{-t-1} ∉ ℚ(φ)' is strictly stronger than Problem 1 for general sequences.
formulations.lean:
Already machine-checked in the repo: Rule30Equivalents.BinaryIrrational.problem1_iff_irrational_base {B} (hB : 2 ≤ B) : Problem1 ↔ Irrational (∑' t, (if c t then 1 else 0)/B^(t+1)), and problem1_iff_irrational_decimal.

- Cardinal.cantorFunction (1/b) center = b·x_b, with Cardinal.cantorFunction_injective (needs 0 < 1/b < 1/2, so b ≥ 3).

formulations.known_results: The window consequences carry over. In base b, for x = p/q in lowest terms: the transient is governed by the primes dividing b, and the period is ord_{q₂}(b), where q₂ is the part of q prime to b. The values above were computed here.

formulations.name: The 2-adic integer Σ c(t)·2^t is not rational (FCSR, 2-adic complexity)
formulations.statement:
α := Σ_{t≥0} c(t)·2^t ∈ ℤ₂ is not in ℚ.
Integer-only form: there are no a, b ∈ ℤ with b ≠ 0 and 2^n | b·S_n − a for all n, where S_n = Σ_{t<n} c(t)·2^t.
Equivalently, c is not the output of any feedback-with-carry shift register (FCSR): its 2-adic complexity profile is unbounded.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
(⇐) Suppose c(t+P) = c(t) for t ≥ T. Put A = S_T, B = Σ_{s<P} c(T+s)·2^s, b = 2^P−1 and a = b·A − 2^T·B. Then b·S_{T+kP} − a = 2^{T+kP}·B, which gives every congruence. Equivalently, α = A + 2^T·B/(1−2^P).
(⇒) Divide out 2^{v₂(b)} so that b is odd. The numbers a_t := (a − b·S_t)/2^t are integers, with a_{t+1} = (a_t − b·c(t))/2 and c(t) ≡ a_t (mod 2). Since |a_{t+1}| ≤ (|a_t|+|b|)/2, eventually |a_t| ≤ |b|. On that finite set the dynamics are deterministic, so a_t, and with it c(t) = a_t mod 2, is eventually periodic.
This is my sketch of the classical fact; textbook versions are in Koblitz and in Goresky–Klapper. The same argument works for Σ c(t)·p^t in ℤ_p for any prime p.
formulations.lean:

- `twoadic_int_iff : Problem1 ↔ ¬ ∃ a b : ℤ, b ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ n, (2:ℤ)^n ∣ b * S n - a`.
The integer form needs only Int, so it is a good core-Lean target: define S by recursion.
formulations.known_results:
Kernel-checked consequence (my derivation). If α = a/b with b odd, then the minimal T ≤ log₂|a| + 3 and P ≤ ord_b(2) ≤ b−1. With transient_add_period_ge this gives α ≠ a/b whenever log₂|a| + b < 16357.
Data (this survey, twoadic.py): Lagrange–Gauss reduction of the lattice {(a,b) : a ≡ b·α mod 2^n} gives log₂(shortest vector) − n/2 ∈ [−4.19, +0.09], for every n ≤ 8192 sampled in steps of 8. That is maximal 2-adic complexity, as for a random sequence.
The project's literature survey lists an unverified third-party 2-adic reformulation (GitHub wryan2986/rule30-lab).

formulations.name: Generating function is not rational: constant-coefficient recurrence, LFSR, linear complexity (over ℚ, ℂ or 𝔽₂)
formulations.proof_of_relation:
(⇐) If c is eventually periodic, (1−z^P)·f is a polynomial.
(⇒) Q·f = P gives a constant-coefficient recurrence for large n. Let j be the largest index with a_j ≠ 0. The window (c(n),…,c(n+j−1)) then determines c(n+j), a deterministic map on {0,1}^j, so c is eventually periodic.
Over 𝔽₂: if c is eventually periodic then L(n) ≤ T+P. If L(n) ≤ d for all n, one of the finitely many LFSRs of length ≤ d generates infinitely many prefixes, hence all of c; no Massey uniqueness is needed. An LFSR output is eventually periodic.
In 𝔽₂((1/X)) a continued fraction is finite iff the element lies in 𝔽₂(X), and the jumps of L(n) are the degrees of the partial quotients (Niederreiter).
(Elementary; my sketches.)
formulations.known_results:
- Project (research/gf2-algebra, Berlekamp–Massey): L(n) = n/2 + O(10) for n ≤ 10^6. Since L ≤ T+P, this gives only T+P ≥ 499,998.
- This survey: max |L(n) − n/2| = 4.5 for n ≤ 1200.
- For a random sequence the partial-quotient degrees are geometric, so |L(n) − n/2| of order log₂ n is expected, and the data fit that.
- The stronger 'almost perfect profile' (bounded partial-quotient degrees) would be atypical.
- In function fields, bounded partial quotients are compatible with algebraicity (the Baum–Sweet cubic). So profile data alone cannot rule out automaticity.
sources: J. L. Massey, Shift-register synthesis and BCH decoding, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 15 (1969) 122–127
H. Niederreiter, Sequences with almost perfect linear complexity profile, EUROCRYPT '87, LNCS 304 (1988) 37–51
Survey: A survey on complexity measures of pseudo-random sequences, arXiv:2405.08479, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08479
L. E. Baum, M. M. Sweet, Continued fractions of algebraic power series in characteristic 2, Ann. of Math. 103 (1976) 593–610
Repo: equivalents/Rule30Equivalents/PowerSeriesF2.lean; research/results/round1.json (algebraic agent)

formulations.name: Not P-recursive: Σ c(t)·z^t is not D-finite
formulations.statement: There are no d, N and polynomials p_0,…,p_d ∈ ℤ[n], not all zero, with Σ_{i=0}^{d} p_i(n)·c(n+i) = 0 for all n ≥ N. Equivalently, f(z) = Σ c(t)·z^t satisfies no linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients over ℚ.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Theorem of van der Poorten–Shparlinski (1996): a ℚ-valued sequence that takes finitely many values and satisfies a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients has a rational generating function. Bell–Chen (2016) extend this to several variables. Formulation 4 then gives eventual periodicity.
Elementary route (my sketch):
- Let D = max deg p_i and let a_i be the coefficient of n^D in p_i (not all 0).
- Dividing by n^D gives Σ a_i·c(n+i) = O(1/n). The left side ranges over a finite set, so it vanishes for large n.
- That is a constant-coefficient recurrence, and Formulation 4 applies.
Conversely, eventually periodic ⇒ rational ⇒ D-finite.
Another route is Pólya–Carlson: a D-finite series has finitely many singularities, so it cannot have a natural boundary.
Consequence (my remark): if Problem 1 holds, every method that needs a linear ODE has nothing to act on. That includes Siegel–Shidlovskii E-/G-functions and Apéry- or Beukers-style Padé constructions.
formulations.lean:
Not in the repo yet. Mathlib has no D-finite, holonomic or P-recursive notion (grep found none), but Polynomial.eval and PowerSeries are available.
Typechecked here: `precursive_iff : Problem1 ↔ ¬ ∃ d N (p : Fin (d+1) → Polynomial ℤ), (∃ i, p i ≠ 0) ∧ ∀ n ≥ N, ∑ i, (p i).eval (n:ℤ) * cz (n+i) = 0`.
The elementary proof needs only integer inequalities, |Σ a_i·c(n+i)|·n^D ≤ C·n^{D−1}, so it is feasible with little machinery.
formulations.known_results: None beyond Formulation 4.
sources: A. J. van der Poorten, I. E. Shparlinski, On linear recurrence sequences with polynomial coefficients, Glasgow Math. J. 38 (1996) 147–155, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/on-linear-recurrence-sequences-with-polynomial-coefficients/749C56946812A17EBFD4C3FFACDB16F4

R. P. Stanley, Differentiably finite power series, European J. Combin. 1 (1980) 175–188

formulations.name: Fatou: Σ c(t)·z^t is transcendental over ℚ(z)
formulations.statement: f(z) = Σ c(t)·z^t is not algebraic over ℚ(z) (equivalently, over ℂ(z)).
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Fatou (1906): a power series with integer coefficients that converges in |z| < 1 is either rational or transcendental. Since f converges there, f algebraic ⇔ f rational ⇔ ¬Problem 1 (Formulation 4).
For 0/1 coefficients there is a shorter route (my sketch). In characteristic 0, algebraic ⇒ D-finite: d/dz extends to the finite extension ℚ(z)(f), so f, f′, f″, … are linearly dependent over ℚ(z) (Stanley 1980). Formulation 5 then applies.
The characteristic matters. Over 𝔽_p(z), algebraic ⇔ p-automatic (Christol), so transcendence of f over 𝔽₂(z) is strictly stronger than Problem 1 (Formulation 15).
formulations.lean:
Not in the repo yet.
Mathlib has Transcendental and IsAlgebraic (RingTheory/Algebraic/Defs.lean), RatFunc, LaurentSeries and Derivation. It lacks Fatou's theorem and 'algebraic ⇒ D-finite'.
Typechecked here: `fatou_iff : Problem1 ↔ Transcendental (RatFunc ℚ) ((f ℚ : PowerSeries ℚ) : LaurentSeries ℚ)`. It needs `open scoped RatFunc` for the algebra RatFunc ℚ → LaurentSeries ℚ.
The practical proof route is Formulation 5 plus 'algebraic ⇒ D-finite'.

formulations.name: Szegő / Pólya–Carlson: the unit circle is a natural boundary of Σ c(t)·z^t
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Szegő (1922): a power series with finitely many distinct coefficients that continues analytically across some arc of the unit circle equals P(z)/(1−z^m), so its coefficients are eventually periodic.
Pólya–Carlson (conjectured by Pólya 1916, proved by Carlson 1921): a power series with integer coefficients and radius 1 is either rational or has the unit circle as natural boundary.
Conversely, an eventually periodic c gives f = P(z)/(1−z^P), meromorphic on ℂ with poles only at P-th roots of unity.
The radius is 1 because c is bounded and not eventually 0.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has AnalyticAt, AnalyticOnNhd, the identity theorem AnalyticOnNhd.eqOn_of_preconnected_of_eventuallyEq (Analysis/Analytic/Uniqueness.lean) and FormalMultilinearSeries.radius. It has nothing on natural boundaries, Szegő or Pólya–Carlson (grep found none). Formalizing Szegő's theorem would be a substantial analytic project.

formulations.name: Hankel determinants of c (Kronecker's rationality criterion)
formulations.statement: H_n := det(c(i+j))_{0≤i,j<n} is nonzero for infinitely many n (over ℤ). The mod-2 version is also equivalent: H_n ≢ 0 (mod 2) for infinitely many n.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
¬Problem 1 ⇒ H_n = 0 for all n > T+P: for such n the columns j = T and j = T+P of the Hankel matrix coincide, because c(i+T+P) = c(i+T).
Conversely, Kronecker (1881): a power series over a field is rational iff its Hankel determinants vanish for all large n. Combine with Formulation 4.
Over 𝔽₂, H_n ≢ 0 exactly when n is one of the values taken by the linear complexity profile L (normal indices of the Padé table; checked here for all n < 600). So the mod-2 version ⇔ L unbounded ⇔ Problem 1.
Since H_n mod 2 ≠ 0 implies H_n ≠ 0, the mod-2 statement directly implies the integer one.
formulations.lean:
Not in the repo yet. Mathlib has Matrix.det and Matrix.of, but no Hankel matrices and no Kronecker criterion (grep 'hankel' found nothing).
Typechecked here: `hankel_iff : Problem1 ↔ ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ hankel ℤ n ≠ 0` and `hankel_F2_iff`, with hankel R n := Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin n => (cz (i+j) : R)).
The direction 'infinitely many nonzero H_n ⇒ Problem 1' is the easy column argument. The converse needs Kronecker, or the repo's linear-complexity theorem plus the normal-index link.
formulations.known_results:
This survey (nt_data.py): H_n ≢ 0 (mod 2) for 305 of the n < 600, exactly the values of L(n). So H_n ≠ 0 over ℤ for those n.
Hankel non-vanishing drives Bugeaud's proof that the Thue–Morse number has irrationality exponent 2, and the Bugeaud–Han–Wen–Yao generalisation. Those proofs also need a Mahler functional equation to bound the Padé approximants, and c has none.

R. Salem, Algebraic Numbers and Fourier Analysis, Heath (1963), Ch. I (Kronecker's criterion)
Y. Bugeaud, On the rational approximation to the Thue–Morse–Mahler numbers, Ann. Inst. Fourier 61 (2011) 2065–2076, https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.2666/
Y. Bugeaud, G.-N. Han, Z.-Y. Wen, J.-Y. Yao, Hankel determinants, Padé approximations, and irrationality exponents, IMRN 2016, https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02797

formulations.name: Not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic (Cobham + Christol)
formulations.statement:
c is not simultaneously 2-automatic and 3-automatic.
Algebraic form: Σ c(t)·z^t is transcendental over 𝔽₂(z), or, with coefficients read in 𝔽₃, transcendental over 𝔽₃(z).
formulations.proof_of_relation:
An eventually periodic sequence is k-automatic for every k: a DFAO reading n tracks n mod P and min(n,T). So ¬Problem 1 ⇒ c is 2-automatic and 3-automatic.
Cobham (1969): a sequence that is k-automatic and l-automatic, with k and l multiplicatively independent, is eventually periodic. So 2-automatic and 3-automatic ⇒ ¬Problem 1.
Christol (1979; Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy 1980): over 𝔽_p, c is p-automatic iff its generating function is algebraic over 𝔽_p(z). The inclusion {0,1} ⊂ 𝔽_p is injective, so this applies to c.
Any multiplicatively independent pair of bases works in place of (2, 3).

formulations.name: The regular continued fraction of x₂ is infinite
formulations.statement: The regular continued fraction of x₂ = 0.c(0)c(1)…₂ does not terminate.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A real number has a terminating regular continued fraction iff it is rational (Euclid's algorithm). Then apply Formulation 1.

formulations.name: Lagrange: θ = [1+c(0); 1+c(1), 1+c(2), …] is not a quadratic irrational
formulations.statement: θ := [1+c(0); 1+c(1), 1+c(2), …] ≈ 2.3693419984984465463470948954606643210774 is not a root of any nonzero integer quadratic polynomial. θ is irrational for every c.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Euler–Lagrange theorem: the regular continued fraction of a real number is eventually periodic iff the number is a quadratic irrational. Hardy–Wright §10.12, Theorem 177, gives Lagrange's direction.
The partial quotients 1+c(t) are eventually periodic iff c is. Any injective encoding {0,1} → ℤ_{≥1} works.
The stronger statement 'θ is transcendental' is open. Two published criteria would give 'θ transcendental ⇔ Problem 1':
- Adamczewski–Bugeaud (2005), if c were 'stammering';
- Bugeaud (2013), automatic continued fractions are quadratic or transcendental, if c were automatic.
The data support neither hypothesis.
formulations.lean:

Target typechecked here: `NotQuadratic θ := ¬ ∃ A B C : ℤ, (A,B,C) ≠ 0 ∧ A·θ² + B·θ + C = 0`. θ can be built with GenContFract from the partial quotients 1 + c(t).
formulations.known_results: The value of θ was computed here. All partial quotients are ≤ 2, so θ is badly approximable (irrationality exponent 2) whatever the answer to Problem 1.

formulations.name: Diophantine and torsion forms: infinite Dirichlet set, LiouvilleWith 2, infinite order in ℝ/ℤ
formulations.statement:
(a) There are infinitely many rationals p/q with |x₂ − p/q| < 1/q².
(b) LiouvilleWith 2 x₂ in Mathlib's sense: there is a C such that, for infinitely many n, some m has x₂ ≠ m/n and |x₂ − m/n| < C/n².
(c) The image of x₂ in ℝ/ℤ has infinite additive order. Equivalently, x₂ is not a preperiodic point of x ↦ 2x mod 1, and e^{2πi·x₂} is not a root of unity.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
(a) Dirichlet/Hurwitz: ξ is irrational iff {q ∈ ℚ : |ξ − q| < 1/den(q)²} is infinite. Mathlib states this as an iff.
(b) Irrational ⇒ (a) ⇒ LiouvilleWith 2 with C = 1. Conversely, LiouvilleWith p with p > 1 ⇒ irrational.
(c) The finite-order points of ℝ/ℤ are exactly ℚ/ℤ. A point x is preperiodic under doubling iff (2^{T+P} − 2^T)·x ∈ ℤ for some T and P > 0.
All three reduce to Formulation 1.
formulations.known_results: As for Formulations 1 and 10.
sources: Mathlib Mathlib/NumberTheory/DiophantineApproximation/Basic.lean and Mathlib/Topology/Instances/AddCircle/Defs.lean

formulations.name: Irrationality exponent of x₂ equals 2
formulations.statement: μ(x₂) = 2: x₂ is irrational and, for every ε > 0, |x₂ − p/q| > q^{−2−ε} for all but finitely many p/q. In Mathlib terms: Irrational x₂ ∧ ∀ p > 2, ¬ LiouvilleWith p x₂.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
The statement contains 'Irrational x₂', which is Problem 1. The converse fails for general digit sequences (Liouville numbers). It holds for Lebesgue-almost every real (Khintchine).
Known tools and why they do not apply:
- The Hankel–Padé method (Bugeaud 2011; Bugeaud–Han–Wen–Yao 2016) needs a Mahler functional equation. For 0/1 sequences that means automaticity (Adamczewski–Bell–Smertnig 2023).
- Repetition-based bounds μ ≥ Dio(c) (Adamczewski–Bugeaud) come from long repetitions near the start of c. Such repetitions would make μ large, not prove μ = 2.
'x₂ is not a Liouville number' is independent of Problem 1, since rationals are not Liouville numbers either.

formulations.name: Transcendence of x₂ (or x_b): Adamczewski–Bugeaud, Loxton–van der Poorten, Mahler's method
formulations.statement: x₂ is transcendental. The same can be asked of x_b for any integer b ≥ 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Transcendental ⇒ irrational ⇒ Problem 1. No converse is known. Each available tool needs structure in c:
(i) Adamczewski–Bugeaud (2007): the b-ary expansion of an algebraic irrational has lim inf p(n)/n = ∞. So 'p_c(n) = O(n) and Problem 1' would give transcendence. But c has p_c(n) = 2^n for every n ≤ 19 in its first 10^7 bits.
(ii) Their stammering criterion needs early repetitions, which are not observed.
(iii) Mahler's method (Mahler 1929; Loxton–van der Poorten 1982, 1988; Nishioka 1996; Philippon 2015; Adamczewski–Faverjon 2017) needs f to satisfy a Mahler equation. For 0/1 coefficients that holds iff c is automatic (Adamczewski–Bell–Smertnig 2023).
Conditional equivalence: if c were automatic, then Problem 1 ⇔ x_b transcendental for every b. That is the Loxton–van der Poorten conjecture, proved by Adamczewski–Bugeaud (2007): irrational automatic numbers are transcendental.

formulations.name: c is not automatic in any base (f is not a Mahler function)
formulations.proof_of_relation:
An eventually periodic sequence is automatic in every base, so this statement implies Problem 1. The Thue–Morse sequence is 2-automatic and not eventually periodic, so the converse fails.
Relation to Problem 3: an automatic sequence is computable in O(log n) steps by a DFAO. So an affirmative Problem 3 implies this statement.
It is also exactly the hypothesis that decides whether Mahler's method and the automatic-number theorems can say anything about x₂. For 0/1 coefficients, Mahler ⇔ automatic (Becker 1994 for one direction; Bell–Chyzak–Coons–Dumas 2019; Adamczewski–Bell–Smertnig 2023).
formulations.lean: Nothing in Mathlib beyond DFA.
formulations.known_results: Kernel lower bounds from this survey (kernel3.py): at least 262,143 elements in the 2-kernel and at least 265,720 in the 3-kernel. Nersissian 2026 showed that any LSD-first 2-DFAO for c needs at least 8191 states.

formulations.name: x₂ is normal in base 2
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Normal ⇒ every finite word occurs (c is disjunctive) ⇒ c is not eventually periodic, because an eventually periodic sequence has at most T+P distinct factors of each length (Morse–Hedlund counting).
Normality also implies Problem 2. Neither converse holds, since Problem 1 says nothing about frequencies.
The weaker statement 'every finite word occurs in c' already implies Problem 1.

formulations.name: Simple normality of x₂ in base 2 (= Problem 2), and its Tauberian form
formulations.statement: x₂ is simply normal to base 2: lim_{N→∞} (1/N)·#{t < N : c(t) = 1} = 1/2. Equivalently, lim_{z→1⁻} (1−z)·Σ c(t)·z^t = 1/2.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
c is not eventually constant, so it is the unique binary expansion of x₂, and simple normality of x₂ is literally Problem 2.
Tauberian form: Cesàro ⇒ Abel is the Abelian theorem. Abel ⇒ Cesàro holds because c ≥ 0, by the Hardy–Littlewood–Karamata Tauberian theorem.
Relation to Problem 1: independent as statements about general 0/1 sequences. (01)^∞ satisfies Problem 2 but not Problem 1, and a non-periodic sequence of density 1/3 satisfies Problem 1 but not Problem 2.
Conditional link: if Borel's conjecture holds (every algebraic irrational is normal in every base), then a failure of Problem 2 would force x₂ to be rational or transcendental.

Grep found no Tauberian theorem.

formulations.name: 2-adic continuity of tails, via Mahler expansions (weaker); profinite continuity (equivalent)
formulations.statement:
Weaker statement: no tail t ↦ c(T+t) extends to a continuous function ℤ₂ → 𝔽₂. Two equivalent forms:
- c has no eventual period of the form 2^k;
- for every T, the 𝔽₂ Mahler coefficients a_T(n) = ⊕_{j ⊆ n} c(T+j) are not eventually 0. Here j ⊆ n means binary-digit containment, by Lucas' theorem.
Equivalent variant: no tail extends continuously to the profinite integers Ẑ.
formulations.proof_of_relation:
A continuous map from ℤ₂ to a discrete space is uniformly locally constant, hence 2^k-periodic. Conversely, a 2^k-periodic tail factors through ℤ/2^k.
Mahler's theorem in this setting: the binomials mod 2 are unitriangular, so a locally constant function has a finite Mahler expansion.
Problem 1 excludes every eventual period, in particular every 2^k. The converse fails: a sequence of period 3 satisfies the weak statement.
The weak statement is still open, because periods 2 and 4 are among the open cases (repo README). With Ẑ instead of ℤ₂, every period is covered, so that variant is equivalent to Problem 1 (my remark).

formulations.name: Mahler's Z-numbers and Kopra's distribution-mod-1 analogy (difficulty calibration)
formulations.statement:
Write X_t := Σ_p cell(t,p)·2^{-p-1}, the row at time t read as a dyadic number (Kopra's real₂). Then c(t) = ⌊2·frac(X_t)⌋ is the first binary digit after the point, and Problem 1 asks that this digit sequence is not eventually periodic.
Mahler's question (1968): is there ξ > 0 with ⌊2·frac(ξ·(3/2)^n)⌋ = 0 for all n ≥ 0, that is, a Z-number?
formulations.proof_of_relation:
Neither question implies the other. Both ask about the first fractional digit along an expanding orbit.
- Multiplication by p/q in base pq is a cellular automaton (Kari 2012).
- Kopra (2023) puts rule 30 and these fractional multiplication automata in one class, the rapidly left-expansive CA.
- Two classical theorems on {ξ(p/q)^n} have proved rule-30 analogs (Kopra 2023): each value of frac(F^t x) occurs only finitely often (Thm 4.5, the analog of Dubickas 2008), and {frac(F^t x)} has infinitely many limit points (Thm 4.7, the analog of Vijayaraghavan 1940 and Pisot 1946).
- The rule-30 analog of 'no eventual Z-number behaviour' is proved: the center column is not eventually constant (Lean no_column_eventually_constant; Condrey 2026 for every finite seed, per the project's notes). Existence of Z-numbers for 3/2 is still open.
- Kopra's Problem 4.8 is exactly Problem 1. He remarks that his Theorem 3.5 already settles the width-1 question for fractional multiplication automata, and that rapid left expansivity alone cannot decide rule 30, because rule 90 is in the class and has an eventually periodic center column.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has nothing on Z-numbers or fractional multiplication automata (Int.fract exists).
formulations.known_results:
- Mahler (1968): at most one Z-number in each interval [n, n+1).
- Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington (1995): lim sup − lim inf of frac(ξ(p/q)^n) is at least 1/p.
- frac((3/2)^n) has infinitely many accumulation points in both [0,1/2) and [1/2,1) (Pisot 1938; Vijayaraghavan, as summarised by MathWorld).
- Density and equidistribution of (3/2)^n mod 1 are unknown. They are the open counterpart of Problem 2.
sources: K. Mahler, An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 8 (1968) 313–321

J. Kopra, Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 946 (2023) 113668, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13809 (local extract: research/literature/kopra2022.txt)

formulations.name: No fast digit extraction for x₂ (no BBP-type or automaton formula)
formulations.statement: No algorithm computes c(n), the n-th binary digit of x₂, in time polylog(n).
formulations.proof_of_relation:
These statements form a chain:
- Problem 3, answered affirmatively (Ω(n) effort), implies this statement.
- This statement implies that c is not automatic in any base, because a DFAO computes c(n) in O(log n) steps.
- That implies Problem 1, because an eventually periodic sequence is computed from n mod P.
So P3 ⇒ [no polylog extraction] ⇒ [c not automatic] ⇒ P1, refining Wolfram's remark that P3 ⇒ P1.
For comparison, BBP-type formulas give binary digits of π in about O(n log n) time and O(log n) space. That is consistent with a linear lower bound in time, so 'BBP-like' and 'polylog' should be kept apart.
formulations.lean: Needs a model of computation. Mathlib has Turing machines, Nat.Partrec and Primrec, but no time-complexity framework suited to this.
formulations.known_results: Wolfram (2019) relates Problems 1–3 and compares the center column with the digits of π. Nothing more specific is known.
sources: S. Wolfram 2019, https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/
D. Bailey, P. Borwein, S. Plouffe, On the rapid computation of various polylogarithmic constants, Math. Comp. 66 (1997) 903–913

perspectives:
Barrier from the equivalences themselves (my synthesis). Every classical irrationality or transcendence method needs a functional equation or a repetition structure, and Problem 1 itself rules these out or the data contradict them.
(i) f is D-finite iff c is eventually periodic (van der Poorten–Shparlinski). So if Problem 1 holds, G-/E-function methods (Siegel–Shidlovskii), Apéry/Beukers-style Padé constructions and Fatou-type arguments have nothing to act on.
(ii) For 0/1 coefficients, f is Mahler iff c is automatic (Adamczewski–Bell–Smertnig 2023). So Mahler's method and the Loxton–van der Poorten/Adamczewski–Bugeaud automatic-number theorems need an automaticity that the kernel data contradict (at least 2.6·10^5 kernel elements in bases 2 and 3).
(iii) Subspace-theorem criteria (Adamczewski–Bugeaud 2005, 2007) need sublinear complexity or early repetitions. Yet every word of length ≤ 19 occurs in the first 10^7 bits, and the convergents of x₂ behave like those of a random real (μ ≈ 2, Lévy and Khinchin statistics).
So a number-theoretic proof of Problem 1 would have to build arithmetic structure out of the CA dynamics. This repository is most useful for translating between formulations; it does not supply an attack.

The center column as a 'naturally defined constant'; Wolfram (2019) compares it with π. Problem 1 is the irrationality question and Problem 2 the simple-normality question for x₂. They sit in the same family as open irrationality problems (Euler's γ, ζ(5), e+π) and open normality problems (√2, π, e; Borel 1950). In that family, irrationality has only ever been proved through explicit rational approximations of arithmetic origin (Hermite, Apéry, Beukers), and x₂ has no such origin.

Distribution modulo one (Kari 2012; Kari–Kopra 2017; Kopra 2021 and 2023). Rule-30 rows are dyadic numbers X_t, and c(t) is the first binary digit of frac(X_t). Rule 30 and multiplication by p/q in base pq are both rapidly left-expansive CA. The theorems on {ξ(p/q)^n} by Dubickas (values repeat finitely often) and by Vijayaraghavan and Pisot (infinitely many limit points) have proved rule-30 analogs. Mahler's Z-number problem (1968) and equidistribution of (3/2)^n mod 1 are the open counterparts of Problems 1–2, which gives a calibrated sense of the difficulty.

Function-field and automatic-sequence arithmetic (Christol; Cobham; the diagonal theorems of Furstenberg 1967, Deligne 1984 and Denef–Lipshitz 1987).
- For linear CA (rules 60, 90, 150) the space-time series is rational over 𝔽₂(x,y). Every column is then a diagonal of a rational function, hence 2-automatic (Litow–Dumas 1993; Rowland–Yassawi 2015).
- Rule 30's OR breaks this. If the space-time series Σ cell(t,p)·x^{p+t}·y^t were algebraic over 𝔽₂(x,y), its diagonal, the center column, would be 2-automatic. So 'c is not 2-automatic' implies that the space-time series is transcendental (my remark).
- Rowland–Yassawi ask whether a column of a nonlinear 2-state CA can be a 3-automatic sequence that is not eventually periodic, as recorded in the project's literature notes.

2-adic and odometer arithmetic. The right diagonals are 2^{e_j}-periodic from t = 0, so they have finite Lucas/Mahler expansions (Rowland 2006; Nersissian 2026; repo Rule30Diagonals). The right-edge orbit closure is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer (Coven–Pivato–Yassawi 2007). Nersissian's support formula gives c(n) = parity of #{r ∈ S_{n+1} : r ⊆ n bitwise}. Rules 90, 150 and 210 share all of this structure (repo barrier Rule30Realization), so it cannot decide Problem 1 on its own.

Complexity profiles from cryptography. LFSR linear complexity (Massey 1969; Niederreiter 1988) and FCSR 2-adic complexity (Klapper–Goresky 1997) both turn Problem 1 into 'the profile is unbounded'. Both profiles of c stay within O(1)–O(log n) of n/2, which is the behaviour of a random sequence. Wolfram (1986) proposed rule 30 as a generator; Meier and Staffelbach (EUROCRYPT 1991) analysed the cipher. Like the window theorems, these profiles give cheap, kernel-checkable finite bounds (L ≤ T+P), but only finite ones.

Normality and ergodic theory. Lebesgue-almost every real has normal binary digits (Borel 1909); in dynamical terms the doubling map is ergodic (Mathlib AddCircle.ergodic_nsmul), though Mathlib has no pointwise ergodic theorem yet. Problem 2 asks for simple normality of one specific number, as for π. Bailey and Crandall (Experiment. Math. 10 (2001) 175–190) reduce normality of BBP-type constants to equidistribution of one explicit dynamical sequence, their 'Hypothesis A'; that is the closest existing program of this kind.

Logical form (my remark). Problem 1, 'x₂ ∉ ℚ', 'α ∉ ℚ', transcendence of x₂ and non-automaticity are all Π⁰₂ statements about a computable sequence; normality is Π⁰₃. A natural Π⁰₁ strengthening of Problem 1 is an explicit witness bound: for all T and P ≥ 1 there is t ∈ [T, T + h(T,P)) with c(t+P) ≠ c(t), for some computable h. The project brief reports that in the billion-bit data the first-witness offsets have geometric tails, with maximum 27. A Π⁰₁ form can be refuted by computation and might be provable by bounded search plus induction, which gives the repository another axis.

formulations.name: Generating series over GF(2) is not rational (function-field irrationality)
formulations.statement: Let C(x) = Σ_{t≥0} c(t) x^t ∈ F_2[[x]]. Problem 1 ⇔ there are no A, Q ∈ F_2[x] with Q ≠ 0 and Q(x)·C(x) = A(x), i.e. C ∉ F_2(x). Equivalent phrasings: (a) ξ := Σ_{t≥0} c(t) x^{−t−1} ∈ F_2((1/x)) is irrational (ξ ∉ F_2(x)). This is the exact function-field analogue of 'the binary real 0.c(0)c(1)c(2)… is irrational'. (b) c is not a torsion element of the F_2[S]-module F_2^ℕ/(finitely supported sequences), where S is the left shift (Sc)(t) = c(t+1).
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c(t+P) = c(t) for t ≥ T, then (1 − x^P)·C(x) is a polynomial of degree < T+P. Conversely, suppose Q·C = A with Q ≠ 0. Let i0 be the least i with q_i = 1, and let d = deg Q. Comparing coefficients of x^n for n > max(deg A, d) gives c(m) = Σ_{i0<i≤d} q_i c(m+i0−i) for all large m. So each window of d−i0 bits determines the next bit: a deterministic map on the finite set F_2^{d−i0}, hence c is eventually periodic. For (a), ξ(x) = x^{−1}C(1/x), and x ↦ 1/x is an automorphism of F_2(x). For (b), if f(S)c is finitely supported and Q(x) = x^{deg f} f(1/x), then Q·C is a polynomial. This is the standard dictionary between linear recurring sequences and rational generating functions (Lidl–Niederreiter, Ch. 8); the write-up is my own.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has: PowerSeries.mk and PowerSeries.coeff (Mathlib/RingTheory/PowerSeries/Basic.lean); the coercion from polynomials (Polynomial.coeToPowerSeries.ringHom, Polynomial.coe_mul); LaurentSeries with the coercion RatFunc F → F⸨X⸩ (instance RatFunc.coeToLaurentSeries := algebraMap (RatFunc F) F⸨X⸩, Mathlib/RingTheory/LaurentSeries.lean); RatFunc.CompletionAtInfty, which is F((1/t)), for the ξ form (Mathlib/FieldTheory/RatFunc/Valuation.lean); geometric series PowerSeries.mk_one_mul_one_sub_eq_one and PowerSeries.invUnitsSub; LinearRecurrence with IsSolution, mkSol and charPoly (Mathlib/Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean, recurrences valid from n = 0 only); torsion API Submodule.torsion' and Module.IsTorsion; pigeonhole Finite.exists_infinite_fiber and Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite. Missing: an eventually-periodic predicate for sequences (only Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic exists, for subsets of ℕ), and the lemma 'a power series over a field with coefficients in a finite set is rational iff its coefficients are eventually periodic'. A suggested RatFunc-free statement: ¬ ∃ A Q : Polynomial (ZMod 2), Q ≠ 0 ∧ (Q : PowerSeries (ZMod 2)) * PowerSeries.mk (fun t => if center t then 1 else 0) = A.
formulations.known_results: Berlekamp–Massey on the first 10^6 bits (round-1 'algebraic' agent, reproduced here) gives linear complexity 499,998. formulations.name: Linear complexity profile unbounded (Berlekamp–Massey / LFSR synthesis)
formulations.statement: For n ≥ 1, let L_n be the least L ≥ 0 such that some a_1, …, a_L ∈ F_2 satisfy c(j) = Σ_{i=1}^{L} a_i c(j−i) for all L ≤ j < n. This is the length of the shortest LFSR, singular ones allowed, that generates c(0..n−1). Problem 1 ⇔ L_n → ∞. Since L_n is nondecreasing, this is the same as sup_n L_n = ∞, and the same as the infinite sequence having infinite linear complexity.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c(t+P) = c(t) for t ≥ T, the LFSR c(j) = c(j−P) of length T+P generates every prefix, so L_n ≤ T+P. If L_n ≤ M for all n, pigeonhole over the finitely many pairs (L ≤ M, a ∈ F_2^L) gives one LFSR that generates infinitely many prefixes, hence all of them. Then c satisfies a linear recurrence and is eventually periodic, as in the rational-series entry. Massey (1969) computes the whole profile in O(N^2). The write-up is my own.
formulations.lean: No LFSR, linear complexity or Berlekamp–Massey in Mathlib (grep for 'Berlekamp', 'Massey', 'shift register' and 'linear complexity' finds nothing relevant). LinearRecurrence covers only fixed recurrences valid from n = 0. The equivalence needs only finite pigeonhole (Finite.exists_infinite_fiber) and fits core Lean, matching the catalog's style. A kernel-checked lower bound on L_n needs a certificate, such as a verified BM or Euclid transcript; direct elimination is O(n^3).
formulations.known_results: L(c[0..10^6)) = 499,998 and |L_n − n/2| ≤ 9.5 for all n ≤ 10^6, with the maximum at n = 937,375. This is the round-1 agent's bm2.c result, reproduced here by an independent Python BM in 21 s. It gives T + P ≥ 499,998 for any eventual period. Columns −1 and +1 behave alike (maximum deviation 8.5 and 9.0 up to n = 199,000; round 1). Random sequences satisfy L_n = n/2 + O(log n) (Rueppel 1986; Niederreiter 1988). Published: Len et al. (2003) applied a linear-complexity test to the center-cell sequences of all ECAs (as reported by Spencer 2013), and rule 30 is among the 12 rules whose LC approaches ℓ/2. Musselman (NKS 2004) found that the single-seed center passes a NIST-derived suite. Caveats (own remark): LC ≈ n/2 does not separate random from automatic sequences. Thue–Morse has L_N = 2⌊(N+2)/4⌋ (Mérai–Winterhof), with deviation ≤ 1 up to N = 20,000 here. As a numeric certificate, LC gives only T+P ≥ ≈ n/2 from n bits, which is weaker per bit than the factor count in Rule30FactorWindow (≈ n).

formulations.name: Continued fraction of ξ in F_2((1/x)) is infinite (partial quotients)
formulations.statement: Write ξ = Σ_{t≥0} c(t) x^{−t−1} = [0; a_1(x), a_2(x), …] as a regular continued fraction with a_k ∈ F_2[x] and deg a_k ≥ 1. Let q_k be the convergent denominators. Problem 1 ⇔ the expansion is infinite. Dictionary: the distinct values of the BM profile L_n are exactly the degrees deg q_k = Σ_{i≤k} deg a_i, and L_n = deg q_k for deg q_{k−1} + deg q_k ≤ n < deg q_k + deg q_{k+1}.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Euclid's algorithm on a rational Laurent series terminates and on an irrational one does not, exactly as for real numbers; rationality of ξ is the GF(2) entry. The link between linear complexity and continued fractions is due to Mills (1975), Welch–Scholtz (1979), Dornstetter (1987) and Niederreiter (1988): BM is the Euclidean algorithm on ξ.
formulations.lean: Mathlib's continued fractions (GenContFract, Mathlib/Algebra/ContinuedFractions/) require a linearly ordered field with FloorRing, so they do not apply to F_2((1/x)). RatFunc.CompletionAtInfty and RatFunc.inftyValuation give the field and its valuation, but there is no continued-fraction API for it.
formulations.known_results: Own computation from the BM profile of the first 10^6 bits. The first 249,628 partial quotients have degrees summing to 499,998. For degrees 1–5 there are 124,501 / 62,734 / 31,074 / 15,601 / 7,813 of them, against 124,814 / 62,407 / 31,204 / 15,602 / 7,801 expected for a random Laurent series (P(deg = d) = 2^−d). The maximum degree is 19. By contrast, every partial quotient of the Thue–Morse series has degree 2 (own computation to N = 20,000), so it is badly approximable.

formulations.name: Hankel determinants mod 2 infinitely often nonzero (Kronecker over F_2)
formulations.statement: Let H_m := det[c(i+j)]_{0≤i,j<m}. Problem 1 ⇔ H_m ≡ 1 (mod 2) for infinitely many m ⇔ the infinite Hankel matrix (c(i+j))_{i,j≥0} has infinite rank over F_2. Refinement: {m ≥ 1 : H_m odd} equals the set of values of the BM profile, i.e. the degrees deg q_k.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Kronecker (1881): a power series over a field is rational iff its infinite Hankel matrix has finite rank, iff H_m = 0 for all large m. Combine this with the GF(2) rationality entry. The easy half (infinitely many odd H_m ⇒ Problem 1, my own write-up): if c(t+P) = c(t) for t ≥ T, then rows T and T+P of H_m coincide when m > T+P, so H_m = 0. The other half needs Kronecker's lemma: if H_r ≠ 0 and H_m = 0 for all m > r, then c satisfies a recurrence of order r. The refinement is the standard Padé/continued-fraction correspondence; I checked it here directly against BM for m ≤ 600 over F_2 and for m ≤ 120 over F_3, F_5, F_7 and F_1000003.
formulations.lean: Matrix.det, Matrix.of, Matrix.rank (Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Matrix/Rank.lean) and ZMod 2 exist. There is no Hankel-matrix API and no Kronecker rationality criterion: grep 'hankel' finds nothing, and 'Kronecker' in Mathlib refers to Kronecker products or to NumberField.Embeddings.pow_eq_one_of_norm_le_one, the roots-of-unity theorem. The easy half is elementary. Each fixed H_m mod 2 is decidable.
formulations.known_results: Own computation: exactly 306 of the m ≤ 600 give odd H_m, and they coincide with the BM values {1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 14, 17, 20, 21, 23, 26, …}. From BM on 10^6 bits, 249,628 values m ≤ 499,998 have odd H_m, including m = 499,998. So the F_2-rank of the infinite Hankel matrix is ≥ 499,998, which by the easy half gives T + P ≥ 499,998.
