formulations.name: p-adic irrationality and 2-adic (FCSR) complexity
formulations.statement: For a prime p let α_p := Σ_{t≥0} c(t) p^t ∈ Z_p. Problem 1 ⇔ α_p ∉ Q, for one p and then for every p. For p = 2, equivalently: the 2-adic complexity φ_n := log_2 min{max(|f|,|g|) : f, g ∈ Z, g odd, g·Σ_{t<n} c(t)2^t ≡ f (mod 2^n)} is unbounded in n.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Own write-up of standard facts. If α_p = f/g, then p ∤ g. The remainders f_k defined by α = Σ_{i<k} c(i)p^i + p^k f_k/g satisfy f_{k+1} = (f_k − c(k)g)/p, so |f_{k+1}| ≤ (|f_k|+|g|)/2. Eventually |f_k| ≤ |g|, so the digit process is finite-state and eventually periodic. Conversely, an eventually periodic c gives α = A + p^T B/(1 − p^P). If φ_n is bounded, only finitely many pairs (f, g) occur, so one pair works for infinitely many n, and then gα = f exactly. Feedback-with-carry shift registers and the rational approximation algorithm, the 2-adic analogue of BM, are due to Klapper–Goresky (1997).
formulations.lean: Mathlib has PadicInt (ℤ_[p], Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/PadicIntegers.lean), Padic, and Mahler expansions (PadicInt.mahler, PadicInt.mahlerSeries, PadicInt.hasSum_mahler). Nothing ties rationality of a p-adic integer to eventual periodicity of its digits (grep finds no 'digit' in Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics). There are no N-adic integers for composite N and nothing on FCSRs. The 2-adic complexity form needs only integers and pigeonhole.

formulations.name: Maximum-order (nonlinear) complexity unbounded; right-special factors of every length
formulations.statement: Let M_n be the least m such that for all m ≤ i, j < n, c(i−m..i−1) = c(j−m..j−1) implies c(i) = c(j). This is the length of the shortest feedback shift register with an arbitrary feedback function that generates c(0..n−1) (Jansen–Boekee 1989). Problem 1 ⇔ M_n → ∞ ⇔ for every m there are i < j with c(i−m..i−1) = c(j−m..j−1) and c(i) ≠ c(j). The same equivalence holds for the k-th order complexity (feedback of algebraic degree ≤ k) for each fixed k ≥ 1, which interpolates between L_n (k = 1) and M_n.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is eventually periodic with transient T and period P, every window of length T+P determines the next bit, so M_n ≤ T+P. If no conflict ever occurs for window length m, then c(i) = F(c(i−m..i−1)) for some F: {0,1}^m → {0,1} and all i ≥ m. That is a finite deterministic system, so c is eventually periodic. For the k-th order version, pigeonhole over the finitely many feedback functions of bounded length. The write-up is my own.
formulations.lean: Nothing specific in Mathlib. The proof is elementary and fits core Lean. A certificate for M_n ≥ m+1 is just two positions (i, j), checkable by decide on a prefix the kernel can evaluate.
formulations.known_results: Own computation (moc.py on the 10^7-bit file, whose first 3·10^5 bits I regenerated independently): M_n = 4, 11, 17, 26, 34, 37, 44 for n = 10, 10^2, …, 10^7. For random sequences M_n ≈ 2 log_2 n, i.e. 39.9 and 46.5 at 10^6 and 10^7 (Jansen). Example witness for M_{10^6} ≥ 37: the length-36 window 011110001011110100001001101101011100 occurs at positions 101,967 and 269,678, followed by 0 and by 1.

formulations.name: No finite-state keystream generator or predictor reproduces c
formulations.statement: There is no finite set S with s_0 ∈ S, F: S → S, g: S → {0,1} and T such that c(t) = g(F^t(s_0)) for all t ≥ T. So no autonomous finite-state generator outputs c from some time on: not an LFSR, NLFSR or FCSR, and not Wolfram's N-cell cyclic rule-30 register with any seed. Equivalently, every deterministic finite automaton that reads c(0..t−1) and outputs a guess for c(t) errs infinitely often.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The outputs of an autonomous finite-state machine are eventually periodic, by pigeonhole on F^t(s_0). Conversely, an eventually periodic c is generated with S = {0, …, T+P−1}. A predictor that is eventually always right becomes autonomous once it reads only its own predictions. Note: c(t) equals the center of the N-cell cyclic single-seed register for t ≤ (N−1)/2 (light cone), so every finite prefix is such an output; Problem 1 says the limit is not. The write-up is my own.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has DFA and Language.IsRegular (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean), Function.IsPeriodicPt and Function.minimalPeriod (Mathlib/Dynamics/PeriodicPts/), and Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite. Autonomous Moore machines and predictors are missing (but see the Presburger entry).
formulations.known_results: Strictly stronger versions: finite-state incompressibility, which is equivalent to Borel normality of c (Becher–Heiber 2013); and finite-state unpredictability at error rate 1/2 (O'Connor 1988). Each implies Problems 1 and 2. Wolfram's finite registers have cycle lengths of roughly 2^{0.61–0.63 N} (Wolfram 1986; NKS notes).

formulations.name: Transcendence of C(x) over Q(x) (equivalently over C(x))
formulations.statement: C(x) = Σ c(t) x^t ∈ Z[[x]] is transcendental over Q(x): no nonzero P ∈ Q[x][y] has P(x, C(x)) = 0.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is eventually periodic, C is rational and hence algebraic. Conversely, an algebraic power series is D-finite (Stanley 1980), and a D-finite series with coefficients from a finite subset of Q is rational (van der Poorten–Shparlinski 1996; multivariate, Bell–Chen 2017). Then the rationality-over-Q entry applies. Alternative routes: (i) algebraic functions have finitely many singularities, so Szegő's theorem (1922) applies; it says a series with finitely many distinct coefficients is either A/(1−x^m) or has natural boundary |x| = 1. (ii) Clear denominators to get a primitive integer relation and reduce it mod 2 and mod 3; then apply Christol and Cobham, as in the Christol–Cobham entry.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has IsAlgebraic, Transcendental and transcendental_iff (Mathlib/RingTheory/Algebraic/), plus PowerSeries, RatFunc and Polynomial.aeval. Missing: D-finite series, van der Poorten–Shparlinski, Szegő, Pólya–Carlson, Christol and Cobham (grep finds none).
formulations.known_results: Own computation. A primitive integer relation reduces to a nonzero F_2 relation of the same size, so the F_2 exclusions apply over Q as well. On the first 16,000 coefficients, C satisfies no Σ_{j≤d} P_j(x) C^j = 0 with deg P_j ≤ h for (d, h) = (2, 5300), (3, 3970), (4, 3175), (8, 1770) or (16, 935).

formulations.name: c is not P-recursive (C is not D-finite)
formulations.statement: There are no r ≥ 0 and polynomials p_0, …, p_r ∈ Q[n], not all zero, with Σ_{i=0}^{r} p_i(n) c(n+i) = 0 for all large n. Equivalently, C(x) satisfies no nonzero linear ODE with coefficients in Q[x].
formulations.proof_of_relation: An eventually periodic c satisfies a constant-coefficient recurrence. Conversely, P-recursive ⇔ D-finite (Stanley 1980), and a D-finite series with coefficients in a finite subset of Q is rational (van der Poorten–Shparlinski 1996; Bell–Chen 2017, characteristic 0). Then the rationality-over-Q entry applies.

formulations.name: Natural boundary of the analytic function C(z) (Szegő / Pólya–Carlson)
formulations.statement: The function C(z) = Σ_{t≥0} c(t) z^t, holomorphic on |z| < 1, has the unit circle as its natural boundary: it continues analytically across no arc of |z| = 1. Equivalently, C does not extend meromorphically to any disk |z| < 1+ε.
formulations.proof_of_relation: c is not eventually 0 (Rule30Prize.no_column_eventually_constant), so the radius of convergence is exactly 1. Szegő (1922): a power series with finitely many distinct coefficients that continues beyond the unit circle equals A(z)/(1−z^m). The Pólya–Carlson theorem (Carlson 1921) gives the same conclusion for integer coefficients and radius 1: rational, or natural boundary |z| = 1. Rational ⇔ eventually periodic, by the rationality-over-Q entry.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has analyticity of power series (FormalMultilinearSeries, AnalyticOnNhd), but no notion of natural boundary and neither theorem (grep 'Carlson' and 'natural boundary': none).
formulations.known_results: I found nothing specific to rule 30. Fatou (1906) was the first to study power series with coefficients from a finite set.
sources: G. Szegő, Sitzungsber. Preuss. Akad. Wiss. (1922) 88–91

formulations.name: Transcendence over F_2(x), i.e. c is not 2-automatic (Christol)
formulations.statement: C(x) ∈ F_2[[x]] is transcendental over F_2(x). Equivalently, by Christol, c is not 2-automatic: its 2-kernel {(c(2^k n + r))_{n≥0} : k ≥ 0, 0 ≤ r < 2^k} is infinite.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Eventually periodic ⇒ rational ⇒ algebraic, so transcendence implies Problem 1; this step is easy. Translating transcendence into non-automaticity needs Christol's theorem (1979; Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy 1980). The statement is strictly stronger: the Thue–Morse series T satisfies (1+x)^3 T^2 + (1+x)^2 T + x = 0 over F_2 (checked here mod x^400) yet is not eventually periodic.
formulations.lean: Transcendental and IsAlgebraic exist. Mathlib has no automatic sequences, k-kernels or Christol's theorem (grep 'Christol' and 'automatic sequence': none), and a web search found no Lean formalization.
formulations.known_results: Own computation (alg_rel.py, first 16,000 coefficients). There is no relation Σ_{j≤d} P_j(x) C^j = 0 over F_2 with deg P_j ≤ h for (d, h) = (2, 5300), (3, 3970), (4, 3175), (8, 1770) or (16, 935). There is no Ore relation Q + Σ_{i≤k} P_i C^{2^i} = 0 with degrees ≤ h for (k, h) = (1, 5300), (2, 3970), (3, 3175) or (7, 1765); every algebraic C of degree d satisfies such a relation with k = d. Sanity check: Thue–Morse is detected at (d, h) = (2, 3) and (k, h) = (1, 3). Round 1: the 2-kernel sequences for k ≤ 13 are pairwise distinct (on n < 64), so an LSD-first 2-DFAO for c would need ≥ 16,383 states. Nersissian (2026) certifies ≥ 8191 states.

formulations.name: Expansion complexity unbounded (Diem's measure)
formulations.statement: Let E_N(c) be the least total degree of a nonzero h ∈ F_2[x, y] with h(x, C(x)) ≡ 0 (mod x^N). Statement: E_N(c) → ∞.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If E_N is bounded, only finitely many h are possible, so one h kills C exactly. Its y-degree is positive, so C is algebraic; the converse also holds. Hence E_N → ∞ ⇔ C transcendental over F_2(x) ⇔ c not 2-automatic (Christol; noted by Mérai–Winterhof), which implies Problem 1. Mérai–Niederreiter–Winterhof also show E_N ≤ L_N + 1.

formulations.name: Shift disagreements of positive density, or vanishing autocorrelations
formulations.statement: (a) For every τ ≥ 1, the set {t : c(t) ≠ c(t+τ)} is infinite; this is literally Problem 1. (b) Stronger: for every τ ≥ 1 this set has positive upper density. (c) Stronger still: A(τ) := lim_N (1/N) Σ_{t<N} (−1)^{c(t)+c(t+τ)} exists and equals 0 for every τ ≥ 1, an analogue of Golomb's autocorrelation postulate. Strongest form: all Mauduit–Sárközy correlation measures of every order are o(N).
formulations.proof_of_relation: (c) ⇒ (b) ⇒ (a), and (a) is Problem 1 written out: for every P > 0, c(t+P) ≠ c(t) for infinitely many t. Borel normality of c would imply (c). The write-up is my own.
formulations.lean: Elementary. Mathlib has Filter.Tendsto; grep found no natural-density predicate (formal-conjectures defines Set.HasDensity separately).
formulations.known_results: Own computation (autocorr.py, first 10^7 bits). For every τ ≤ 300, at least 49.96% of t < N−τ have c(t) ≠ c(t+τ). The largest |Σ_{t<N−τ} (−1)^{c(t)+c(t+τ)}| is 8261, at τ = 103, about 2.6√N, which is consistent with randomness.

formulations.name: No pure 2-power period (Lucas–Mahler / binomial transform over GF(2))
formulations.statement: There is no k with c(t + 2^k) = c(t) for all t ≥ 0. Equivalently, the F_2 binomial (Mahler) transform μ_m := Σ_{j ⊆ m} c(j) mod 2, where j ⊆ m is bitwise inclusion, has infinitely many nonzero terms. Equivalently, c is not of the form t ↦ f(t mod 2^k), i.e. not the restriction to ℕ of a locally constant function on Z_2.

formulations.name: ANF degree of the t-step center map (Boolean-function / stream-cipher view)
formulations.statement: Let Φ_t: F_2^{[−t,t]} → F_2 be the center cell after t steps as a function of the initial cells x_{−t..t}. Then c(t) = Φ_t(e_0) is the coefficient of x_0 in the algebraic normal form of Φ_t, since Φ_t(0) = 0. Fact: deg Φ_t = 2t−1 for t ≥ 2, and for t ≥ 3 the unique top monomial is x_{−t+2}⋯x_t. Φ_t is balanced and uncorrelated with every affine function not involving x_{−t}: it is 0-resilient, and numerically not 1-resilient for 2 ≤ t ≤ 11.

The fact concerns all seeds at once. Round-1 barrier: all 34 ECAs of maximal degree have eventually periodic single-seed centers, so degree says nothing about Problem 1.

formulations.name: Problem 3 ⇒ non-automatic ⇒ transcendental over F_2(x) ⇒ Problem 1
formulations.statement: Suppose computing c(n) from n (given in binary) needs more than O(log n) time; any reasonable form of Problem 3 says at least this. Then c is not 2-automatic, so C(x) is transcendental over F_2(x) by Christol, so Problem 1 holds. Conversely, the cryptographic profiles (LC ≈ n/2, 2-adic complexity ≈ n/2, maximum-order complexity ≈ 2 log_2 n, maximal E_N) are not evidence for Problem 3.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A 2-automatic sequence is computed by a DFA that reads the ≈ log_2 n digits of n, in O(log n) time; eventually periodic sequences are a special case (Wolfram 2019 notes that a positive answer to Problem 3 gives a positive answer to Problem 1). Linear complexity cannot certify hardness: Thue–Morse has L_N = 2⌊(N+2)/4⌋ (Mérai–Winterhof) and is computable in O(log N). The write-up is my own.

perspectives: Function-field Diophantine approximation. ξ = Σ c(t) x^{−t−1} ∈ F_2((1/x)) is the exact analogue of the binary real 0.c(0)c(1)…, and Problem 1 is its irrationality. Berlekamp–Massey is the Euclidean (continued-fraction) algorithm for ξ (Mills 1975; Welch–Scholtz 1979; Dornstetter 1987), and the linear complexity profile is read off the partial-quotient degrees (Niederreiter 1988). Irrationality exponents, badly approximable series and Hankel determinants all carry over. Rule 30's ξ looks like a random Laurent series, with geometrically distributed partial-quotient degrees up to 19 in the first 10^6 bits. Automatic series such as Thue–Morse are badly approximable instead: all their partial quotients have degree 2.

Hierarchy of stream-cipher complexity measures (C. Li's 2024 survey): linear, 2-adic (FCSR), k-th order, maximum-order and expansion complexity. For any sequence with values in a finite set, every finite-register model — LFSR, FCSR, NLFSR, any autonomous finite-state machine — gives 'profile bounded ⇔ eventually periodic'. Problem 1 is therefore exactly 'the center column defeats every finite-register model'. Expansion complexity alone measures algebraicity, i.e. automaticity (Diem 2012; Mérai–Niederreiter–Winterhof 2017), the next rung up. For c, every measure tested matches a random sequence.

Transcendence dichotomy across characteristics. For a {0,1} power series, algebraic over Q(x) implies rational (Pólya–Carlson, Szegő, van der Poorten–Shparlinski, Bell–Chen). Over F_p(x), algebraic means p-automatic (Christol). So Problem 1 equals 'transcendental over Q(x)', and also equals 'not algebraic over both F_2(x) and F_3(x)' (Christol + Cobham). It is strictly weaker than 'transcendental over F_2(x)'.

Furstenberg–Deligne diagonals. For linear rules the space-time series is rational, so the center column, a constant term or diagonal, is algebraic and hence automatic (Furstenberg 1967; Allouche–von Haeseler–Peitgen–Skordev 1996); this is why rules 90 and 150 have automatic centers. For rule 30 the series F(x,z) = Σ_t X_t(z) x^t is not known to be algebraic; if it were, c would be 2-automatic. The right diagonals are individually rational: they are purely 2^{e_j}-periodic, with exact linear complexities known from round 1 and Nersissian (2026). c is a moving diagonal of this odometer-like array (Coven–Pivato–Yassawi 2007 give the odometer structure).

Wolfram's rule-30 stream cipher and its cryptanalysis (Wolfram 1985/86; Meier–Staffelbach 1991; Koç–Apohan 1997; Spencer 2013; Mariot 2024). The attacks use three facts: rule 30 is affine in one extreme input (left-permutive), which makes leftward reconstruction from two adjacent temporal sequences deterministic; the local rule is not first-order correlation immune; and its nonlinearity is low (Martin 2008). Meier–Staffelbach report that for n = 300 about 18 bits of entropy suffice to recover the seed. The left-permutive identity is the same one behind Jen's theorem (Rule30Jen.cell_left). Their observation that a run of 0s in the observed column forces the right-adjacent column to read 0*1* is the monotonicity step in Rule30Prize.no_column_eventually_constant. The cryptographic setting uses finite registers and random keys, so every output is eventually periodic by construction, and none of this reaches Problem 1 directly.

Boolean-function view of the t-step map Φ_t. It has exact algebraic degree 2t−1 and is balanced, 0-resilient but not 1-resilient. The single-seed center is the x_0-coefficient of its ANF. Degree and nonlinearity are properties of all seeds jointly, and the round-1 barrier (maximal-degree ECAs have eventually periodic single-seed centers) shows they cannot decide Problem 1. Mariot (2024) flags the algebraic degree of CA generators as an open question in cryptography, so the degree theorem may be publishable on its own.

Lucas–Mahler (binomial) calculus over GF(2). Purely 2^k-periodic sequences are exactly those with finitely supported binomial transforms. This controls the right diagonals and the 2-adic odometer (round 1; Nersissian 2026, where c(n) is an XOR of binomials over a Newton support), but reaches only the pure 2-power case of Problem 1.

Hankel-determinant technology from transcendence theory (Han's Hankel continued fractions; Bugeaud–Han–Wen–Yao 2016; Adiceam–Nesharim–Lunnon on the t-adic Littlewood conjecture, arXiv:1806.04478) computes Hankel determinants of automatic sequences modulo p with finite automata. Rule 30's Hankel determinants show no such structure: mod 2 they are nonzero exactly at the BM jump values, and over Z they are nonzero except at m = 7, 8. These tools would gain a foothold only if c were automatic.
surveys.notes:
Scope and conventions. My angle was algebra, coding theory and cryptography. c(t) ∈ {0,1} is Rule30Prize.center t, and C(x) = Σ c(t) x^t. The 'difficulty' field rates how hard it is to prove the stated relation to Problem 1; for 'related' and 'about Problem 2/3' entries it rates the stated fact or implication. All the stronger statements are themselves open. Anything marked 'own' is my reasoning or my computation; everything else cites a source.

Own computations. All ran in under 60 s on the laptop, with python3 -I. Scripts are in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/algebra-crypto/:
- gen_center.py: an independent rule-30 generator. Its output matches /Users/swish/src/wolfram/Ruliology/build/rule30/center-1e7.bin (MSB-first) on the first 300,000 bits, and center-1e6.bin is a prefix of that file.
- bm_profile.py: BM over GF(2). It reproduces round 1 (L = 499,998 at 10^6 bits; maximum deviation 9.5 at n = 937,375) and adds the partial-quotient statistics.
- hankel.py, hankel_check_modp.py, bm_modp.py: Hankel determinants over GF(2), Z and GF(p). The correspondence 'nonzero H_m ⇔ BM value' was checked directly for p = 2, 3, 5, 7 and 1000003.
- twoadic.py: 2-adic complexity up to n = 65,536.
- moc.py: maximum-order complexity up to 10^7 bits.
- alg_rel.py and expansion.py: exclusion of small algebraic relations and expansion complexity over GF(2), sanity-checked on Thue–Morse and on a periodic sequence.
- precursive.py: exclusion of P-recursive relations, modulo the prime 2147483629.
- autocorr.py: autocorrelations on 10^7 bits.
- anf_degree.py: ANF degree of Φ_t for t ≤ 10.
Downloads were treated as untrusted and only text-extracted with pdftotext; they are in dl_spencer2013/ and dl_mariot2024/. The PDF in dl_wolfram1986/ turned out to be a different, scanned Wolfram note, so I did not read Wolfram's 1986 paper itself.

Main conclusions.
(1) Every finite-memory complexity measure from stream-cipher theory gives an elementary, easily formalized equivalent of Problem 1: 'the profile is unbounded'. This covers linear complexity (BM, Hankel determinants and continued fractions are three views of the same object), 2-adic (FCSR) complexity, k-th order and maximum-order complexity, and finite-state generation. Expansion complexity is the exception: it is unbounded iff c is not 2-automatic, which is strictly stronger.
(2) In characteristic 0, the conditions 'C rational', 'C algebraic', 'C D-finite' and 'C continues across the unit circle' all coincide for a {0,1} sequence. Those equivalents need classical analysis (Szegő, Pólya–Carlson, van der Poorten–Shparlinski). Over GF(p), algebraic means p-automatic (Christol), and Problem 1 is equivalent to 'not algebraic over both F_2(x) and F_3(x)' (Christol + Cobham).
(3) Numerically, c looks random under every measure I tested:
- linear complexity n/2 ± 9.5;
- partial-quotient degrees with a geometric distribution;
- integer Hankel determinants nonzero for 9 ≤ m < 45,000, and zero at m = 7, 8;
- 2-adic complexity n/2 ± 3.6;
- maximum-order complexity 37 and 44 at 10^6 and 10^7 bits, close to 2 log_2 n;
- expansion complexity at its maximum, 178, for N = 16,000;
- no algebraic relation over F_2 of degree ≤ 16 with heights up to 935, and no P-recursive relation of order and degree ≤ 44.
(4) As numeric certificates, LC and 2-adic complexity give only T+P ≥ ≈ n/2 from n bits. That is weaker per bit than the factor-count certificate already in Lean (Rule30FactorWindow: T+P ≥ 16,359 from 16,384 bits). Their value is conceptual, not numeric. One odd Hankel determinant H_m certifies T+P ≥ m by the easy half of Kronecker, but a nonsingularity certificate for large m would need a verified BM or Euclid transcript. I did not attempt this.
(5) The cryptanalysis of Wolfram's generator concerns finite registers and random seeds. It shares the left-permutive reconstruction with Jen's theorem, but none of it bears on single-seed periodicity.

Lean planning. The Ruliology catalog is core Lean without Mathlib. The Mathlib-based equivalents (PowerSeries/RatFunc, Matrix.det, PadicInt, Transcendental, Presburger) therefore need a separate Mathlib-dependent package that restates center. My suggested order, easiest first:
- (a) Presburger/semilinear: Mathlib already proves Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic and FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic.
- (b) LFSR linear complexity, maximum-order complexity and finite-state generation: finite pigeonhole only; core Lean suffices.
- (c) Rationality over GF(2) and over Q, stated as ∃ A Q, Q ≠ 0 ∧ Q·C = A in PowerSeries.
- (d) p-adic irrationality.
- (e) The easy half of the Hankel criterion, then Kronecker's criterion.
- Long projects: Christol, Cobham, Szegő/Pólya–Carlson, van der Poorten–Shparlinski, Hardy–Littlewood. None of these is in Mathlib.

Citations from secondary sources or not fully checked:
- Meier–Staffelbach details come from Spencer (2013, arXiv:1306.3546) and Mariot (2024); I did not access the original.
- Len et al. (2003) is cited via Spencer.
- The journal details for Bell–Chen, and the content of O'Connor (1988), were not checked.
- The ANF degree theorem is a round-1 paper proof that no verifier checked; I re-checked it numerically for t ≤ 10 and found no published proof.
- Apart from Len et al.'s ECA-wide LC test (via Spencer) and Musselman's NIST-derived tests (NKS 2004), I found no published computation of the linear complexity profile of the single-seed center column.

formulations.name: Infinite shift orbit (c is not a preperiodic point of the shift)
formulations.statement: Write (σ^n c)(t) = c(n+t). Problem 1 ⟺ n ↦ σ^n c is injective ⟺ the forward orbit {σ^n c : n ∈ ℕ} is infinite ⟺ for no m is σ^m c a periodic point of σ (σ^m c ∉ Function.periodicPts σ for every m). Word form, already in the catalog: Problem 1 ⟺ for no nonempty word w is c eventually w w w ⋯ (Rule30StripCertificates.problem1_iff_no_word).
formulations.proof_of_relation: By funext, σ^{T+P} c = σ^T c says exactly that c(t+P) = c(t) for all t ≥ T. So two equal iterates σ^m c = σ^n c with m < n give T = m and P = n − m, and conversely. A finite orbit has two equal iterates by pigeonhole, and an injective orbit is infinite. No named theorem is needed. Checked in core Lean in my scratch file CoreEquiv.lean as Scratch2.problem1_iff_shift_injective; axioms are propext and Quot.sound only.

formulations.name: Morse–Hedlund factor complexity
formulations.statement: Let p_c(n) = #{c[i, i+n) : i ∈ ℕ}, the number of distinct length-n factors. Problem 1 ⟺ p_c(n) ≥ n+1 for every n ≥ 1 ⟺ p_c is unbounded ⟺ p_c is strictly increasing ⟺ for every n some length-n factor u is right-special (both u0 and u1 occur). For a binary sequence, p_c(n+1) − p_c(n) is exactly the number of right-special factors of length n. Quantitative form: if c(t+P) = c(t) for all t ≥ T, then p_c(n) ≤ T + P for every n; with T and P minimal, p_c(n) = T + P for all large n, so sup_n p_c(n) = T_min + P_min.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Counting direction: a factor starting at i ≥ T equals the one starting at T + ((i − T) mod P), so every factor starts below T + P. Morse–Hedlund direction: p_c is nondecreasing because every factor extends to the right, and p_c(1) = 2 because c is not eventually constant (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant, already in Lean). If p_c(n) ≤ n, then p_c(m) = p_c(m+1) for some m < n. Each length-m factor then has a unique right extension, so c(i+m) is a function of c[i, i+m), and the windows follow a self-map of a finite set, hence are eventually periodic. The sup identity is my own reasoning: for large n, the factors starting at i < j < T+P must differ, since otherwise σ^i c = σ^j c would contradict minimality. I brute-force checked it on 600 random eventually periodic words (check_claims.py). Named theorems: Morse–Hedlund (1938), Coven–Hedlund (1973).
formulations.lean: Mathlib has no factor complexity, special factors or Morse–Hedlund theorem; grepping for Hedlund, Sturmian and subword/factor complexity found nothing beyond docstrings. Usable pieces: List.IsInfix (<:+:), Finset.card, Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt, SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.LanguageOn and MulSubshift.languageOn (patterns of a given shape), and finite_setOf_pattern_support_eq. The counting direction already sits inside Rule30FactorWindow.transient_add_period_ge (core Lean). Missing: the Morse–Hedlund direction, which I estimate at 150–250 lines of core Lean.
formulations.known_results: Kernel-checked: p_c(26) ≥ 16359 (Rule30FactorWindow), hence T + P ≥ 16359. From the 10^7-bit prefix (my recount, which agrees with the project's mh-rigor-verify): p_c(n) = 2^n for n ≤ 19; p_c(20) ≥ 1,048,480 = 2^20 − 96; p_c(21) ≥ 2,079,158; p_c(22) ≥ 3,806,484; p_c(23) ≥ 5,839,590; p_c(24) ≥ 7,529,936. These are prefix lower bounds and say nothing about the tail.

E. M. Coven, G. A. Hedlund, Sequences with minimal block growth, Math. Systems Theory 7 (1973) 138–153, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01762232 (checked via Crossref)

formulations.name: Finite-certificate (Π₂) form
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ for every N there are n and M such that the prefix c[0, M) contains at least N+1 distinct factors of length n. For each fixed N, the inner statement is equivalent to 'c has no eventual period (T, P) with T + P ≤ N'. That inner statement is Σ₁ and can be verified by a finite computation; Problem 1 itself is Π₂.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Both directions come from the Morse–Hedlund entry. N+1 distinct factors contradict p_c ≤ T + P ≤ N. Conversely, suppose no eventual period has T + P ≤ N. Then either c is not eventually periodic, so p_c is unbounded by Morse–Hedlund, or sup p_c = T_min + P_min ≥ N+1. In both cases N+1 distinct factors of one length already occur in some finite prefix. Only the sup identity is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: Same as the Morse–Hedlund entry. Rule30FactorWindow is exactly such a certificate for N = 16358: a kernel-checked sorted permutation of the 16359 windows of length 26, in core Lean without native_decide.
formulations.known_results: N = 16358 is kernel-checked. N = 9,999,956 follows from the 10^7-bit file (round 1, data only). The project brief adds a result from Wen's 10^9-bit dataset: every P ≤ 2.5·10^8 has a witness t ∈ [5·10^8, 10^9 − P) with c(t) ≠ c(t+P). That excludes eventual periods P ≤ 2.5·10^8 with transient ≤ 5·10^8.

formulations.name: Infinite right-special branch (König form)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ there is a left-infinite word ⋯a₃a₂a₁ such that every suffix aₙ⋯a₁ is right-special in c, i.e. both aₙ⋯a₁0 and aₙ⋯a₁1 occur in c. The same holds with 'occur infinitely often', i.e. right-special in the tail language L∞(c).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Suffixes of right-special factors are right-special, so the right-special factors form a binary tree under extension to the left. By the Morse–Hedlund entry this tree has nodes at every depth, so König's lemma gives an infinite branch. Conversely, an infinite branch gives right-special factors of every length, so p_c strictly increases. Named theorem: König's infinity lemma.

formulations.known_results: In the 10^7-bit prefix every word of length ≤ 18 is right-special (p(n+1) − p(n) = 2^n for n ≤ 18). This is prefix data only.

formulations.name: Tail language and ω-limit subshift
formulations.statement: Let L∞(c) be the set of words occurring infinitely often in c, and p∞(n) = |L∞(c) ∩ {0,1}^n|. Let Ω(c) ⊆ {0,1}^ℤ be the two-sided subshift with language L∞(c), and ω(c) ⊆ {0,1}^ℕ the set of limit points of (σ^n c). Problem 1 ⟺ p∞(n) ≥ n+1 for all n ⟺ Ω(c) is infinite ⟺ Ω(c) contains a non-periodic point ⟺ ω(c) is not a single periodic orbit ⟺ ω(c) contains a non-periodic point. If c is eventually periodic with minimal period P, then Ω(c) has exactly P points and p∞(n) = P for every n ≥ P − 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is eventually periodic, Ω(c) is the orbit of the bi-infinite periodic word. Then p∞(n) = P for n ≥ P − 1, because two rotations of a primitive word with the same first P − 1 letters coincide; this is my reasoning, brute-force checked. For the converse: L∞(c) is factorial and extends on both sides, and by compactness the length-n prefixes of points of ω(c) are exactly L∞(c) ∩ {0,1}^n. If p∞(n) ≤ n, the Morse–Hedlund flat step inside L∞ gives unique right extensions. Only finitely many length-(m+1) words occur finitely often; after their last occurrence c follows the extension map, so it is eventually periodic. An infinite one-dimensional subshift contains a non-periodic point: Meyerovitch–Salo cite Ballier for the fact that a subshift on a finitely generated group whose points all have finite orbits is finite, and a right-special-branch argument also works. For the one-sided ω(c): if every right half of a non-periodic point of Ω(c) were periodic, they would share one period and the point would be periodic (my reasoning). The project's round-1 rigor check verified the p∞ and finiteness clauses; the non-periodic-point clauses are my additions.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has omegaLimit (notation ω) with mem_omegaLimit_iff_frequently, isClosed_omegaLimit, nonempty_omegaLimit and isInvariant_omegaLimit (Mathlib/Dynamics/OmegaLimit.lean). Missing: the language of a subshift as a set of words, Morse–Hedlund for subshifts, and the theorem that a subshift with only periodic points is finite.

formulations.name: Rauzy graphs of the tail language
formulations.statement: For n ≥ 1 let Γₙ have vertex set L∞(c) ∩ {0,1}^n, with one edge u → v for each w ∈ L∞(c) ∩ {0,1}^{n+1} whose prefix is u and whose suffix is v. Every Γₙ is strongly connected. Problem 1 ⟺ no Γₙ is a single directed cycle ⟺ every Γₙ has a vertex of out-degree 2 ⟺ p∞(n+1) > p∞(n) for every n.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Strong connectivity is my own reasoning: from some time on, the path of length-n windows of c uses only edges of Γₙ and visits every vertex and edge infinitely often. A strongly connected graph whose out-degrees are all 1 is a single cycle, which happens exactly when p∞(n+1) = p∞(n); the tail-language entry then gives eventual periodicity. Conversely, for an eventually periodic c, Γₙ is a single cycle of length P once n ≥ P − 1.

formulations.known_results: None; this is a tail property.

formulations.name: Return words, gaps between equal letters, run lengths
formulations.statement: Let u be a word occurring infinitely often, with occurrences i₁ < i₂ < ⋯. Its derived sequence D_u(c) = (c[i_k, i_{k+1}))_k lists the return words to u. Problem 1 ⟺ D_u(c) is not eventually periodic, for one (equivalently every) such u. Both letters recur, so concretely: Problem 1 ⟺ the gaps between consecutive 1s (OEIS A327981) are not eventually periodic ⟺ the gaps between consecutive 0s (A327980) are not eventually periodic ⟺ the run-length sequence of c (A327983) is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is periodic from T with period P, the occurrences of u after T fall into finitely many residue classes mod P, so D_u(c) is eventually periodic. If D_u(c) has period q from k₀ on, then from position i_{k₀} the sequence c is the infinite repetition of r_{k₀}⋯r_{k₀+q−1}. The same argument works for gaps and runs over the alphabet ℕ. All runs are finite because c is not eventually constant (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant). No named theorem is needed; Durand's derived sequences are the background.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has Nat.nth (Mathlib/Data/Nat/Nth.lean), which gives the k-th black time once the set of black times is shown infinite. It has no API for return words, derived sequences or run lengths. In core Lean the positions can be defined by search, using the proved non-constancy for termination.
formulations.known_results: OEIS A327980, A327981 and A327983 (Karttunen, 2019) are tabulated to n = 100000. I checked that the project's 10^7-bit file reproduces their first 33–40 terms. The first 10^7 bits contain 2,500,412 runs of each color, with mean run length 1.9997.

formulations.name: Decimation form: every modulus has a non-constant residue class
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ for every P ≥ 1 there is r < P such that k ↦ c(r + kP) is not eventually constant. The case P = 1 is Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant.
formulations.proof_of_relation: c is periodic from T with period P iff every residue class mod P is constant from k = T on. For the converse, take the largest of the P class transients. formulations.name: Invariance under permutive recodings (XOR derivative)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ Δc is not eventually periodic, where Δc(t) = c(t) xor c(t+1). More generally, Problem 1 ⟺ φ(c) is not eventually periodic for any sliding block code φ(c)(t) = f(c(t), …, c(t+r)) in which f is a bijection in its last argument for each fixed value of the others (for example c(t) xor c(t+k), or iterated derivatives).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Sliding block codes preserve eventual periodicity. Converse for Δ: if Δc has period P from T, then S(t) = c(t+P) xor c(t) is constant for t ≥ T, so c has period P (if S = 0) or 2P (if S = 1). For a general permutive f, c(t+r) is a function of c[t, t+r) and φ(c)(t), so the pair (c[t, t+r), (t − T) mod P) follows a self-map of a finite set. The Δ case is machine-checked in core Lean as Scratch2.problem1_iff_deriv (axioms propext, Quot.sound). With minimal periods, P_c ∈ {P_Δc, 2·P_Δc}, brute-force checked on 600 random words. The general case is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: The Δ case is done in core Lean. Mathlib has no sliding block codes and no cellular automata (grepping for 'cellular automat' found nothing).
formulations.known_results: Nothing beyond the equivalence itself.
sources: D. Lind, B. Marcus, An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding, CUP 1995 (sliding block codes)
G. A. Hedlund, Endomorphisms and automorphisms of the shift dynamical system, Math. Systems Theory 3 (1969) 320–375, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01691062 (checked via Crossref)

formulations.name: Orbit closure is infinite
formulations.statement: Let X̄_c be the closure of {σ^n c : n ∈ ℕ} in {0,1}^ℕ (product topology). Problem 1 ⟺ X̄_c is infinite ⟺ X̄_c has an accumulation point.
formulations.proof_of_relation: An eventually periodic c has a finite orbit; a finite set is closed, so it equals X̄_c. An infinite orbit makes X̄_c infinite, and an infinite compact space has an accumulation point, while a finite one has none.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has closure, Set.Infinite, AccPt and Function.compactSpace. An orbit closure is a SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.Subshift with G = ℕ, since it is closed and shift-invariant; the constructor is one short lemma, which is the only missing piece.
formulations.known_results: X̄_c has at least 16359 points, by the shift-orbit entry.
sources: D. Lind, B. Marcus, An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding, CUP 1995
P. Kůrka, Topological and Symbolic Dynamics, Cours Spécialisés 11, SMF 2003

formulations.name: Irrationality / doubling map (the user's example)
formulations.statement: Let x_c = Σ_{t≥0} c(t)·2^{−(t+1)}, i.e. Real.ofDigits (b := 2) applied to c. Problem 1 ⟺ x_c is irrational ⟺ x_c has infinite order in ℝ/ℤ (¬ IsOfFinAddOrder (x_c : AddCircle 1)) ⟺ x_c is not a preperiodic point of the doubling map D(y) = 2y mod 1. The same holds with base 2 replaced by any integer base b ≥ 2, keeping the digits 0 and 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Digits conjugate σ to D: x_{σc} = 2·x_c − c(0), from Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits with n = 1. Eventually periodic digits give a rational number (geometric series). If x_c = a/q, the D-orbit of x_c lies in the finite set (1/q)ℤ/ℤ, so D^m x_c = D^n x_c for some m < n. Two digit sequences with the same value are equal unless one ends in 0^∞ and the other in 1^∞. That is excluded because c is not eventually constant (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant), so σ^m c = σ^n c. Infinite order ⟺ irrational is AddCircle.isOfFinAddOrder_iff_exists_rat_eq_div. Preperiodic ⟺ finite order: 2^m y = 2^n y gives (2^n − 2^m)·y = 0, and a point of order q has its orbit in the finite set {z : q·z = 0} (AddCircle.finite_torsion). For b ≥ 3, the 0/1 expansion is unique outright.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has Real.ofDigits, Real.ofDigitsTerm (term d_i·b^{−(i+1)}), Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits, Real.digits, Real.ofDigits_digits and Real.continuous_ofDigits (Mathlib/Analysis/Real/OfDigits.lean); Irrational (Mathlib/NumberTheory/Real/Irrational.lean); AddCircle.isOfFinAddOrder_iff_exists_rat_eq_div, AddCircle.not_isOfFinAddOrder_iff_forall_rat_ne_div, AddCircle.finite_torsion and AddCircle.addOrderOf_coe_rat (Mathlib/Topology/Instances/AddCircle/Defs.lean); and AddCircle.ergodic_nsmul (Mathlib/Dynamics/Ergodic/AddCircle.lean), which says the doubling map is ergodic. Missing: the lemma 'eventually periodic digits ⟺ rational' (grep found none) and uniqueness of expansions that are not eventually constant.
formulations.known_results: This is equivalent to the shift-orbit, Morse–Hedlund and certificate entries, so a rational x_c would need T + P ≥ 16359 in its binary expansion (kernel-checked). OEIS A092539 lists the binary prefixes as integers. The number-theory sibling covers the number side.
sources: Mathlib: Mathlib/Analysis/Real/OfDigits.lean, Mathlib/Topology/Instances/AddCircle/Defs.lean, Mathlib/Dynamics/Ergodic/AddCircle.lean
OEIS A092539, https://oeis.org/A092539
B. Adamczewski, Y. Bugeaud, On the complexity of algebraic numbers I. Expansions in integer bases, Ann. of Math. 165 (2007) 547–565

formulations.name: Black times are not Presburger-definable
formulations.statement: Let B = {t ∈ ℕ : c(t) = 1}. Problem 1 ⟺ B is not definable in Presburger arithmetic (ℕ, 0, 1, +), with any set of parameters ⟺ B is not a semilinear subset of ℕ.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Ginsburg–Spanier: a subset of ℕ is Presburger-definable iff it is semilinear iff it is ultimately periodic. Mathlib states this as FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic: A.Definable₁ presburger s ↔ ∃ k, ∃ p > 0, ∀ x ≥ k, x ∈ s ↔ x + p ∈ s. Unfolding EventuallyPeriodic finishes the proof. Machine-checked against the built Mathlib in my scratch file PresburgerCheck.lean as Scratch.problem1_iff_not_presburger : Problem1 ↔ ¬ (∅ : Set ℕ).Definable₁ FirstOrder.Language.presburger {t | center t = true}. A general version for any f : ℕ → Bool and any parameter set is in the same file. It compiled in 8 s with axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic and FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable_iff_isSemilinearSet (Mathlib/ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/Definability.lean), Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic (Mathlib/ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/Semilinear/Defs.lean) and Set.Definable₁ (Mathlib/ModelTheory/Definability.lean). Nothing is missing. The only obstacle is packaging: the Ruliology catalog is core Lean without Mathlib, so this needs a Mathlib-dependent companion project that restates cell and center.
formulations.known_results: Same certificates as the finite-certificate entry.
sources: S. Ginsburg, E. H. Spanier, Semigroups, Presburger formulas, and languages, Pacific J. Math. 16 (1966) 285–296
Mathlib: Mathlib/ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/Definability.lean (D. Zhang, 2025)

formulations.name: Cobham two-base form
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ c is not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic. More generally, Problem 1 ⟺ c is not both k- and l-automatic, for any one pair of multiplicatively independent k, l ≥ 2 ⟺ c is not k-automatic for some k ≥ 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation: ⟸ is Cobham's theorem (1969): a sequence that is both k- and l-automatic, with k and l multiplicatively independent, is eventually periodic. ⟹: an eventually periodic sequence is k-automatic for every k, since a DFAO reading base-k digits can track t mod P and whether t < T. Third form: being k-automatic for every k includes k = 2 and k = 3.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has DFA, NFA, εNFA, Language and RegularExpression (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean, NFA.lean, MyhillNerode.lean). It has no automatic sequences, k-kernels or Cobham's theorem; grepping for 'Cobham' and 'automatic sequence' found nothing. All of it is missing, and Cobham's theorem would be a substantial formalization project.
formulations.known_results: From the project's literature notes (Nersissian 2026, unrefereed): the 8191 words (c(2^a·j + r))_{1≤j≤31}, for a ≤ 12 and r < 2^a, are pairwise distinct within the first 131072 bits. So an LSD-first 2-DFAO generating c needs at least 8191 states. No proof of non-automaticity is known in any base.
sources: A. Cobham, On the base-dependence of sets of numbers recognizable by finite automata, Math. Systems Theory 3 (1969) 186–192, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01746527 (checked via Crossref)
J.-P. Allouche, J. Shallit, Automatic Sequences, CUP 2003
H. Nersissian, Diagonal Periods and Newton Supports of Rules 30, 86 and 135, arXiv:2609.25077 (unrefereed), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25077

formulations.name: Width-1 trace of rule 30 and ω-limit sets
formulations.statement: Let F be rule 30 on {0,1}^ℤ, and let Tr_W(x) = ((F^t x)|_W)_{t≥0} be the trace on a window W. Tr_{0} is a factor map from ({0,1}^ℤ, F) onto ({0,1}^ℕ, σ), and c = Tr_{0}(δ₀). Problem 1 ⟺ Tr_{0}(δ₀) is not σ-preperiodic ⟺ Tr_{0}(ω_F(δ₀)) is infinite, where ω_F(δ₀) is the ω-limit set of the single seed under F. Jen's theorem is the width-2 version: for every i, Tr_{[i,i+1]}(δ₀) is not eventually periodic, i.e. Tr_{[i,i+1]}(ω_F(δ₀)) is infinite.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Tr_{0} is continuous with Tr_{0}∘F = σ∘Tr_{0}, and it is onto by left-permutivity (Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique). For a factor map π between compact metric systems, π(ω_F(x)) = ω_σ(π x): one inclusion by continuity, the other by passing to a convergent subsequence. This identity is my own reasoning. The tail-language and orbit-closure entries then apply. A width-2 trace is eventually periodic iff both columns are (common period, Rule30Jen.common_period), so Rule30Jen.not_adjacent is exactly the width-2 case.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has omegaLimit, mapsTo_omegaLimit and isInvariant_omegaLimit (Mathlib/Dynamics/OmegaLimit.lean), Function.Semiconj and Function.IsPeriodicPt.map. Missing: cellular automata, traces, and the identity π(ω(x)) = ω(π x). The project has, in core Lean, Rule30Jen.jen, Rule30Jen.not_adjacent, Rule30Realization.evol and Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique.
formulations.known_results: Width 2 is Jen 1986, proved in Lean. Kopra 2023 extends width 2 to every number-like configuration (nonzero and eventually 0 to the left) via rapid left expansivity, and states width 1 for the seed as an open problem (Problem 4.8 in arXiv v1). Barrier: rules 90, 150 and 210 satisfy the same width-2 theorem but have eventually constant center columns (Rule30Realization.barrier).
sources: J. Kopra, Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 946 (2023) 113668, arXiv:2202.13809, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13809
E. Jen, Global properties of cellular automata, J. Stat. Phys. 43 (1986) 219–242, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01010579
J. Cervelle, E. Formenti, P. Guillon, Ultimate traces of cellular automata, STACS 2010, arXiv:1001.0251, https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0251
P. Kůrka, Topological dynamics of cellular automata (survey), https://www.cts.cuni.cz/~kurka/cantor.pdf

formulations.name: Unbounded runs (unbounded return times to one letter)
formulations.statement: S0: 0^n occurs in c for every n; equivalently, the gaps between consecutive 1s (A327981) are unbounded, or 0^∞ ∈ X̄_c. S1: the same for runs of 1s (A327980). Either S0 or S1 implies Problem 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is periodic from T with period P and not eventually constant (proved in Lean), every run has length < T + P. As a statement about binary sequences this is strictly stronger: the Thue–Morse word is not eventually periodic, yet it has no run longer than 2.
formulations.lean: The statement is core Lean, and S0 ⟹ Problem 1 is a short proof from Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant.
formulations.known_results: S0 and S1 are open. My count on the first 10^7 bits: the longest 0-run is 22 (first at t = 5,241,994) and the longest 1-run is 23 (first at t = 1,174,512). Record 0-runs of lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 19, 20, 22 first start at t = 2, 6, 10, 43, 86, 117, 292, 1269, 11109, 26216, 32198, 2810107, 5241994. Record 1-runs of lengths 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 16, 21, 22, 23 first start at t = 0, 3, 62, 191, 1053, 4646, 6531, 22711, 37260, 731772, 1174512. Fair coin flips give a longest run near log₂(10^7) ≈ 23. A related project result: Theorem B (Rule30BlackRuns.no_long_black_run) excludes eventual periods P that contain a black run of length r ≥ about 0.82·P + 8.2.
sources: OEIS A327980 https://oeis.org/A327980, A327981 https://oeis.org/A327981
Project: Rule30BlackRuns.lean; round-1 verifier note on Thue–Morse (research/results/round1.json)

formulations.name: Unbounded abelian complexity (c is not C-balanced)
formulations.statement: Let a_c(n) be the number of distinct Parikh vectors of length-n factors; for binary c this is max_i |c[i, i+n)|₁ − min_i |c[i, i+n)|₁ + 1. If a_c is unbounded (equivalently, c is not C-balanced for any C), then Problem 1 holds.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is periodic from T with period P, the weights of tail windows repeat with period P and change by at most 1 per shift. Windows starting before T differ in weight from the window at T by at most T. So a_c(n) ≤ T + P + 1 for all n. For binary words, bounded abelian complexity is the same as C-balance, by the max − min formula. Strictly stronger: Thue–Morse has abelian complexity in {2, 3} and Sturmian words have abelian complexity 2, yet both are aperiodic.
formulations.lean: The statement is core Lean; Mathlib has nothing on abelian complexity.
formulations.known_results: Open. Prefix values from 10^7 bits (my computation): a(n) = n+1 for n ≤ 5 and for n = 8 and 16; a(32) = 29, a(64) = 39, a(128) = 55, a(256) = 74, a(512) = 107, a(1024) = 144, a(4096) = 266, a(16384) = 516, a(65536) = 874. This growth is what random bits give.
sources: G. Richomme, K. Saari, L. Q. Zamboni, Abelian complexity of minimal subshifts, J. London Math. Soc. 83 (2011) 79–95, arXiv:0911.2914, https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.2914

formulations.name: No eventually constant arithmetic progression (anti-Toeplitz), and Problem 2 along progressions
formulations.statement: A: for every P ≥ 1 and every r < P, k ↦ c(r + kP) is not eventually constant, so c has no Toeplitz-type skeleton. B (Problem 2 along progressions): for every P ≥ 1 and r < P, the 1s have density 1/2 among c(r), c(r+P), c(r+2P), …. Then B ⟹ A ⟹ Problem 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A ⟹ Problem 1 by the decimation form, which needs only one non-constant class per modulus where A asks for all of them. B ⟹ A because an eventually constant class has density 0 or 1. Strictly stronger: non-periodic Toeplitz sequences (Jacobs–Keane) satisfy Problem 1, yet every position lies on an eventually constant progression. Normal sequences satisfy B by Wall's theorem (1949): normality survives restriction to arithmetic progressions.
formulations.lean: Both are core-Lean statements, and A ⟹ Problem 1 follows at once from Scratch2.problem1_iff_decimations.
formulations.known_results: Both are open. The P = 1 case of A is proved (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant). The P = 2 case of A asks that neither c(2k) nor c(2k+1) be eventually constant. As far as I know it is open, and it is stronger than excluding eventual period 2, which the project reduced to Q01. Data (my computation, 10^7 bits): the worst class mod P ≤ 64 has density 0.504454 (P = 63, r = 1, |z| = 3.55 over 2080 classes), and the overall density is 0.500222. Project brief: 500,025,038 ones in the first 10^9 bits (1.6 sd).
sources: K. Jacobs, M. Keane, 0-1-sequences of Toeplitz type, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Geb. 13 (1969) 123–131
T. Downarowicz, Survey of odometers and Toeplitz flows, Contemp. Math. 385 (2005) 7–37
D. D. Wall, Normal numbers, PhD thesis, University of California, Berkeley, 1949
Project research/BRIEF.md (data section)

formulations.name: Positive Besicovitch distance from periodic sequences
formulations.statement: Let d_B(c, e) = limsup_N (1/N)·#{t < N : c(t) ≠ e(t)}. Statement: the infimum of d_B(c, e) over periodic e is positive. A weaker variant that still suffices: no quasi-generic measure of c (weak-* limit point of (1/N)·Σ_{t<N} δ_{σ^t c}) is a periodic-orbit measure.
formulations.proof_of_relation: An eventually periodic c agrees with a periodic e from T on, so d_B(c, e) = 0, and its only quasi-generic measure is the uniform measure on the periodic orbit. Strictly stronger: a periodic sequence changed on an infinite set of density 0 is not eventually periodic, yet its distance to that periodic sequence is 0. For a normal c, d_B(c, e) = 1/2 for every periodic e, by Wall's theorem.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure with its weak-* topology, and birkhoffAverage. Missing: the Besicovitch pseudometric and quasi-generic measures.
formulations.known_results: Open. My computation on bits [5·10^6, 10^7): for every P ≤ 1024, the best agreement with a P-periodic sequence is at most 0.505942 (at P = 1014). Normalized by the mean excess of random bits, sqrt(P/(2πL)), the excess averages 1.003 over P ≤ 1024 and is at most 1.64 (at P = 1). That is exactly the random-model size.
sources: F. Blanchard, E. Formenti, P. Kůrka, Cellular automata in the Cantor, Besicovitch and Weyl topological spaces, Complex Systems 11 (1997) 107–123
D. D. Wall, Normal numbers, PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1949

formulations.name: Positive entropy, or uncountable orbit closure
formulations.statement: h(c) = lim_n (1/n)·log p_c(n), the topological entropy of σ on X̄_c, is positive. A weaker statement that still implies Problem 1: X̄_c is uncountable (has a nonempty perfect kernel).
formulations.proof_of_relation: h > 0 ⟹ X̄_c is uncountable: on a countable compact system every invariant measure is atomic, so h = 0 by the variational principle. Uncountable ⟹ infinite ⟹ Problem 1, by the orbit-closure entry. Both statements are strictly stronger than Problem 1: Sturmian words have h = 0 and are aperiodic, and 0 1 0² 1 0³ 1 ⋯ is aperiodic with a countable orbit closure. Also h_top(X̄_c) = h_top(ω(c)), because every invariant measure on X̄_c gives full mass to ω(c): orbit points outside ω(c) are non-periodic, so they would need infinitely many atoms of equal mass. This last identity is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has Dynamics.coverEntropy, Dynamics.coverEntropyInf and Dynamics.netEntropyEntourage, the Bowen–Dinaburg entropy of a subset under a map (Mathlib/Dynamics/TopologicalEntropy/CoverEntropy.lean, NetEntropy.lean, Semiconj.lean, Subset.lean). So 'coverEntropy (shift 1) X̄_c > 0' can already be stated. Missing: the block-count formula h = lim log p(n)/n for subshifts, and the variational principle.
formulations.known_results: Open. Only prefix data exist: p_c(n) = 2^n for n ≤ 19 in the first 10^7 bits. The conjecture is h = log 2, i.e. X̄_c is the full shift.
sources: D. Lind, B. Marcus, An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding, CUP 1995
S. Ferenczi, Complexity of sequences and dynamical systems, Discrete Math. 206 (1999) 145–154
P. Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory, GTM 79, Springer 1982 (variational principle)

formulations.name: Disjunctive (rich) center column
formulations.statement: Every finite binary word occurs in c: p_c(n) = 2^n for all n, i.e. X̄_c = {0,1}^ℕ (x_c is disjunctive in base 2).
formulations.proof_of_relation: For large n, 2^n exceeds the bound T + P from the Morse–Hedlund entry. The statement is strictly stronger than Problem 1 (consider Sturmian words). Each instance 'all 2^n words occur' is Σ₁ and finitely checkable; the whole statement is Π₂.
formulations.lean: The statement is core Lean; Mathlib adds nothing specific.
formulations.known_results: Open. It holds for n ≤ 19 in the first 10^7 bits. There, 96 words of length 20 are missing (for example 00000010101111110100, found by the project's mh-rigor-verify); random bits would miss about 76.
sources: Project research/mh-rigor-verify (recount.py)
C. Calude, L. Priese, L. Staiger, Disjunctive sequences: an overview, CDMTCS Research Report 063, 1997

formulations.name: Normality of c; genericity of the single seed for rule 30
formulations.statement: N: every u ∈ {0,1}^k has frequency 2^{−k} in c; that is, c is generic for the uniform Bernoulli measure, and x_c is normal in base 2. G: δ₀ is a generic point of (rule 30, μ), with μ the uniform Bernoulli measure on {0,1}^ℤ, i.e. (1/N)·Σ_{t<N} δ_{F^t δ₀} → μ weak-*. G ⟹ N ⟹ Problem 1 and Problem 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation: N ⟹ disjunctive ⟹ Problem 1, and N ⟹ Problem 2 (take k = 1). G ⟹ N: Tr_{0} is a continuous factor map that sends μ to the uniform Bernoulli measure on {0,1}^ℕ. By left-permutivity, (F^t x)_0 = x_{−t} xor h_t(x_{−t+1}, …, x_t), so for a fixed right half the map x_{[−n,0]} ↦ (Tr_{0} x)_{[0,n]} is a triangular bijection. This is my own reasoning; it is the measure form of Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique. Empirical measures push forward along Tr_{0} because Tr_{0}∘F = σ∘Tr_{0}. Strictly stronger than Problem 1 (Sturmian words).
formulations.lean: Mathlib has MeasureTheory.Measure.infinitePi and infinitePiNat (Mathlib/Probability/ProductMeasure.lean), birkhoffAverage (Mathlib/Dynamics/BirkhoffSum/Average.lean), Ergodic and MeasurePreserving. Missing: normal numbers (grep found none), Borel's normal number theorem, the pointwise ergodic theorem (grep found only the mean ergodic theorem, Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/MeanErgodic.lean) and cellular automata.
formulations.known_results: Open. Wolfram (1986, 2019) reports that c passes standard randomness tests. The project brief reports 500,025,038 ones in 10^9 bits and uniform-looking block statistics. My 10^7-bit counts: every word of length ≤ 19 occurs, and the longest return time to a word of length k ≤ 16 is 0.75–1.47 × 2^k·ln N, as for random bits. By the pushforward argument above, the trace Tr_{0}(x) is normal for μ-almost every x, but δ₀ is not a typical configuration.
sources: S. Wolfram, Random sequence generation by cellular automata, Adv. Appl. Math. 7 (1986) 123–169
S. Wolfram, Announcing the Rule 30 Prizes (2019), https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/
M. Shirvani, T. D. Rogers, On ergodic one-dimensional cellular automata, Comm. Math. Phys. 136 (1991) 599–605, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02099076 (checked via Crossref)
É. Borel, Les probabilités dénombrables et leurs applications arithmétiques, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 27 (1909) 247–271

formulations.name: Not automatic / transcendental generating series / not morphic
formulations.statement: (a) c is not 2-automatic; by Christol's theorem this says C(X) = Σ c(t)X^t ∈ F₂[[X]] is transcendental over F₂(X). (b) c is not morphic, i.e. not a coding of a fixed point of a morphism. Either implies Problem 1. Problem 1 itself is equivalent to C(X) ∉ F₂(X), since a power series over a finite field is rational iff its coefficients are eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Eventually periodic sequences are automatic in every base, and morphic. Strictly stronger: Thue–Morse is 2-automatic and aperiodic, and the Fibonacci word is morphic and aperiodic. Context: ultimate periodicity is decidable for morphic sequences (Harju–Linna 1986 and Pansiot 1986 for D0L; Durand 2013 and Mitrofanov 2013 for HD0L). So a substitutive description of c would turn Problem 1 into a finite computation. Durand 1998: a uniformly recurrent sequence is primitive substitutive iff it has finitely many derived sequences.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has PowerSeries, RatFunc and Polynomial, so algebraicity can be stated, and it has DFA. Missing: automatic sequences, Christol's theorem and morphic words.
formulations.known_results: Open. The only quantitative result I found is the 2-DFAO lower bound of 8191 states (Nersissian 2026, unrefereed).
sources: G. Christol, T. Kamae, M. Mendès France, G. Rauzy, Suites algébriques, automates et substitutions, Bull. SMF 108 (1980) 401–419, http://www.numdam.org/item/BSMF_1980__108__401_0/
T. Harju, M. Linna, On the periodicity of morphisms on free monoids, RAIRO ITA 20 (1986) 47–54, https://www.numdam.org/item/ITA_1986__20_1_47_0.pdf
F. Durand, Decidability of the HD0L ultimate periodicity problem, RAIRO ITA 47 (2013) 201–214, https://doi.org/10.1051/ita/2013035, arXiv:1111.3268
I. Mitrofanov, Periodicity of morphic words, arXiv:1110.4780 (Fundam. Prikl. Mat. 18(4) (2013) 107–119)
F. Durand, Discrete Math. 179 (1998) 89–101, arXiv:0807.3322

formulations.name: Every nonzero finite configuration has an aperiodic column-0 trace (GP1)
formulations.statement: For every configuration x ∈ {0,1}^ℤ with finite nonzero support, t ↦ (F^t x)_0 is not eventually periodic, where F is rule 30. A stronger version asks the same for every column.
formulations.proof_of_relation: δ₀ is one such x. Measure and category arguments cannot help. The finite configurations form a countable, μ-null, dense, F-invariant set. Meanwhile E = {x : Tr_{0}(x) eventually periodic} is a dense, meager, μ-null F_σ set. It is dense because any cylinder contains a point realizing any column with any right half (Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique). It is meager because each E_{T,P} is closed with empty interior. These facts are my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: The project has Rule30Realization.evol (rule 30 on arbitrary configurations), Rule30DrivenLeft and Rule30WhiteSeed. Mathlib has nothing on cellular automata.
formulations.known_results: Open. Period 1 is known for every finite configuration (Condrey 2026, unrefereed, consistent with Jen 1986 Thm 7a) and for every column of the seed (Rule30Prize.no_column_eventually_constant). Width 2 is known for every number-like configuration (Kopra 2023). A project search found no nonzero finite configuration supported in [−9, 9] whose center column is periodic with period ≤ 512 on times [1024, 2048) (research/lit-recent, finite_configs.c). The round-1 Left-half Conjecture implies this statement.
sources: D. L. Condrey, Finite Configurations Cannot Generate a Constant Trace in Rule 30, arXiv:2609.09431 (unrefereed), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09431
Project research/lit-recent/NOTES.txt and research/results/round1.json

formulations.name: Not purely periodic (the T = 0 case)
formulations.statement: For no P ≥ 1 is c(t+P) = c(t) for all t ≥ 0, i.e. σ^P c ≠ c. If c is recurrent (every factor occurs infinitely often), this is equivalent to Problem 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: This is the T = 0 case of Problem 1. Under recurrence: if c is periodic from T with period P, the prefix c[0, T+P) reoccurs at some i ≥ T, inside the periodic tail. So the prefix has period P as well, and c is purely periodic. This argument is my own reasoning.
formulations.lean: Core Lean; the implication from Problem 1 is one line.
formulations.known_results: Open in general. P ≥ 16359 is kernel-checked (Rule30FactorWindow with T = 0). Data (my computation): every prefix c[0, k) with k ≤ 26 reoccurs within the first 10^7 bits, and c[0, 26) first reoccurs at t = 2,085,567.
sources: Project: Rule30FactorWindow.lean
Own computation, scratch stats2.py

formulations.name: Recurrence and uniform recurrence of c
formulations.statement: R: every factor of c occurs infinitely often (c ∈ ω(c)). UR: every factor occurs with bounded gaps (X̄_c is minimal).
formulations.proof_of_relation: As statements about sequences, neither R nor UR implies or follows from Problem 1: periodic words are uniformly recurrent, and aperiodic words need not be recurrent. Links: R together with 'not purely periodic' implies Problem 1 (see the T = 0 entry). A normal sequence is R but not UR, because it contains every 0^n and the only minimal subshift containing all 0^n is {0^∞}. So the conjectured truth for c is R and not UR, and any proof route through UR would contradict normality.
formulations.lean: Mathlib states MulAction.IsMinimal (Mathlib/Dynamics/Minimal.lean) and topological transitivity (Mathlib/Dynamics/Transitive.lean) for monoid actions, so a single map needs the ℕ-action by iterates. Mathlib has no recurrence notions for sequences.
formulations.known_results: Both are open. Data (my computation): within 10^7 bits, the longest return time to any word of length k ≤ 16 is at most 0.75–1.47 × 2^k·ln N, as for random bits, and every prefix of length ≤ 26 recurs.
sources: H. Furstenberg, Recurrence in Ergodic Theory and Combinatorial Number Theory, Princeton 1981
F. Durand 1998, arXiv:0807.3322
L. Vuillon, European J. Combin. 22 (2001) 263–275

formulations.name: Problem 2 in words-and-dynamics form
formulations.statement: Problem 2 ⟺ x_c is simply normal in base 2 ⟺ every quasi-generic measure ν of c satisfies ν([1]) = 1/2. As statements about sequences, Problems 1 and 2 are independent: (01)^∞ has density 1/2, and Sturmian words with slope ≠ 1/2 are aperiodic. Problem 2 along all arithmetic progressions does imply Problem 1 (see the anti-Toeplitz entry).
formulations.proof_of_relation: The frequency of 1s in c[0, N) is the mass of the clopen cylinder [1] under the N-th empirical measure. The space of probability measures on {0,1}^ℕ is compact, so the frequency tends to 1/2 iff every limit point gives [1] mass 1/2.
formulations.lean: The project has Rule30Prize.Problem2 (integer form). Mathlib has MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure and birkhoffAverage. Missing: quasi-generic measures and simple normality.
formulations.known_results: Open. There are 500,025,038 ones in the first 10^9 bits (project brief), and the fraction in the first 10^7 bits is 0.500222 (my count).
sources: S. Wolfram 2019, https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/
L. Kuipers, H. Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences, Wiley 1974

perspectives: Language versus tail. Every complexity reformulation (Morse–Hedlund, special factors, Rauzy graphs, return words) is decided by the tail language L∞(c), which no finite computation reaches. Finite data can certify each instance 'no eventual period with T + P ≤ N', a Σ₁ fact; Rule30FactorWindow does this for N = 16358. Problem 1 needs only the Sturmian threshold p∞(n) ≥ n+1, while every computed prefix shows 2^n. So the gap is not quantitative: what is missing is a mechanism tying the tail of c to the rule.

Generic point versus special point. Rule 30 is surjective and left-permutive, so it preserves the uniform Bernoulli measure μ (Hedlund 1969). It is strongly mixing for μ. Shirvani–Rogers 1991 state this for permutive two-state CA, though I read only secondary citations. My own short proof: for cylinders on [−k, k] and n > 2k, the triangular structure of F^n makes (F^n x)_{[−k,k]} uniform and independent of x_{[−k,k]}. Shereshevsky 1992 proves the natural extension is K or Bernoulli under one-sided neighbourhood conditions; rule 30's [−1, 1] neighbourhood needs a moving frame to meet them. Rule 30 is rapidly left-expansive (Kopra 2023). Its topological entropy lies between log 2 (the column factor is the full 2-shift) and 2·log 2 (radius 1); I found no source with the exact value. The column trace sends μ to the uniform Bernoulli measure. So μ-almost every configuration, and also a comeager set of them, has a normal (hence aperiodic and balanced) center trace. The single seed lies in the countable μ-null set of finite configurations, which these arguments never see. Compare: the doubling map is ergodic (Mathlib's AddCircle.ergodic_nsmul), yet this says nothing about the digits of any particular number.

Width of traces, from Jen to Kopra. Width-2 traces are aperiodic for every number-like configuration, by rapid left expansivity (Jen 1986; Kopra 2023). Width 1 is open; Kopra lists it as a problem. Rules 90, 150 and 210 share all of this width-2 structure, yet their center columns are eventually constant (Rule30Realization.barrier). For the ×p/q fractional multiplication automata width 1 is known (Kopra 2021, arXiv:2005.05112), because they are left-expansive with width 1. Problem 1 therefore sits next to Mahler-type questions about digits of (p/q)^n. A related preprint is R. Stephan, arXiv:2607.14774 (unrefereed; I read only the abstract): quantitative aperiodicity and p(n) ≥ n+1 for the low-order binary digits of 3^m.

Odometer and Toeplitz frame. In the frame of the right diagonals, the seed's orbit closure is the 2-adic odometer (Coven–Pivato–Yassawi 2007, arXiv:math/0511030). Each right diagonal R_j(t) = cell(t, t−j) is periodic from t = 0, with least period 2^{e_j} and e_j ≈ 0.43·j (project data for j ≤ 74; Rule30Diagonals.R_periodic proves the period divides 2^j). Left diagonals are eventually periodic with transients T_j > j. The center column c(t) = R_t(t) = D_t(t) is the diagonal of this Toeplitz-like array. For 3 ≤ t ≤ 74 it reads each right diagonal inside its first period; Nersissian's unrefereed bound on least periods gives 'within the first two periods' for all t. It also reads each left diagonal inside its transient. That is why diagonal periodicity cannot reach c. Toeplitz sequences also explain why the decimation form needs only one non-constant class per modulus, and why the anti-Toeplitz statement is the natural strengthening.

Sturmian contrast and renormalization. Sturmian words are the extremal aperiodic words: p(n) = n+1, exactly two return words per factor (Vuillon 2001), and they are codings of irrational rotations. c is as far from them as possible at every computed scale (p = 2^n for n ≤ 19; abelian complexity n+1 for n ≤ 16). Problem 1 is invariant under passing to derived sequences and under permutive recodings. This renormalization closes up only for substitutive words, which have finitely many derived sequences (Durand 1998); for those, ultimate periodicity is decidable (Harju–Linna, Pansiot, Durand 2013, Mitrofanov). Nothing suggests c is substitutive.

Logic and automata. Problem 1 ⟺ the set of black times is not Presburger-definable; I machine-checked this against Mathlib. Problem 1 ⟺ c is not both 2- and 3-automatic (Cobham). Stronger statements: c is not 2-automatic (by Christol, the series is transcendental over F₂(X)), and c is not morphic. Cervelle–Formenti–Guillon 2010 prove that properties of cellular-automaton traces which are stable under ultimate coincidence are undecidable in general, and eventual periodicity is such a property. That is a uniform statement over all automata and does not bar a proof for rule 30. It does mean any proof must use structure specific to rule 30, and the project's barrier theorems show that every structural fact used so far is shared by rules with eventually constant center columns.

Ladder of strengthenings (my synthesis). Problem 1 is implied by each of: unbounded runs, unbounded abelian complexity, anti-Toeplitz, positive Besicovitch distance, uncountable orbit closure. These follow from positive entropy, which follows from disjunctive, which follows from normal, which follows from the seed being μ-generic for rule 30. On the number side, x_c irrational (Problem 1) is implied by C(X) being transcendental over F₂(X) (c not 2-automatic). Adamczewski–Bugeaud 2007 show that an algebraic irrational has p(n)/n → ∞; so Problem 1 together with linear complexity would make x_c transcendental. Every rung is conjectured true. The only proved results on the ladder are period 1 (no column is eventually constant) and finite windows (T + P ≥ 16359 in the kernel).

Strengthenings to avoid. Several natural strengthenings are probably false, because normal sequences fail them: c uniformly recurrent; X̄_c not sofic, or not an SFT (if c is disjunctive, X̄_c is the full shift); c Toeplitz; Ω(c) minimal.

Space-time as a 2D word. Problem 1 asks that one column of a configuration of the rule-30 space-time subshift of finite type be vertically aperiodic. Jen's theorem rules out vertical eventual periodicity on every strip of width 2. Nivat-type theorems (Cyr & Kra, Nonexpansive Z²-subdynamics and Nivat's conjecture, Trans. AMS 367 (2015) 6487–6537) go the other way, from low rectangular complexity to periodicity. They do not apply here, since the single-seed diagram has exponential pattern complexity.
surveys.notes:
Scope: I covered combinatorics on words and dynamics only. Sibling agents cover number theory, logic, algebra/crypto, CA structure and Wolfram's writings. Where their topics overlap mine (irrationality, Presburger, Cobham, rational power series), I include them only in their word or dynamical form.

What 'difficulty' means here: it rates the proof of the stated relation to Problem 1, not the statement itself. Every stronger or weaker statement in the list is itself open unless its known_results say otherwise.

Machine checks done here (scratch files, not in the catalog):
- /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/words-dynamics/CoreEquiv.lean, core Lean 4.30, no Mathlib. It proves Scratch2.problem1_iff_shift_injective, Scratch2.problem1_iff_decimations and Scratch2.problem1_iff_deriv. Compile with ~/.elan/toolchains/leanprover--lean4---v4.30.0/bin/lean CoreEquiv.lean.
- /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/words-dynamics/PresburgerCheck.lean, against the built Mathlib at /Users/swish/src/mathlib4 (commit c5ea00351c). It proves Scratch.problem1_iff_not_presburger. Run the same lean binary with LEAN_PATH set to .lake/build/lib/lean plus every .lake/packages/*/.lake/build/lib/lean. It takes 8 s and 2.1 GB RSS, and builds nothing.
- All four theorems use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
- rule, cell, EventuallyPeriodic, center and Problem1 are copied verbatim from Rule30Jen and Rule30Prize. Porting the core proofs into the catalog is a rename. The Presburger proof needs a Mathlib-dependent companion project, because the catalog is core-only.

Suggested formalization order for the repository:
1. Done above: shift orbit, decimation, derivative, Presburger.
2. Morse–Hedlund with the sup identity, plus the finite-certificate form, in core Lean. This is the most valuable next target: it subsumes the counting in Rule30FactorWindow and gives the Π₂ certificate form.
3. Gaps and run lengths, once positions of 1s are defined.
4. Irrationality / doubling map, in Mathlib. It needs the missing lemma 'eventually periodic digits ⟺ rational' and uniqueness of expansions that are not eventually constant.
5. ω-limit sets, Rauzy graphs and traces. These need a language-of-subshift API.
6. Cobham is a large project; I do not recommend it.

Data:
- All statistics come from the project's own file /Users/swish/src/wolfram/Ruliology/build/rule30/center-1e7.bin.
- I cross-checked that file against a fresh rule 30 simulation (first 6000 bits) and against the OEIS A327980, A327981 and A327983 prefixes.

- Every prefix statistic looks like random bits, and none bears on any tail statement.
- Correction of my own draft: the best raw agreement with a P-periodic sequence (P ≤ 1024) on the second half is 0.505942 at P = 1014, not 0.5008. That is the random-model size.

Claims that are my own reasoning, not taken from a source:
- sup p_c = T_min + P_min;
- p∞ = P for n ≥ P − 1;
- strong connectivity of the tail Rauzy graphs;
- the non-periodic-point clauses for ω-limit sets;
- π(ω(x)) = ω(π x) for factor maps;
- the trace map sends μ to the Bernoulli measure, and the short proof that rule 30 is mixing;
- E is dense and meager;
- invariant measures on X̄_c are carried by ω(c);
- the entropy bounds for rule 30;
- the general permutive-recoding equivalence;
- the strictness examples.

The sup identity, the p∞ value, the derivative period relation and the decimation criterion were brute-force checked.

formulations.name: Mirror image: rule 86 from a single black cell
formulations.statement: Let cell86 be rule 86 (new cell = right XOR (left OR center)) started from a single black cell at 0. Then cell86(t,p) = cell(t,-p) for all t and p, so its center column is exactly c(t). Problem 1 holds iff there are no T and P > 0 with cell86(t+P,0) = cell86(t,0) for all t >= T.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Rule 86 is rule 30 with left and right swapped, and the seed is symmetric, so induction on t gives cell86(t,p) = cell(t,-p). This is machine-checked in scratch as R30EquivScratch.cell86_eq, center86 and problem1_iff_86 (axioms propext, Quot.sound). Simulation (scripts/symclass.py, 400 steps) agrees.

formulations.name: Complement conjugates: rules 135 and 149 from a single white cell on a black background
formulations.statement: Rule 135 (new = NOT left XOR (center AND right)) and its mirror rule 149 (new = NOT right XOR (center AND left)), started from a single white cell at 0 on an all-black background, have patterns NOT cell(t,p) and NOT cell(t,-p). Their center column is therefore exactly NOT c(t). Problem 1 holds iff these columns are not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: F135 = NOT o F30 o NOT (complement conjugation), and F149 is the mirror of F135. Induction on t gives the patterns, and eventual periodicity is invariant under complement. Simulation (scripts/symclass.py) confirms that rule 30 and rule 86 from a black seed give c, and rule 135 and rule 149 from a white seed give NOT c.

formulations.name: White-seed problem: column -1 (rules 30 and 86 from a white cell, rules 135 and 149 from a black cell)
formulations.statement: Let c_{-1}(t) = cell(t,-1). Rules 30 and 86 from a single white cell on a black background have center column 0, c_{-1}(0), c_{-1}(1), .... Rules 135 and 149 from a single black cell on a white background have center column 1, NOT c_{-1}(0), NOT c_{-1}(1), .... White-seed Problem 1: c_{-1} is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: In Lean, cellW(t+1,p) = cell(t,p-1) and cell135(t+1,p) = NOT cell(t,p-1); the rule-86 and rule-149 versions follow by mirroring. Jen's theorem for columns 0 and -1 gives Problem 1 OR white-seed Problem 1 (Lean: problem1_black_or_white, problem1_30_or_135). So (Problem 1 iff white-seed Problem 1) is equivalent to (Problem 1 AND white-seed Problem 1): proving the equivalence would solve both. This consequence is my own observation; it is machine-checked in scratch as problem1_iff_column_iff_both with j = -1. As a result, the eight single-seed center columns of the class {30, 86, 135, 149} fall into two families: {c, NOT c} and {c_{-1} delayed one step, its complement} (simulated).

formulations.name: Stripe seeds 1, 11, 101, 1011, 10101, ...: finite seeds with exactly the same center column
formulations.statement: For n >= 0 let s_n be the row whose black cells are exactly the even positions of [0,n) and the position n (s_0 = 1, s_1 = 11, s_2 = 101, s_3 = 1011, s_4 = 10101, ...). Under rule 30, its evolution agrees with the single-seed pattern at every cell (t,p) with p < t. On t <= p < t+n it is the fixed stripe (black iff p is even), and its right edge is at t+n. Hence its center column is exactly c(t) for all t, and Problem 1 holds iff the center column of s_n is not eventually periodic, for any n. The same holds for F^s(s_n), whose center column is c(t+s).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Induction on t with the explicit pattern. The mechanism is my own observation. The stripe ...1010... is a fixed point of rule 30, and it always shows x_p OR x_{p+1} = 1 to its left neighbour (the OR latch that Condrey uses). So the light cone left of the diagonal p = t never sees the stripe. Equivalently, the right diagonals of s_n coincide with those of the seed from index n+1 on. Machine-checked in scratch: R30EquivScratch.evol_stripeSeed, stripeSeed_center, problem1_iff_stripeSeed (axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). Changes on the left never preserve the column: flipping the cell at -m flips c(m) (triangular uniqueness).
formulations.lean: Project: none; the scratch proof uses Rule30Realization.evol for general rows. Scratch: SymSeeds.lean (stripeSeed, pat, pat_left, pat_band, pat_edge, pat_or, evol_stripeSeed, stripeSeed_center, problem1_iff_stripeSeed), about 150 lines of core Lean. Mathlib: not needed.

Among all 4095 rows supported in [-3,8], only s_0..s_8 have a center column eventually equal to c or to NOT c with transient <= 200, checked to t = 800. The pattern identity was checked for n <= 51 up to t = 2500 (scripts/stripeseed.py). Two-cell seeds delta_0 + delta_p with p >= 3 change the center column by t <= 280 (scripts/twocell.py). Not found in any source read.
