formulations.name: No column is eventually periodic, and the barrier for single other columns
formulations.statement: Strong form: for every j in Z, t -> cell(t,j) is not eventually periodic. Single-column form CP(j): column j is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The strong form gives Problem 1 by taking j = 0. Since at most one column is eventually periodic (Jen), the strong form says the one possible exception does not exist. For fixed j != 0, Jen gives Problem 1 OR CP(j), so 'Problem 1 iff CP(j)' is equivalent to 'Problem 1 AND CP(j)'. This is my own observation, machine-checked in scratch (problem1_or_column, problem1_iff_column_iff_both): no other column can be proved equivalent to the center without solving Problem 1. Conversely, 'some column j != 0 is eventually periodic' would imply Problem 1, but it is presumably false.

formulations.name: Diagonals (45-degree lines): the solved analogue
formulations.statement: For every j, the right diagonal R_j(t) = cell(t,t-j) is purely periodic with period 2^j (least period 2^{e_j}, with e_{j+1} - e_j in {0,1}), and the left diagonal D_j(t) = cell(t,j-t) is eventually periodic with period 2^j. The center column is the moving diagonal c(t) = R_t(t) = D_t(t).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Jen 1986, Thm 4 (one-sided rules started from a rightful row have eventually periodic columns; cited via Rowland) and Rowland 2006, Lemma 2 (right-bijective rules give purely periodic columns); in Lean, R_periodic and D_periodic. So the diagonal analogue of Problem 1 has the answer 'periodic', and it says nothing about c: c(t) lies in the first period of R_t whenever c(t) = 1, and in the transient of D_t. In Rowland's shifted frame (rule 86 as a range-[2,0] right-bijective rule) these diagonals are columns and the rule-30 center column is a diagonal. 'Problem 1 for a diagonal' in that frame is therefore Problem 1 itself, only re-coordinatized (own remark).
formulations.lean: Project: Rule30Diagonals.R, D, R_periodic, D_periodic, center_eq_R, center_eq_D, center_eq_parity; Rule30RightPeriods (per_step, shift_formula, restart, center_restart, column_continuity, row_restart). Mathlib: nothing relevant.
formulations.known_results: Right periods: e_j <= floor((2j+1)/3) (project). The period divides 2^{ceil log2 F_{j+2}} (Nersissian 2609.25078). The least period is at least floor((j+1)/2)+1 (Nersissian 2609.25077). Left period records are at 1, 4, 9, 30, 401, 87868 (OEIS A364239), and left periods are unbounded (Nersissian). Wolfram (2019) says that at 45 degrees any sequence must be periodic.

formulations.name: Main diagonal of the right-diagonal array (2-adic odometer)
formulations.statement: Let A: N x N -> Bool be the unique array with A(0,t) = 1, A(1,t) = [t odd], A(j,0) = 0 for j >= 1, and A(j+2,t+1) = A(j+2,t) XOR (A(j+1,t) OR A(j,t)). Then A(j,t) = cell(t,t-j), every row j is purely periodic with period 2^j, and c(t) = A(t,t). Problem 1 holds iff t -> A(t,t) is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: In Lean, R_zero, R_one_succ and R_step give the recurrence, and center_eq_R gives c(t) = R t t. Coven-Pivato-Yassawi: in the frame moving with the right edge (G = shift o F, G(x)_i = x_i XOR (x_{i+1} OR x_{i+2})), the orbit closure of the seed is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer. So t -> (A(j,t))_j extends to a homeomorphism psi from Z_2 onto that orbit closure with psi(x+1) = G(psi(x)), and c(t) = psi(t)_t is the diagonal of an odometer orbit. Algebraic form (Nersissian): A(j,t) is the parity of #{r in S_{j+1} : r is a bitwise subset of t}.
formulations.lean: Project: R, R_zero, R_one_succ, R_step, R_periodic, center_eq_R, center_eq_parity. A standalone array statement takes a few lines. Mathlib: no odometer and no cellular automata (grep). Z_2 exists as PadicInt. Mathlib/Dynamics/SymbolicDynamics/Basic.lean has SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.Subshift, shift, cylinder and Pattern, but no CA.
formulations.known_results: Lean: center_eq_parity, i.e. c(t) is the parity of the number of rows s < t with a black cell at s-t+1 or s-t+2. Nersissian: any LSD-first 2-DFAO generating c needs at least 8191 states (from 131072 bits); his fixed-diagonal theorems explicitly do not reach c.
sources: E. M. Coven, M. Pivato, R. Yassawi, Prevalence of odometers in cellular automata, Proc. AMS 135 (2007) 815-821, arXiv:math/0511030, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511030

formulations.name: Lines of other slopes
formulations.statement: For coprime q >= 1 and |p| < q, the sequence s_{p/q}(n) = cell(qn, pn), or any translate of it, is not eventually periodic. Slope 0 is Problem 1; slopes +-1 (diagonals) are periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: No implication between different slopes is known. Jen's argument rebuilds columns sideways by left-permutivity and does not transfer to non-vertical lines (own remark).

This includes slopes inside the 'ordered' left region. Only slopes +-1 are periodic.

formulations.name: Inverse problem: the center column determines the initial row (Realization)
formulations.statement: For u: N -> Bool, let Lambda(u) be the unique row that is white at every p >= 1 and whose rule-30 evolution has center column u. It exists and is unique by left-permutivity. Lambda(u)(-m) depends only on u(0..m) and flips when u(m) flips, and Lambda(c) is the single seed. Problem 1 holds iff no eventually periodic u has Lambda(u) = single seed. Sideways form: with S(a,b) = (shift(a) XOR (a OR b), a) acting on pairs of time sequences, (col_{i-1}, col_i) = S(col_i, col_{i+1}). Problem 1 says that, for eventually periodic u, the S-orbit of (u, column 1 of the right half driven by u from white) never reproduces the moving left edge (col_{-m} white before time m and black at time m).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique gives existence and uniqueness for every right half and every target column; evol_seed identifies the seed. Machine-checked in scratch: R30EquivScratch.problem1_iff_realization (SymSeeds.lean; axioms propext, Quot.sound). The flip property follows from triangular uniqueness (Condrey, Lemma 1) together with lc_congr.

Missing: the flip (permutivity) property of Lambda as a standalone lemma. Mathlib: not needed.
formulations.known_results: Barriers: seed_perturbation (for every n, some row agreeing with the seed on [-n, infinity) has center column c up to n and white afterwards); Rule30DrivenLeft.barrier_exists and barrier_unique; Rule30ZeroBoundary.edge_region_barrier; Condrey's H(2,w) >= w. Condrey computes Lambda_R of both constant columns for every right half R (alternating or checkerboard left halves). This settles period 1 for finite rows.

formulations.name: 2-adic irrationality of the trace map at 1 (and the real binary number)
formulations.statement: Read a row that is white at p >= 1 as the 2-adic integer X = sum_{m>=0} x_{-m} 2^m, and its center column as C = sum_t c_t 2^t. The trace map Tr_0: X -> C is a bijective isometry of Z_2, and the single seed is X = 1. Problem 1 holds iff Tr_0(1) is not rational. Real form (the user's example): Problem 1 holds iff sum_t c(t) 2^{-t-1} is irrational.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A real number in [0,1], or a 2-adic integer, is rational iff its base-2 digit sequence is eventually periodic (standard). Tr_0 is an isometry because c_t depends only on x_0..x_{-t} (light cone with a white right half) and flips when x_{-t} flips (left-permutivity, triangular uniqueness), so Tr_0 permutes the residues mod 2^n for every n. The same holds for every fixed right half R. In this language, the finite-configuration problem at column 0 says: Tr_R(n) is irrational for every natural number n and every finite R, except (n,R) = (0,0). Condrey's fibers become Tr_R(-1/3) = -1 for every R (the checkerboard 1+4+16+... = -1/3 gives the all-ones trace), and the preimages of the zero trace are rationals such as -2/3 (when R_1 = 1). The 2-adic reformulation and these translations are my own reasoning; a search found nothing on them in the literature.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has Real.ofDigits, Real.digits, Real.ofDigits_digits, Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits and Real.continuous_ofDigits (Mathlib/Analysis/Real/OfDigits.lean), Irrational and irrational_iff_ne_rational (Mathlib/NumberTheory/Real/Irrational.lean), and PadicInt (Z_[p]) with PadicInt.appr, appr_spec, toZModPow, nthHom and nthHomSeq (Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/RingHoms.lean). The project has its ingredients (Rule30Realization.lc_congr, Rule30ZeroBoundary.pivot) but is core Lean without Mathlib.
formulations.known_results: As for Problem 1. In the analogue for Kopra's fractional multiplication automata (x p/q), width-1 traces of number-like configurations are never eventually periodic (Kopra 2021). The reason is that those automata are left expansive with width 1, which rule 30 is not: every column is realizable.

formulations.name: Coupled driven halves: a causal fixed point
formulations.statement: For u: N -> Bool, let Lft(u)(t) be cell -1 at time t of rule 30 on p <= -1, started all white and driven at position 0 by the effective boundary e(t) = u(t) AND u(t+1). Let Rgt(u)(t) be cell 1 at time t of rule 30 on p >= 1, started all white and driven at position 0 by u. The equation u(0) = 1, u(t+1) = Lft(u)(t) XOR (u(t) OR Rgt(u)(t)) is causal, and its unique solution is u = c. Problem 1 holds iff this solution is not eventually periodic.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The left half sees the center only through c(t) AND c(t+1) (Rule30MaskedJen.effective_step; Rule30DrivenLeft.cell_eq_L_effective with T = 0). The right half is driven by c (Rule30Ether.cell_eq_drv with T = 0), and the center update is the rule itself. Since u(t+1) depends only on u(0..t), the solution is unique. This packaging of the project's driven-halves framework is my own. Replacing the white starts by arbitrary finite halves gives the finite-configuration problem. Dropping the right half (column 1 arbitrary) gives the left-only relaxations Q01, Q001, C3, C3w and C3s001. Dropping the left half gives the right-only absorption statements, which masked Jen closes.

formulations.known_results: Every period-specific reduction in the project is a relaxation of this system; see the Q01, CQ01, LHC and Absorption entries.

formulations.proof_of_relation: Finite rows are number-like, so NumberLike implies FinConf, which implies Problem 1.

formulations.name: CQ01 is the period-2 case of the finite-configuration problem
formulations.statement: CQ01 (Rule30PeriodTwoCoupled.CQ01) holds iff no row x with finitely many black cells has center column 1,0,1,0,... from time 0. Together with Condrey's Cor 5, this is FinConf for period 2: no nonzero finite row has an eventually 2-periodic column.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Forward: in such a row the effective boundary of the center is white, so the left half is a ZBL orbit whose column -1 is black at even steps. The right half is the half driven by the alternating column, and the center update forces column -1 = NOT column 1 at odd steps. Backward: glue L, a black center and R, and check the rule cell by cell. Machine-checked in scratch: R30EquivScratch2.CQ01_iff_no_finite_alternating (/Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/ca-structure/lean/CQ01Finite.lean; axioms propext, Quot.sound). A prefix-by-prefix check over all 4096 pairs of widths (7,5) also agrees (scripts/cq01check.py). Relations: Q01 implies CQ01 (CQ01_of_Q01), which implies c is not eventually 2-periodic (no_eventual_period_two_of_CQ01). FinConf implies CQ01. Neither CQ01 nor Problem 1 is known to imply the other.

formulations.statement: Q01: no finitely supported start of rule 30 on p <= -1, with position 0 held white, keeps cell -1 black at every even time.

formulations.name: Left-half conjecture for every period (LHC)
formulations.statement: For every primitive word w of length >= 2: no finitely supported start of rule 30 on p <= -1, driven at position 0 by the effective boundary e_w(t) = w(t) AND w(t+1) (indices mod |w|, any phase), has cell -1 at time t equal to NOT w(t+1) at every black phase t of w from some time on.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Suppose c = w^infinity from time T. The row at T restricted to p < 0 is finite. From then on the left half runs driven by e_w (effective_step, cell_eq_L_effective), and a black center cell forces cell -1 = NOT the next center cell (left_of_black). This contradicts LHC(w). Period 1 is excluded separately (no_column_eventually_constant). The same argument works for every left-finite row (using Condrey for period 1), so LHC implies NumberLike, which implies FinConf, which implies Problem 1. Q01 is LHC(10) and Q001 is LHC(001). C3w(011), C3(0001/0011/0111) and C3s001 add right-half skeleton constraints at white phases, so LHC(w) implies each of them.
formulations.lean: Project special cases: Rule30PeriodTwo.Q01; Rule30EtherThree.Q001, C3w, C3s001; Rule30PeriodFourSkeleton.C3, each with its exclusion theorem. The constraint itself is Rule30MaskedJen.left_of_black. Neither the general LHC(w) nor 'LHC implies Problem 1' is formalized.
formulations.known_results: Project round-1 complexity study: exhaustive searches up to support 36 for w = 10, and up to 14-20 for every primitive w of length <= 5, found no survivors; maximal survival was about L divided by the density of 1s in w. Q001 was checked to width 37 and the 011 constraint to width 70 (C programs, not kernel-checked). Finiteness is essential: the stripe and the left part of the period-3 ether are witnesses.

formulations.name: Problem 3 under the same symmetries and seeds; Problem 3 implies Problem 1
formulations.statement: Problem 3 (computing c(n) needs at least O(n) effort) is equivalent to the same question for rule 86 from a black cell, for the stripe seeds s_n, and for rules 135 and 149 from a white cell. An affirmative answer to Problem 3 implies Problem 1.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The columns are identical or complementary, so their computational effort differs by O(1). An eventually periodic column is computable in time O(log n) (read n mod P from a table), which contradicts both the prose and the formal version of Problem 3.
formulations.lean: Not formalizable in the project without a machine model; Problem 3 is not stated in Lean.

perspectives: Symmetry and same-column seeds (own synthesis). Reflection, complement and both map rule 30 to rules 86, 135 and 149. Of the eight single-seed center columns in this class, four are c or NOT c and four are a shifted c_{-1} or its complement. Beyond the symmetries, the OR latch gives an infinite family of finite seeds (1, 11, 101, 1011, ...) with literally the same column. More generally, two finite seeds have eventually equal center columns whenever their right-diagonal families synchronize: two consecutive diagonals agree and all deeper initial values agree. Every right diagonal of a finite row is purely periodic with a 2-power period, so this is a finite check, and it could be used to enumerate the seed's 'same-column class' systematically.

Jen's dichotomy blocks some equivalences (own observation). If A OR B is a theorem, then proving A iff B is as hard as proving A AND B. So column -1 (the white seed, or rule 135 from a black cell), any other column, and any statement already known to hold in disjunction with Problem 1 cannot be proved equivalent to Problem 1 without solving it. Equivalents that can be proved now must stay consistent with c being eventually periodic: symmetries, recodings, same-column seeds, and the inverse-problem and 2-adic restatements.

Uniformity hierarchy: Problem 1 (one seed), then FinConf (all finite rows), then NumberLike (all left-finite rows), then LHC (left half only), each stronger than the last. Every classical partial result (Jen, Kopra's width 2, Condrey's period 1) and every project reduction (Q01, CQ01, C3, Absorption) is uniform over finite or left-finite rows. CQ01 is exactly the period-2 case of FinConf (machine-checked from time 0). So a finite row with a periodic column would refute these reductions without settling Problem 1. Conversely, a proof of Problem 1 that does not also prove FinConf would have to use something specific to the seed's orbit, such as its right-edge odometer structure.

Inverse problems. Left-permutivity makes the trace map from left halves, with any fixed right half, a triangular permutive bijection: an automorphism of the binary tree, or equivalently an isometry of Z_2. Problem 1 asks whether this map sends the 2-adic integer 1 (the seed) to an irrational number. Condrey's theorems compute the preimages of the two constant traces, which are rationals such as -1/3. This places Problem 1 next to Mahler's 3/2 problem and the Kari-Kopra x p/q automata. For those automata the width-1 analogue is solved, because they are left expansive with width 1; rule 30 is not, since every column is realizable (Rule30Realization).

Coupled half-lines. The seed pattern is the unique solution of a causal equation that couples a left half, which sees the center only through c AND shift(c), with a right half driven by c. The period-specific programs each drop one half. Left-only statements (Q01, Q001, C3, C3w) have infinite witnesses: the stripe and the ether. Right-only statements use absorption traps plus masked Jen. The barriers say that each half alone is blind: Realization and seed_perturbation (the right half and any left window), Condrey's H(2,w) >= w, and Rule30ZeroBoundaryBarriers (no local or finite-state ranking proves Q01).

Diagonal and odometer structure. In the right-edge frame, the seed's orbit closure is the 2-adic odometer (Coven-Pivato-Yassawi 2007). All 45-degree lines are periodic (Jen 1986 Thm 4, Rowland 2006), and c is the main diagonal of the odometer array, c(t) = A(t,t). Lines of every other slope look aperiodic numerically. Wolfram (2019) poses them as a family of Problem-1 analogues, but nothing is known to relate different slopes.

Space-time subshift view. The rule-30 space-time diagrams form a Z^2 subshift of finite type in which two adjacent columns determine everything to their left: rule 30 is left expansive with width 2 (Kopra 2023). Problem 1 is the width-1 trace question for a single point. Rowland's Prop 1 gives the seed's diagram a canonical backward extension: the unique history with white right tails, whose rows are ...1110000, then the (100)^infinity row, and so on. In it the center is white at all negative times, so the extension adds nothing.

Barrier rules. Rules 90, 150 and 210 (and 154, the mirror of 210) share left-permutivity, 001 -> 1 and Jen's theorem with rule 30, yet their single-seed center columns are eventually constant (Rule30Realization.barrier). Any proof must therefore use rule 30's OR latch: the mechanism behind Condrey's period-1 theorem, and also the reason the stripe seeds share c.

Finite rings. On a ring of n cells every column is eventually periodic, with periods of roughly 2^{0.63n} from the seed (Wolfram 2019). The ring's center column agrees with c for t <= (n-1)/2, but no finite-size statement is equivalent to Problem 1.

Rowland's Conjecture 1 (2006) is a rigidity statement about the right edge of the same pattern: up to time shifts, the single seed is the only central row with white tails whose right-edge statistic I_R(t) is nonperiodic. It is not known to be related to Problem 1. The stripe seeds, which have the same center column but a different right edge, show that the center column does not determine the right edge.

formulations.name: Existing formal statements of Problem 1 (formal-conjectures, Wolfram's WL statement, our Lean, others)
formulations.statement: All of these say: there are no T ≥ 0 and P ≥ 1 with c(t+P) = c(t) for every t ≥ T. (1) google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, FormalConjectures/Other/Rule30.lean, namespace Rule30, current main = commit 7db2ea3 (2026-10-14, PR #6762). Every declaration in the file: `def step (row : ℤ → Bool) : ℤ → Bool := fun i => xor (row (i - 1)) (row i || row (i + 1))`; `def state : ℕ → ℤ → Bool | 0 => fun i => decide (i = 0) | t + 1 => step (state t)`; `@[simp, category API, AMS 37 68] theorem state_zero (i : ℤ) : state 0 i = decide (i = 0) := rfl`; `@[simp, category API, AMS 37 68] theorem state_succ (t : ℕ) : state (t + 1) = step (state t) := rfl`; `def centerColumn (t : ℕ) : Bool := state t 0`; `@[category test, AMS 37 68] theorem centerColumn_prefix : (List.range 8).map centerColumn = [true, true, false, true, true, true, false, false] := by decide`; `@[category research open, question, AMS 37 68] theorem centerColumn_not_eventually_periodic : ¬ ∃ p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ t : ℕ, N ≤ t → centerColumn (t + p) = centerColumn t := by sorry`; `@[category research open, question, AMS 37 68] theorem centerColumn_frequency_half : {t : ℕ | centerColumn t}.HasDensity (1 / 2) := by sorry`. History of the file: (a) 84063d6, 2026-09-07, PR #4377: both research theorems had the form `answer(sorry) ↔ <statement>` with `@[category research open, AMS 37 68]`, and the file used plain `import FormalConjecturesUtil`; (b) 6fbb54f, 2026-09-18, PR #4688: added the module system (`module`, `public import`, `@[expose] public section`), statements unchanged; (c) 75a6d3d, 2026-10-14, PR #6740: added `question` to both research attributes; (d) 7db2ea3, 2026-10-14, PR #6762: removed `answer(sorry) ↔`. The docstring omits Problem 3 as 'model-relative and has no canonical model-independent phrasing'. (2) Ours: `Ruliology.CellularAutomata.Rule30Prize.Problem1 : Prop := ¬ EventuallyPeriodic center`, where `EventuallyPeriodic f := ∃ T P : Nat, 0 < P ∧ ∀ t, T ≤ t → f (t + P) = f t`. The catalog also has `Rule30StripCertificates.problem1_iff_no_word : Problem1 ↔ ∀ w : List Bool, w ≠ [] → ¬ EventuallyWord w`. (3) Wolfram 2019, in Wolfram Language: `c[t_] := CellularAutomaton[30, {{1}, 0}, {t, {{0}}}]` and `NotExists[{p, i}, ForAll[t, t > i, c[t + p] == c[t]]]`. (4) Dibujaron/rule30 (Lean 4.33 with Mathlib) states the problem with `IsEventuallyPeriodic centerColumn`; its statement files contain sorry.
formulations.proof_of_relation: formal-conjectures against ours: `state t = fun i => cell t i` by induction on t; both use the same rule `xor l (c || r)` and the same seed. After that the statements differ only in quantifier order (∃p ∃N against ∃T ∃P). Wolfram's WL formula, my own reading: c[t] is the list of the first t+1 values. I checked this by evaluating `c[5]`, which returns {1,1,0,1,1,1}. So `c[t+p] == c[t]` compares lists of different lengths and is False whenever p ≠ 0. The formula also does not exclude p = 0, where it is True. Taken literally, the formula is therefore false (p = 0 is a witness), or vacuously true if p is restricted to p ≥ 1. The intended reading is `Last[c[t+p]] == Last[c[t]]` with p ≥ 1, which is what formal-conjectures and our Lean state.
formulations.lean: formal-conjectures defines `Rule30.state`, `Rule30.centerColumn`, `Rule30.centerColumn_not_eventually_periodic` and `Rule30.centerColumn_frequency_half`. Its `Set.HasDensity` is in FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Data/Set/Density.lean and is not in Mathlib: `HasDensity S α := Tendsto (fun b => ((S ∩ A) ∩ Iio b).ncard / (A ∩ Iio b).ncard) atTop (𝓝 α)` with A = univ. Missing: a bridge lemma `state t i = cell t i` and `Problem1 ↔ ¬∃ p, 0 < p ∧ ∃ N, …`, about 10 lines (core Lean plus the formal-conjectures definitions). The parent's library `Rule30Equivalents.Basic.problem1_iff` may already contain it.
formulations.known_results: formal-conjectures checks the first 8 bits (`centerColumn_prefix`, by decide). OEIS A051023 gives c(0..100000) (b-file). The Wolfram Data Repository has a million bits (Wolfram 2017) and a billion bits (Xiangdong Wen 2019). Searches on 2026-10-15 found no Isabelle (AFP) or Coq formalization of rule 30.

formulations.name: Presburger non-definability of the black times
formulations.statement: Let S = {t ∈ ℕ : c(t) = 1}. Problem 1 ⟺ S is not first-order definable in Presburger arithmetic (ℕ, 0, 1, +), with or without parameters. Equivalently, S is not a semilinear set. For comparison, FO(ℕ,<) defines only finite and cofinite sets, so order alone is too weak. MSO(ℕ,<) defines exactly the same subsets of ℕ as FO(ℕ,+), namely the ultimately periodic ones.
formulations.proof_of_relation: The subsets of ℕ definable in (ℕ,+) are exactly the ultimately periodic sets. This follows from Presburger's quantifier elimination, or from Ginsburg–Spanier (definable ⟺ semilinear, and in dimension 1 semilinear ⟺ ultimately periodic). For a Bool sequence, 'S is ultimately periodic' is the same as 'c is eventually periodic'. Mathlib proves the definability theorem, and the bridge is a 10-line case split. I machine-checked the equivalence.
formulations.lean: Mathlib (c5ea00351c) already has: `FirstOrder.Language.presburger`; `FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic : A.Definable₁ presburger s ↔ ∃ k, ∃ p > 0, ∀ x ≥ k, x ∈ s ↔ x + p ∈ s`; `FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable_iff_isSemilinearSet`; `Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic`; `IsSemilinearSet`; `Set.Definable₁` (Mathlib/ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/*). I proved `R30Test.problem1_iff_not_presburger (A : Set ℕ) : Problem1 ↔ ¬ A.Definable₁ presburger {t | center t = true}` in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/logic-computation/lean/PresburgerTest.lean. It compiles in 1.7 s against the built Mathlib with axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Missing in Mathlib: the theory of Presburger arithmetic and its quantifier elimination and decidability, which Presburger/Basic.lean lists as a TODO, and MSO logic.
formulations.known_results: Every finite exclusion transfers verbatim. For example, by Rule30FactorWindow, a Presburger formula defining S would give an eventual period with T+P ≥ 16359. Because the Mathlib theorem allows any parameter set A, even adding every natural number as a constant does not help define S unless Problem 1 fails.

formulations.name: Unary regular language / finite shift orbit / unary DFA (also context-free)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ the unary language L₁ = {1ⁿ : c(n) = 1} is not regular ⟺ L₁ is not context-free ⟺ no deterministic finite automaton with output reading n in unary outputs c(n) for every n ⟺ the shift orbit {(c(n+m))_{m≥0} : n ∈ ℕ} is infinite, that is, c is not a preperiodic point of the shift.
formulations.proof_of_relation: By Myhill–Nerode, the left quotient of L₁ by 1ⁿ is the unary language of the n-th shift of c, and distinct sequences give distinct languages. So L₁ is regular ⟺ c has finitely many shifts. If c has finitely many shifts, pigeonhole gives i < j with equal shifts, so c is eventually (j−i)-periodic from i; the converse is immediate. For context-free: every unary context-free language is regular (Ginsburg–Rice 1962; also a corollary of Parikh's theorem).
formulations.lean: Mathlib has `Language.IsRegular`, `Language.leftQuotient` and `Language.isRegular_iff_finite_range_leftQuotient` (Mathlib/Computability/MyhillNerode.lean, DFA.lean). I proved `R30Test.problem1_iff_not_regular : Problem1 ↔ ¬ (unaryLang center).IsRegular` and the general `R30Test.eventuallyPeriodic_iff_finite_shifts` in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/logic-computation/lean/RegularTest.lean (1.3 s; standard axioms only). Mathlib has `Language.IsContextFree` (ContextFreeGrammar.lean) but neither Parikh's theorem nor Ginsburg–Rice, so the context-free variant is missing. The parent's `Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit` already covers the shift-orbit forms (`problem1_iff_infinite_shifts`, `problem1_iff_not_preperiodic`).
formulations.known_results: Rule30FactorWindow gives T+P ≥ 16359 for any eventual period. A unary DFA with s states produces an eventual period with T+P ≤ s. So no unary DFA with fewer than 16,359 states outputs c, and the shifts c(·+n), n ≤ 16358, are pairwise distinct.

formulations.name: Language of prefixes (regular, context-free, 'determined by a language')
formulations.statement: Let Pref(c) = {c(0)c(1)…c(n−1) : n ∈ ℕ} ⊆ {0,1}*. Problem 1 ⟺ Pref(c) is not regular ⟺ Pref(c) is not context-free ⟺ no infinite context-free language consists only of prefixes of c (c is not 'determined' by a context-free language).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Myhill–Nerode: the left quotient of Pref(c) by a word x is the prefix language of the |x|-th shift if x is a prefix of c, and the empty language otherwise. Prefix languages of distinct sequences are distinct, so regularity ⟺ finitely many shifts ⟺ eventually periodic. I machine-checked this. For context-free: Book (1977) showed, using the context-free pumping lemma, that every context-free prefix language is regular, so an infinite word determined by a context-free language is ultimately periodic (as summarized by Smith 2014).
formulations.lean: I proved `R30Test.problem1_iff_prefixes_not_regular : Problem1 ↔ ¬ (prefLang center).IsRegular` in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/logic-computation/lean/PrefixTest.lean, using the Mathlib names from the previous item. Here `prefLang f := {l | l = (List.range l.length).map f}`; the file compiles in 3.3 s with standard axioms only. The context-free part needs the context-free pumping lemma, which this Mathlib checkout does not have (it only has `Language.IsContextFree`). That part counts as hard: it needs a classical theorem.
formulations.known_results: The minimal DFA for Pref(c), if one existed, would need at least 16,360 states (16,359 distinct shifts plus a dead state).
sources: R. V. Book, On languages with a certain prefix property, Math. Systems Theory 10 (1977) 229–237
M. Latteux, Une note sur la propriété de préfixe, Math. Systems Theory 11 (1977/78) 235–238
T. Smith, On infinite words determined by indexed languages, MFCS 2014; arXiv:1406.3373 (states Book's result)

formulations.name: ω-regular singleton / monadic second-order definability (S1S)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ the ω-language {c} ⊆ {0,1}^ω is not ω-regular (no Büchi automaton accepts exactly c) ⟺ S = {t : c(t) = 1} is not definable in the monadic second-order theory of (ℕ,<), either by a formula φ(x) or as the unique X satisfying a formula ψ(X).
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c = u·v^ω, then {c} = u·v^ω is ω-regular. Conversely, every nonempty ω-regular language contains an ultimately periodic word (take an accepting lasso in a Büchi automaton), so if {c} is ω-regular then c is ultimately periodic. Büchi's theorem (MSO over (ℕ,<) ⟺ Büchi automata) gives the MSO forms.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has no ω-words, Büchi automata or MSO logic. An external Lean 4 project, ctchou/AutomataTheory, has ω-regular languages and Büchi complementation without sorry and is being ported to CSLib. I did not check whether it contains the lasso lemma. With such a library the first form is a short proof; the MSO form needs Büchi's theorem, which is hard and classical.
formulations.known_results: Nothing specific to c. Finite exclusions transfer: a Büchi automaton accepting exactly {c} needs at least 16,359 states, because a lasso of length T+P cannot beat Rule30FactorWindow.

formulations.name: No linear recurrence over any field / infinite linear complexity / non-rational generating series
formulations.statement: For every field K (for example F₂ or ℚ), Problem 1 ⟺ the 0/1 sequence c, read in K, satisfies no linear recurrence c(n+d) = Σ_{i<d} a_i c(n+i) for all n ⟺ Σ c(n)xⁿ ∉ K(x) ⟺ the GF(2) linear-complexity profile L_n(c) (Berlekamp–Massey) is unbounded ⟺ the Hankel determinants det(c(i+j))_{0≤i,j<n} are nonzero for infinitely many n (Kronecker).
formulations.proof_of_relation: If c is eventually periodic, then c(n+T+P) = c(n+T) is a recurrence of order T+P. Conversely, a recurrence makes the window (c(n),…,c(n+d−1)), which lies in the finite set {0,1}^d, determine the future, so pigeonhole and strong induction give eventual periodicity. This works over any field, because 0 ≠ 1 there. Rational series ⟺ linear recurrence is standard. For Berlekamp–Massey: if L_n ≤ L for all n, then for n ≥ 2L any discrepancy would raise the length to n+1−L > L, so one register generates all of c. Kronecker's Hankel criterion characterizes rational series.
formulations.lean: Mathlib has `LinearRecurrence`, `LinearRecurrence.IsSolution`, `LinearRecurrence.charPoly` and `mkSol` (Mathlib/Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean). I proved `R30Test.problem1_iff_no_recurrence : Problem1 ↔ ∀ E : LinearRecurrence K, ¬ E.IsSolution (toK center)` for every field K in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/logic-computation/lean/LinRecTest.lean (1.7 s; standard axioms). The parent's `Rule30Equivalents.PowerSeriesF2` covers ZMod 2 (`problem1_iff_series_not_rational`, `problem1_iff_no_lfsr`, `eventuallyPeriodic_iff_linearComplexity_bounded`). Mathlib has no Berlekamp–Massey and no Kronecker Hankel criterion.
formulations.known_results: My Berlekamp–Massey run on c(0..10⁵−1): L_n stays within 7 of n/2 for every n ≤ 10⁵, and L = 50001 at n = 10⁵. This is the profile of a random sequence. Hence c satisfies no GF(2) linear recurrence, valid from index 0, of order ≤ 50000. The project's research/gf2-algebra studied the linear complexity of the diagonals.
sources: J. L. Massey, Shift-register synthesis and BCH decoding, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 15 (1969) 122–127
L. Kronecker (1881) Hankel criterion for rational series; see e.g. Salem, Algebraic Numbers and Fourier Analysis (1963), ch. I

formulations.name: Lempel–Ziv (1976) complexity of prefixes is unbounded
formulations.statement: Let C_LZ(w) be the Lempel–Ziv 1976 production complexity: the number of components in the exhaustive history of w, where copy sources may overlap the phrase being built. Problem 1 ⟺ C_LZ(c(0)…c(n−1)) → ∞.
formulations.proof_of_relation: My own reasoning. If c is P-periodic from T, every component starting after position T+P copies from P positions back with overlap and never ends, so the count is bounded. If the count is bounded, the last component is infinite: every prefix of the tail is a copy from some start position ≤ h. Some start p₀ works for infinitely many prefixes, hence for all of them, so c(m) = c(m−d) for all m > h with d = h+1−p₀ ≥ 1. The count is nondecreasing in n.
formulations.lean: Nothing in Mathlib. The definitions take about 30 lines; the proof is a pigeonhole argument like the shift-orbit one.
formulations.known_results: My computation: C_LZ(c↾20000) = 1433. A pseudorandom 20000-bit sample gives 1437, and n/log₂n = 1400. The implementation reproduces Lempel–Ziv's example 0001101001000101 → 6, and gives 4 for 111(1101001)^200.
sources: A. Lempel, J. Ziv, On the complexity of finite sequences, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 22 (1976) 75–81

formulations.name: Finite-state prediction (every finite-state predictor errs infinitely often)
formulations.statement: A finite-state predictor is a finite set Q with q₀ ∈ Q, δ : Q×{0,1} → Q and a guess map g : Q → {0,1}. It reads c(0),…,c(n−1), reaches q_n, and guesses g(q_n) for c(n). Problem 1 ⟺ every finite-state predictor guesses wrong for infinitely many n. A stronger, quantitative form is that every finite-state predictor errs with asymptotic frequency 1/2 (finite-state unpredictability); this implies both Problem 1 and Problem 2.
formulations.proof_of_relation: My own reasoning. (⇐) If c is eventually periodic, a predictor whose T+P states count the position up to T and then mod P, ignoring the input, is always right. (⇒) If a predictor is right for all n ≥ N, then q_{n+1} = δ(q_n, g(q_n)) for n ≥ N. That is autonomous dynamics on a finite set, so q_n is eventually periodic, and so is c(n) = g(q_n). For the quantitative form: the constant predictors 'always 1' and 'always 0' have error rates equal to the densities of 0s and 1s, which gives Problem 2. Normality implies finite-state unpredictability (Feder–Merhav–Gutman, Schnorr–Stimm).
formulations.lean: Mathlib's `DFA` has no output map; define predictors directly. Nothing exists yet.
formulations.known_results: None specific to c.
sources: M. Feder, N. Merhav, M. Gutman, Universal prediction of individual sequences, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 38 (1992) 1258–1270
C. P. Schnorr, H. Stimm, Endliche Automaten und Zufallsfolgen, Acta Informatica 1 (1972) 345–359

formulations.name: Cobham: not automatic in two independent bases (and Cobham–Semenov definability)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ c is not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic. More generally, for any multiplicatively independent k, l ≥ 2: Problem 1 ⟺ c is not both k- and l-automatic. In logical form (Büchi–Bruyère plus Cobham–Semenov): Problem 1 ⟺ S is not definable in both Büchi arithmetics (ℕ,+,V₂) and (ℕ,+,V₃), where V_k(x) is the largest power of k dividing x.
formulations.proof_of_relation: An eventually periodic sequence has a finite k-kernel for every k (kernel elements n ↦ c(kᵉn+r) with kᵉ ≥ T are determined by c(r), kᵉ mod P and r mod P), so it is k-automatic for every k. Conversely, Cobham's theorem (1969) says that a sequence that is k- and l-automatic for multiplicatively independent k, l is eventually periodic. Büchi–Bruyère: k-automatic ⟺ definable in (ℕ,+,V_k).
formulations.lean: formal-conjectures has `AutomaticSequence.kKernel` and `AutomaticSequence.IsAutomatic k a := (kKernel k a).Finite` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Computability/AutomaticSequence.lean, Eilenberg's kernel criterion), `AutomaticSequence.IsAutomatic.finite_range` and `isAutomatic_const`. formulations.name: Problem 1 as an effort lower bound for unary input (time and space gap theorems)
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ no one-tape deterministic Turing machine decides {1ⁿ : c(n) = 1} in time o(n log n) ⟺ no deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape decides it in work space o(log log n). Binary-input analogue (strictly stronger than Problem 1): c is not 2-automatic ⟺ no one-tape DTM decides {bin(n) : c(n) = 1} in time o(m log m), where m ≈ log₂ n is the input length.
formulations.proof_of_relation: Combine the unary-regular item with two gap theorems. Trakhtenbrot (1964) and Hartmanis (1968): every language accepted by a one-tape DTM in time o(n log n) is regular; the bound is tight. Stearns–Hartmanis–Lewis (1965): space o(log log n) gives only regular languages. Conversely, a regular language is decided in real time and constant space. This exactly matches Problem 1 to a lower bound on computational effort, in the spirit of Problem 3 but for unary input. The identification is my own; the theorems are classical.

It has no crossing-sequence theory, so neither gap theorem is available.

formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ the structure (ℕ,+,S), with S = {t : c(t) = 1}, defines without parameters an infinite set whose gaps between consecutive elements are unbounded. By Milchior, one fixed formula ν(x), independent of S, defines such a set whenever S is not Presburger-definable.
formulations.proof_of_relation: (⇐) If S is Presburger-definable, every set definable in (ℕ,+,S) is Presburger-definable, hence ultimately periodic, hence has bounded gaps if infinite. (⇒) Michaux–Villemaire (1996): every relation that is not Presburger-definable defines a non-ultimately-periodic subset of ℕ. Milchior strengthened this to a uniform formula defining an expanding set.

formulations.name: Π⁰₂ normal form: total defect function / a machine that beeps infinitely often
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ ∀T ∀P ≥ 1 ∃t ≥ T : c(t+P) ≠ c(t). Equivalently, the defect function W(T,P) = min{d ≥ 0 : c(T+d+P) ≠ c(T+d)} is total. Equivalently, the machine that runs through all pairs (T,P) in order, searches for the defect and beeps when it finds one, beeps infinitely often (it never 'quasihalts', in the sense of Aaronson's Beeping Busy Beaver).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Pure logic. c is primitive recursive: c(t) is bit t of Fᵗ(1), with F(x) = x XOR (2x OR 4x) (OEIS A269160, A110240). So Problem 1 is a Π⁰₂ sentence with a decidable matrix, and its negation, eventual periodicity, is Σ⁰₂. Each instance (T,P) is Σ⁰₁ and can be confirmed by finite computation. Neither Problem 1 nor its negation can in general be settled by finite computation alone. Unlike a Π⁰₁ statement, Problem 1 would not become true merely by being unprovable. For comparison (my own analysis): Problem 2 as stated is Π⁰₃, and Wolfram's literal Problem 3 is Π⁰₂ (∀m ∀B ∃n: machine m on n does not output c(n) within B·n steps).

formulations.name: Irrationality of the binary reading ξ = 0.c(0)c(1)c(2)…₂ = 0.862389783947384… (the user's example), 2-adic and automatic-number variants
formulations.statement: Problem 1 ⟺ ξ = Σ_{n≥0} c(n)·2^{−(n+1)} = 0.86238978394738404864080024608675112810853296362455061526195… (OEIS A365254) is irrational. The same holds for the reading in any base B ≥ 2. 2-adic variant: Problem 1 ⟺ Σ c(n)2ⁿ ∈ ℤ₂ is not in ℚ. Automata-related strengthenings: 'ξ is not an automatic number' (the digit sequence is not k-automatic for any k), and 'ξ is transcendental'.
formulations.proof_of_relation: A real number has an eventually periodic base-B digit sequence iff it is rational: one direction is a geometric series, the other is pigeonhole on remainders. The proven fact that c is not eventually constant rules out the dual expansion ending in 1^∞. The 2-adic analogue (rational ⟺ eventually periodic digits) is classical. Link to automata (Adamczewski–Bugeaud 2007): an irrational algebraic number has block complexity p(n)/n → ∞, while automatic sequences have p(n) = O(n). So if c were automatic and Problem 1 held, ξ would be transcendental.

formulations.name: Π⁰₁ strengthening with an explicit defect bound
formulations.statement: For all T ≥ 0 and P ≥ 1: W(T,P) ≤ 3·log₂(T+P+1). That is, some t with T ≤ t ≤ T + 3·log₂(T+P+1) satisfies c(t+P) ≠ c(t).

With coefficient 2, the expected number of violations grows like ln N, so that version should eventually fail. With coefficient 3 the expected count beyond T+P = 2¹⁶ is about 8·10⁻⁶. formulations.name: Automaticity hierarchy: not k-automatic for any k, transcendental series over F₂(x), not morphic
formulations.statement: (a) c is not k-automatic for any k ≥ 2; for a fixed k, equivalently S is not definable in Büchi arithmetic (ℕ,+,V_k). (b) Christol form for k = 2: Σ c(n)xⁿ is transcendental over F₂(x). (c) Stronger still: c is not morphic ⟺ c is not determined by any indexed language (Smith 2014).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Eventually periodic ⟹ k-automatic for every k (finite kernel) ⟹ morphic (Cobham 1972). So each statement implies Problem 1. Christol (1979; Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy 1980): a sequence over F_p is p-automatic ⟺ its series is algebraic over F_p(x). For the implication alone, 'transcendental ⟹ not rational ⟹ Problem 1' suffices. Strictness: Thue–Morse is 2-automatic and not eventually periodic.
formulations.lean: formal-conjectures has `AutomaticSequence.IsAutomatic`. Missing: `EventuallyPeriodic → IsAutomatic k`, which is easy. For (b) the parent's `PowerSeriesF2.problem1_iff_series_not_rational` gives the implication. Christol, Büchi–Bruyère and Smith's theorem are not formalized anywhere I found.
formulations.known_results: The kernel lower bounds in the Cobham item (at least 65,535 for base 2 and at least 29,524 for base 3). Litow–Dumas (1993) and Rowland–Yassawi (2015): columns of linear CA from finite seeds are p-automatic, and every p-automatic sequence arises this way. Rowland–Yassawi ask whether a non-eventually-periodic 3-automatic sequence can be a column of a nonlinear 2-state CA. If c had a known automaton or morphism, Problem 1 would be mechanically decidable (Honkala 1986 for automatic sequences, e.g. in Walnut; Durand 2013 and Mitrofanov 2011 for morphic words).

formulations.name: Undecidability of the first-order theory of (ℕ,+,S)
formulations.statement: The first-order theory Th(ℕ,+,S), with S = {t : c(t) = 1}, is undecidable. A stronger form: (ℕ,+,S) defines multiplication.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If Problem 1 fails, S is Presburger-definable and Th(ℕ,+,S) is decidable (Presburger 1929). If c is 2-automatic, Th(ℕ,+,S) is also decidable (Büchi; Bruyère et al. 1994). So undecidability implies 'not k-automatic for any k', which implies Problem 1. Plausibility, my own reasoning: if c is disjunctive (every finite word occurs, as it would if c is normal), each finite F ⊆ [0,y) equals {i < y : x₀+i ∈ S} for some x₀. So (ℕ,+,S) can quantify over finite sets. It then defines squaring (z = x² iff some finite F starting 0, 1 has consecutive differences rising by 2 and last difference 2x−1), hence multiplication, hence it is undecidable. Karimov–Nieuwveld–Ouaknine (2026) give a general framework of this kind ('simulating counter machines').
formulations.lean: formal-conjectures has `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsDecidable` and `IsRecursive` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/ModelTheory/Decidability.lean). Mathlib has `FirstOrder.Language.completeTheory` and the Presburger language, but not decidability of Presburger arithmetic, which the implication needs.

formulations.name: Undecidable monadic theory of (ℕ,<,S): a stronger statement that is probably false
formulations.statement: The monadic second-order theory of (ℕ,<,S) is undecidable.
formulations.proof_of_relation: If Problem 1 fails, S is MSO-definable and the theory reduces to S1S, which is decidable (Büchi). Caution, my own reasoning from Semenov's criterion (MTh(ℕ,<,P) is decidable ⟺ P is recursive and has a recursive weak indicator of recurrence): if c is disjunctive, a satisfiable MSO sentence is satisfied by factors at infinitely many positions. The indicator is then computable, because satisfiability over finite words is decidable, so the monadic theory is decidable. Under the normality conjecture this strengthening is therefore false. Monadic decidability does not separate the periodic and random scenarios; use the first-order item instead.

formulations.name: Circuit-complexity strengthening
formulations.statement: Let g_m : {0,1}^m → {0,1} send the binary digits of n < 2^m to c(n). The strengthening: g_m has no Boolean circuits of size O(m). Variant: the family (g_m) is not in non-uniform NC¹.

That gives circuits of size O(m) and membership in NC¹, since regular languages are in NC¹ (Barrington). So a superlinear lower bound implies 'not 2-automatic', which implies Problem 1. 'Not in AC⁰' would not suffice, because a sequence of period 3 needs n mod 3, which is not in AC⁰.

formulations.statement: K(c(0)…c(n−1)) = K(n) + O(1) for prefix complexity, and C(c↾n | n) = O(1). This holds for every computable sequence, periodic or not.

Hence Problem 1 has no formulation in terms of unbounded-resource Kolmogorov complexity: c is trivially K-trivial and is not Martin-Löf random or even computably random. The useful substitutes bound resources. Lempel–Ziv 1976 complexity and linear complexity are exactly equivalent to Problem 1 (separate items); finite-state dimension > 0 is stronger; time-bounded complexity and prediction lead toward Problem 3.

formulations.name: Problem 3 (computational irreducibility), its literal formalization, and what it implies for Problem 1
formulations.statement: Verbal: 'Does computing the nth cell of the center column require at least O(n) computational effort?' Wolfram's formal statement: NotExists m: (ForAll n: machine[m][n][[1]] == Last[c[n]]) ∧ MaxLimit[machine[m][n][[2]]/n, n → ∞] < ∞, that is, 'there does not exist a machine m which for all n gives c[n], and for which the lim sup of the amount of computational effort spent, divided by n, is finite'. Here machine[m][n] = {value, effort}, a Turing machine reads the digits of n, and m must be finite. In terms of c: every Turing machine M that outputs c(n) on input n in binary has limsup t_M(n)/n = ∞ (literal reading), or > 0 (reading 'at least O(n)' as Ω(n)).
formulations.proof_of_relation: Problem 3 implies Problem 1; Wolfram writes: 'If the answer to Problem 3 is affirmative …, then it implies that the answer to Problem 1 must also be affirmative.' If c were P-periodic from T, a Turing machine reading binary n computes n mod P with a finite automaton and looks up c in O(log n) steps, so t(n)/n → 0. That contradicts both readings, and also a unary-input reading, since O(n) steps contradict the literal one. Problem 1 does not imply Problem 3: Thue–Morse-like sequences are aperiodic yet take O(log n) time. Intermediate statements that imply Problem 1: not k-automatic (equivalently not decidable by an automaton on binary n, or in o(log log m) space); not computable in O(log n) time. My own observation on model dependence: on a unit-cost RAM with bitwise operations on unbounded integers, c(n) = bit n of Fⁿ(1), F(x) = x XOR (2x OR 4x), takes O(n) operations. So the literal statement is false in that model, while on Turing machines the naive simulation costs O(n²). This is why the model must be fixed, as Wolfram does ('For definiteness … Turing machine'). The literal statement is Π⁰₂.

Formalizing 'Problem 3 ⟹ Problem 1' requires building an explicit FinTM2 for n mod P on binary input; that is laborious but routine.
formulations.known_results: Open. Wolfram suggests partial results: effort O(n^γ) with γ < 2, and lower bounds such as Ω(log n) time or memory. As stated, Problem 2 is Π⁰₃.
formulations.lean: `Set.HasDensity` is in formal-conjectures (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Data/Set/Density.lean), not in Mathlib. The bridge between our integer form and `HasDensity (1/2)` is routine real analysis; Dibujaron has a proof of a similar equivalence.
formulations.known_results: Open. The first 2²⁰ bits contain 524,976 ones (my count). OEIS A327982 (partial sums) remarks that proving lim a(n)/n = 1/2 solves Problem 2.

perspectives: Formal-language hierarchy. Problem 1 sits exactly at the regular/context-free level, in four equivalent forms: unary regular (Myhill–Nerode) or context-free (Ginsburg–Rice); prefix language regular, or context-free by Book 1977; singleton ω-regular (Büchi). One level up are strictly stronger statements: binary-input regularity is 2-automaticity, and indexed-language determination is morphicity (Smith 2014). Three of these equivalences are now kernel-checked against Mathlib in scratch files.

Definability and decidability. 'S is not Presburger-definable' is exactly Problem 1 and is a one-step corollary of Mathlib's presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic. Büchi arithmetic (ℕ,+,V_k) captures k-automaticity; Cobham–Semenov makes two bases jointly equivalent to Problem 1; Michaux–Villemaire–Milchior gives an 'expanding set' form. Decidability gives the right strengthening in first-order logic: Th(ℕ,+,S) undecidable, which holds if c is disjunctive (my argument). In monadic logic it gives the wrong one: MSO(ℕ,<,S) is decidable both when c is eventually periodic and when c is disjunctive (Semenov's criterion).

Arithmetical hierarchy and proof theory. Problem 1 is Π⁰₂ with a primitive-recursive matrix; c(t) is bit t of Fᵗ(1), F(x) = x XOR (2x OR 4x). It is the totality of the defect function W(T,P), and in Busy-Beaver terms it says a specific machine beeps infinitely often (Π⁰₂, not halting-type Π⁰₁). Explicit Π⁰₁ strengthenings such as W(T,P) ≤ 3·log₂(T+P+1) hold for T+P ≤ 65536 in my computation. A proof of Problem 1 in a standard theory would yield such a bound by proof mining. Literal Problem 3 is also Π⁰₂ and Problem 2 is Π⁰₃.

Computational complexity and irreducibility. Problem 3 (any reading with binary input) implies 'not automatic' implies Problem 1. Problem 1 itself is exactly an effort lower bound for unary input: one-tape time not o(n log n), or space not o(log log n), by the Trakhtenbrot/Hartmanis and Stearns–Hartmanis–Lewis gap theorems. Circuit-size strengthenings of the binary version are far beyond current lower-bound technology. The model matters: on a unit-cost bitwise RAM, c(n) costs O(n) operations, so Wolfram's literal Problem 3 is false there. Wolfram himself notes that known explicit lower bounds are information-theoretic.

Compression, prediction and randomness. Plain and prefix Kolmogorov complexity cannot see Problem 1, since c is computable and K(c↾n) = K(n) + O(1). Resource-bounded measures can. Lempel–Ziv 1976 complexity, GF(2) linear complexity (Berlekamp–Massey) and finite-state prediction are each exactly equivalent. Finite-state dimension > 0, disjunctiveness and normality are strictly stronger, and normality also gives Problem 2. On prefixes up to 10⁵ bits the center column behaves like a random sequence: LZ 1433 against 1437, L_n = n/2 ± 7.

Number-theoretic readings via automata. ξ = 0.c(0)c(1)…₂ (A365254) is irrational ⟺ Problem 1, and the parent's library proves this for any base. The 2-adic analogue holds as well. Christol: the series Σ c(n)xⁿ is rational over F₂ ⟺ eventually periodic, and algebraic ⟺ 2-automatic. Adamczewski–Bugeaud: if c were automatic, Problem 1 would force ξ to be transcendental.

Linear and nonlinear CA. Columns of linear CA (rules 90 and 150) from finite seeds are p-automatic (Litow–Dumas; Rowland–Yassawi), so their eventual periodicity is decidable through rationality. The project's barrier theorem shows rules 90, 150 and 210 share rule 30's structural facts but have eventually constant centers. Rowland–Yassawi's open question, whether a non-eventually-periodic automatic sequence can be a column of a nonlinear 2-state CA, marks the frontier. Moore-style decomposition methods explicitly fail for rule 30.

Decision procedures for structured candidates. If c had any automatic or morphic description, Problem 1 would be mechanically decidable: Honkala 1986 for automatic sequences (and Walnut), Durand 2013 and Mitrofanov 2011 for morphic words. The kernel bounds of at least 65,535 states in base 2 and 29,524 in base 3 indicate that no small automaton exists.

Cryptographic view. Rule 30 was proposed as a stream cipher and PRNG (Wolfram 1985/1986) and was attacked by Meier–Staffelbach (EUROCRYPT 1991) through left-permutivity: the center column and the right half determine the left half. That is the same fact as the project's Rule30Realization, and it runs in the 'easy' direction opposite to Problem 3.

Formalization infrastructure. Mathlib (c5ea003) already contains the hard part of three equivalences: Presburger definability ⟺ ultimate periodicity, Myhill–Nerode, and LinearRecurrence. formal-conjectures' ForMathlib layer supplies definitions for automatic sequences, automatic and normal numbers, block complexity and entropy, decidable theories, and the complexity classes P, NP and BPP. Big missing theorems: Cobham, Christol, Büchi (S1S), Book, Ginsburg–Rice and Parikh, Presburger decidability and quantifier elimination, and the one-tape and sublog-space gap theorems.

# Rule 30 Prize, Problem 1: a catalog of equivalent, stronger, weaker and related problems

Merged on 2026-10-15 from six surveys, each written from one angle:

1. Wolfram's writings.
2. Number theory.
3. Algebra, coding and cryptography.
4. Combinatorics on words and dynamics.
5. Cellular-automaton (CA) structure.
6. Logic and computation.

For this merge, every classification was re-derived and every Lean statement was typechecked against Mathlib `c5ea00351c` (2026-05-26), the core catalog `VibeProof/Rule30Prize/lean`, and the equivalents library `VibeProof/Rule30Prize/equivalents`. Section 10 lists what was checked and where the files are.

---

## 0. The problem and the conventions

**Problem 1.** Let c(t) be the center cell at time t of rule 30 started from a single black cell. The update is new = left XOR (center OR right). The column begins c = 11011100110001011001001110101110011101010110000110010101101… (OEIS A051023). Problem 1 says c is not eventually periodic (EP):

```lean
-- lean/Ruliology/CellularAutomata/Rule30Jen.lean and Rule30Prize.lean (core Lean, no Mathlib)
def Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (f : Nat → Bool) : Prop :=
  ∃ T P : Nat, 0 < P ∧ ∀ t, T ≤ t → f (t + P) = f t
def Rule30Prize.center (t : Nat) : Bool := Rule30Jen.cell t 0
def Rule30Prize.Problem1 : Prop := ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic Rule30Prize.center
```

Problems 2 and 3 are in Section 7.

**Relations.**
- *Equivalent*: provably ⟺ Problem 1. Proving the equivalence does not solve the problem.
- *Stronger*: implies Problem 1. Every stronger statement listed is open.
- *Weaker*: implied by Problem 1.
- *Related*: no implication is known.

**Difficulty** rates how hard it is to machine-check the *relation*, not the problem.

**Status labels.**
- **Library**: proved in the untracked Mathlib-based Lake project `VibeProof/Rule30Prize/equivalents`, namespace `Rule30Equivalents`. It has 25 `problem1_iff_*` theorems, no `sorry`, and uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; see `scripts/CheckAxioms.lean`.
- **Catalog**: proved in the core-Lean snapshot `VibeProof/Rule30Prize/lean`.
- **Scratch proof**: a complete, axiom-clean proof exists in a scratch file (Section 10). Porting it is mechanical.
- **Stated**: the Lean statement below typechecks, with `sorry`.
- **Sketch**: the statement needs a definition that Mathlib lacks.

All Lean below assumes `open Ruliology.CellularAutomata` and `import Rule30Equivalents`, plus the Mathlib modules named under "Mathlib".

**The common pattern.** Every equivalence here is an instance of a general theorem: `∀ b : ℕ → Bool, EventuallyPeriodic b ↔ X b`, specialized to `b = center`. Only a few need a fact about rule 30 itself: that c is not eventually constant (`Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant`). Those are the forms blind to constant tails, such as greedy binary digits, gaps and run lengths.

Three mechanisms produce almost every entry:

1. **Pigeonhole on a finite state.** The state is a shift, a remainder mod q, a recurrence window or an automaton state.
2. **Digit expansions.** A number is rational iff its digits are eventually periodic. This holds in ℝ, ℚ_p and F_q((1/X)).
3. **Definability.** The ultimately periodic subsets of ℕ are exactly the Presburger-definable, semilinear, unary-regular, MSO(ℕ,<)-definable and Büchi-recognizable ones.

## 2. Formalization priority and repository plan

**Ranking.** Priority is value times ease.

- **Value** is high when the statement is classical and recognizable in another field, is a hub that other entries reduce to, links the project to Mathlib or formal-conjectures, or could become an attack route.
- **Ease** is the length of the proof, given Mathlib and the existing library.

Completed items keep their rank. The user's example ranks first. The list of first targets starts with it, because it is machine-checked but still untracked and needs committing, followed by the best items that are not yet done:

1. binary-irrational: done (Library). Commit it. Its generic lemma `eventuallyPeriodic_iff_not_irrational` is the hub for items 2, 10, 11, 12 and 39.
2. base-b-irrational: add the 15-line `Real.ofDigits` bridge (scratch proof) and the one-line `cantorFunction` corollary.
3. fc-bridge: scratch proof. It makes the project's `Problem1` provably the formal-conjectures statement.
4. presburger: scratch proof, 3 lines on top of Mathlib's `definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic`.
5. circle-rotation: two parts are proved in scratch; the doubling-map part needs about 20 lines.
6. continued-fraction: scratch proof, 5 lines.
7. dirichlet-liouville: the Dirichlet part is proved in scratch; LiouvilleWith 2 needs about 20 lines.
8. orbit-closure: scratch proof, 6 lines.
9. pi2-normal-form: the Π⁰₂ part is proved in scratch; the k! part is about 10 lines.
10. two-adic: about 100 lines (integer congruence form first).
11. integer-digits: the core-Lean (Mathlib-free) version of the user's example, for the core catalog.
12. rational-any-field: the recurrence form is proved in scratch; the power-series form generalizes PowerSeriesF2.
13. regular-languages: scratch proofs exist.
14. simple-transforms: derivative proved in scratch; parity and shift are easy.
15. decimations: one form proved in scratch.
16. stripe-seeds: scratch proof.
17. realization: scratch proof.

After that, in priority order:
- **Easy:** special-factors, finite-certificates, nks-integer-rows, diagonal-array, finite-state-machines, nlfsr, return-words, fcsr-complexity.
- **Moderate:** p-recursive, the easy half of hankel, coupled-halves, omega-limit, tail-language, omega-regular, lz76.
- **Classical-theorem projects** (each is also a Mathlib contribution): Kronecker (hankel), Fatou, Lagrange, Parikh and Book (context-free), Szegő and Pólya–Carlson (natural-boundary), Christol and Cobham, the gap theorems.

**Proposed repository layout.** Every file proves a general statement `∀ b : ℕ → Bool, EventuallyPeriodic b ↔ X b` and specializes it to c.

- `Basic.lean` (exists): add an `EventuallyPeriodic` API with transfer lemmas (equal or complemented sequences, index shift, period multiples).
- `BinaryIrrational.lean` (exists): add the `Real.ofDigits` and `cantorFunction` bridges. The integer-digits form could also go into the core catalog.
- `Diophantine.lean` (new): continued fraction, Dirichlet, LiouvilleWith, circle and doubling map; Lagrange later.
- `Padic.lean` (new): the 2-adic and p-adic forms, and FCSR complexity.

- `Logic.lean` (new): FC bridge, Π⁰₂ form, Presburger, regular languages, finite-state machines, NLFSR, LZ76, Büchi.
- `Classical/` (long term): the named classical theorems.

**Candidates for upstreaming to Mathlib:**
- `Real.ofDigits d` is rational iff d is eventually periodic, for arbitrary digits ℕ → Fin b.
- Morse–Hedlund.
- An eventually-periodic predicate.
- Finite-valued power series are rational iff eventually periodic.

---

## 3. Equivalent formulations, grouped by field

Where an entry uses x₂ it means `noncomputable abbrev x₂ : ℝ := ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℝ) else 0) / 2 ^ (t + 1)`; this is definitionally `Rule30Equivalents.BinaryIrrational.centerBinary`. Where it uses `series K` it means `noncomputable def series (K : Type*) [Field K] : PowerSeries K := PowerSeries.mk fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : K) else 0`.

### 3.1 Restatements and bookkeeping

**[7] eventual-word: no eventual word.**
- *Statement.* For no nonempty word w and no time T is c(T+n) = w[n mod abs(w)] for all n. So Problem 1 is the conjunction, over primitive words w, of "c is not eventually w w w …". The project's period-specific reductions attack these conjuncts one at a time.
- *Lean* (Catalog):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_no_word : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ w : List Bool, w ≠ [] → ¬ Rule30StripCertificates.EventuallyWord w :=
    Rule30StripCertificates.problem1_iff_no_word
  ```

**[8] fc-bridge: the formal-conjectures and Wolfram statements.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 is equivalent to `Rule30.centerColumn_not_eventually_periodic` in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, `FormalConjectures/Other/Rule30.lean`, commit 7db2ea3 of 2026-10-14. That file's `state t i` is our `cell t i`, and it quantifies ∃p ∃N where we quantify ∃T ∃P. Problem 1 is also equivalent to Wolfram's 2019 formal statement, read as intended: there are no p ≥ 1 and i with c(t+p) = c(t) for all t > i.
- *Caveat.* As printed, Wolfram's Wolfram Language formula is degenerate. It is `NotExists[{p, i}, ForAll[t, t > i, c[t + p] == c[t]]]` with `c[t_] := CellularAutomaton[30, {{1}, 0}, {t, {{0}}}]`. Two things go wrong:
  - p = 0 is not excluded, so the literal NotExists is false.
  - `c[t]` is the list of the first t+1 values (`c[5]` = {1,1,0,1,1,1}), so for p ≥ 1 the two sides are lists of different lengths.

  The intended reading needs p ≥ 1 and `Last[c[t]]`.
- *Route.* Prove `state t = fun i => cell t i` by induction (each step is `rfl`), then swap the quantifiers. Note t > i ⟺ t ≥ i+1.
- *Lean.* The first theorem is a scratch proof using only the axiom Quot.sound; the second is stated:

  ```lean
  namespace FC
  def step (row : ℤ → Bool) : ℤ → Bool := fun i => xor (row (i - 1)) (row i || row (i + 1))
  def state : ℕ → ℤ → Bool
    | 0 => fun i => decide (i = 0)
    | t + 1 => step (state t)
  def centerColumn (t : ℕ) : Bool := state t 0
  theorem state_eq : ∀ t, state t = fun i => Rule30Jen.cell t i
    | 0 => rfl
    | t + 1 => by rw [state, state_eq t]; rfl
  theorem problem1_iff_fc : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ t : ℕ, N ≤ t → centerColumn (t + p) = centerColumn t := by
    have hc : centerColumn = Rule30Prize.center := funext fun t => by
      rw [centerColumn, state_eq]; rfl
    rw [hc]
    constructor
    · rintro h ⟨p, hp, N, hN⟩; exact h ⟨N, p, hp, hN⟩
    · rintro h ⟨N, p, hp, hN⟩; exact h ⟨p, hp, N, hN⟩
  end FC
  theorem problem1_iff_wolfram : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ p i : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ t, i < t → Rule30Prize.center (t + p) = Rule30Prize.center t := sorry
  ```

- *Sources:* [FC], [W19].

**[14] pi2-normal-form: Π⁰₂ form, cofinal periods, Diophantine form.**
- *Statement.*
  - (a) For all T and all P ≥ 1 there is t ≥ T with c(t+P) ≠ c(t). Since c is primitive recursive, Problem 1 is Π⁰₂ and its negation is Σ⁰₂. Each instance (T, P) is Σ⁰₁, so it is finitely checkable; `Rule30Window` and `Rule30FactorWindow` are kernel-checked bundles of such instances.
  - (b) For every k ≥ 1, c has no eventual period k!. Any family of periods that is cofinal under divisibility works.
  - (c) Diophantine form. The set S = {t : c(t)=1} is Diophantine (by DPRM, since c is computable). So Problem 1 becomes a sentence of the form ∀P ∀T ∃t, x, y with polynomial equations in the matrix. Wolfram (2019) raises possible independence from PA or ZFC. In busy-beaver terms, Problem 1 says a specific machine "beeps" infinitely often [Aar20].
- *Route.*
  - (a) Push the negation inward.
  - (b) A period P gives the period P!, because P divides P!.
  - (c) Use MRDP, or a direct encoding. One rule-30 step on integer rows is a ↦ a XOR 2(a OR 2a) [NKS p. 1160]. Bit operations are Diophantine through Lucas' theorem: binom(x, y) is odd iff the bits of y are a subset of those of x. Iterating needs Matiyasevich's exponential-Diophantine machinery.
- *Lean.* (a) is a scratch proof; (b) and (c) are stated:

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_pi2 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ T P : ℕ, 0 < P → ∃ t, T ≤ t ∧ Rule30Prize.center (t + P) ≠ Rule30Prize.center t := by
    unfold Rule30Prize.Problem1 Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic
    push Not
    rfl
  theorem problem1_iff_factorial_periods : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ k : ℕ, ¬ ∃ T, ∀ t, T ≤ t → Rule30Prize.center (t + (k + 1).factorial) = Rule30Prize.center t := sorry
  theorem center_dioph : Dioph {v : Fin 1 → ℕ | Rule30Prize.center (v 0) = true} := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Has `Dioph`, `DiophFn`, `Dioph.pow_dioph` (Matiyasevich; NumberTheory/Dioph.lean), `Choose.choose_modEq_prod_range_choose` (Lucas; Data/Nat/Choose/Lucas.lean), `Primrec` and `REPred`. Missing: DPRM, and Diophantine definitions of bitwise operations.
- *Sources:* [W19], [NKS] p. 1160, [Dav73], [Aar20].

**[25] nks-integer-rows: rows as integers (NKS p. 871).**
- *Statement.* Let a(0) = 1 and a(t+1) = a(t) XOR (2a(t) OR 4a(t)) (OEIS A110240). One step is A269160, n ↦ n XOR (2n OR 4n). Then cell(t, p) = bit (t − p) of a(t), so c(t) = bit t of a(t). Problem 1 ⟺ t ↦ testBit(a(t), t) is not EP.
- *Checks.* A Lean `#eval` reproduces 60 bits of A051023; Python reproduces 400 bits against a direct simulation.
- *Route.* Induction on t with the core lemmas `Nat.testBit_xor`, `Nat.testBit_or` and `Nat.testBit_shiftLeft`. The catalog's `Rule30Window.stepRow` and `row_testBit` encode rows with the opposite bit order.
- *Lean* (stated; the `let` avoids exponential evaluation):

  ```lean
  def nksRow : ℕ → ℕ
    | 0 => 1
    | t + 1 => let a := nksRow t; a ^^^ (2 * a ||| 4 * a)
  theorem problem1_iff_nksRow : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => (nksRow t).testBit t) := sorry
  ```

- *Why it is useful.* Fast evaluation and certificates. It also gives a 2-adic reading: f(n) = n XOR (2n OR 4n) is 1-Lipschitz on ℤ₂, and c(t) is bit t of fᵗ(1).
- *Sources:* [NKS] p. 871 note, [W19], OEIS A110240, A269160, A051023.

**[26] diagonal-array: the main diagonal of the right-diagonal array.**
- *Statement.* Let A(j, t) = cell(t, t − j). It satisfies:
  - A(0, t) = 1;
  - A(1, t) = [t odd];
  - A(j+2, 0) = 0;
  - A(j+2, t+1) = A(j+2, t) XOR (A(j+1, t) OR A(j, t)).

  Each row j is purely periodic with period 2^j, and c(t) = A(t, t) (OEIS A363343; periods in A094605). Problem 1 ⟺ the main diagonal of this array is not EP.
- *Route.* A equals `Rule30Diagonals.R`, using `R_zero`, `R_one_succ` and `R_step`; then apply `center_eq_R`. In the frame moving with the right edge, the orbit closure of the seed is the 2-adic odometer [CPY07], so c is the diagonal of an odometer orbit.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  def diagArray : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
    | 0, _ => true
    | 1, t => decide (t % 2 = 1)
    | _ + 2, 0 => false
    | j + 2, t + 1 => xor (diagArray (j + 2) t) (diagArray (j + 1) t || diagArray j t)
  theorem problem1_iff_diagArray : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => diagArray t t) := sorry
  ```

- *Sources:* [Row06], [CPY07], [Ner26a], [Ner26b]; the catalog's `Rule30Diagonals`.

### 3.2 Real numbers and Diophantine approximation

**[1] binary-irrational: the user's example.**
- *Statement.* x₂ = Σ_{t≥0} c(t)·2^−(t+1) = 0.11011100110001011001…₂ = 0.862389783947384048640800246086751128108532963624… (OEIS A365254). Problem 1 ⟺ x₂ ∉ ℚ.
- *Route.* The classical theorem: a real number is rational iff its expansion in an integer base is eventually periodic (Wallis 1685, Euler, Gauss *Disq.* art. 312 ff.; [HW] ch. IX).
  - EP ⟹ rational: by the geometric series, x₂ = (N_T + N/(2^P − 1))/2^T.
  - Rational ⟹ EP: if x₂ = p/q, the tail values x_t = 2ᵗx₂ − N_t lie in the finite set (1/q)ℤ ∩ [0, 1], so x_i = x_j for some i < j. If c has infinitely many 1s, then c(t) = [2x_t > 1] and x_{t+1} = 2x_t − c(t) are functions of x_t, so c has period j − i from i on. Otherwise c is eventually 0. This case split handles double expansions such as 0.0111…₂ = 0.1₂.
- *Lean* (Library):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_irrational_binary : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      Irrational (∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℝ) else 0) / 2 ^ (t + 1)) :=
    Rule30Equivalents.BinaryIrrational.problem1_iff_irrational_binary
  -- generic: BinaryIrrational.eventuallyPeriodic_iff_not_irrational (hB : 2 ≤ B) (b : ℕ → Bool)
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Used: `Irrational`, `exists_rat_of_not_irrational`, `Rat.not_irrational`, `tsum_geometric_two'`, `Summable.tsum_eq_zero_add`, `Set.Finite.exists_lt_map_eq_of_forall_mem`. Missing: "eventually periodic digits ⟺ rational" for arbitrary digits ℕ → Fin b (an upstream candidate).
- *Consequences.* The kernel bound T + P ≥ 16359 (`Rule30FactorWindow`) gives x₂ ≠ p/q for every q ≤ 16359. Reason: write p/q in lowest terms with q = 2^a·q′, q′ odd; the expansion has preperiod a and period ord_q′(2), so T_min + P_min ≤ q − 1. Data: c has no period within the first 10^9 bits [W19].
- *Sources:* [HW] ch. IX, [Dic19] ch. VI, [W19] (section "The Digits of Pi"), OEIS A365254, A092539.

**[2] base-b-irrational: every base, `Real.ofDigits`, the Cantor function.**
- *Statement.* For each integer b ≥ 2, Problem 1 ⟺ x_b = Σ c(t)·b^−(t+1) is irrational. Examples: the decimal number 0.11011100110001011001…₁₀, and x₃ = 0.462345072609503417371211…. The same holds in Mathlib's vocabulary, for `Real.ofDigits` of the digit sequence c, and for `Cardinal.cantorFunction (1/b) c`, which equals b·x_b.
- *Route.* As in [1]. For b ≥ 3 the 0/1 expansion is unique.
- *Caution.* Only positional readings in an integer base are equivalent.
  - Σ c(t)/t! is irrational, and Σ c(t)·2^−t! is a Liouville number, for *any* sequence with infinitely many 1s. These say nothing about Problem 1.
  - In base φ (the golden ratio) the blocks 100 and 011 have the same value, so the corresponding statement is a different one.

  ```lean
      Irrational (Real.ofDigits (b := b) fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then 1 else 0) := by
  ```

**[16] integer-digits: the user's example without real numbers (core Lean).**

Conversely, if c is EP then c is the greedy expansion of its rational value, because c is not eventually 1 (`center_not_eventually_constant`). This form fits the Mathlib-free core catalog.

### 3.3 p-adic numbers

**[15] two-adic.**
- *Statement.* α = Σ c(t)·2ᵗ ∈ ℤ₂ is not in ℚ. There is an integer form for any prime p (reading the 0/1 digits p-adically): there are no a, b ∈ ℤ with b ≠ 0 and pⁿ divides b·S_p(n) − a for all n, where S_p(n) = Σ_{t<n} c(t)·pᵗ.
- *Route.* A p-adic integer is rational iff its digits are eventually periodic [Gou97], [Kob].
  - EP ⟹ rational: α = A + p^T·B/(1 − p^P).
  - Rational ⟹ EP: the congruences say bα = a in ℤ_p. First divide out the p-power of b; it must also divide a. The remainders a_n = (a − b·S_n)/pⁿ are then integers with a_{n+1} = (a_n − b·c(n))/p and abs(a_{n+1}) ≤ (abs(a_n) + abs(b))/2. So eventually abs(a_n) ≤ abs(b). Since p does not divide b, c(n) ≡ a_n·b⁻¹ (mod p), and the system is finite and deterministic.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  noncomputable def α₂ : ℤ_[2] := ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℤ_[2]) else 0) * 2 ^ t
  theorem problem1_iff_padic_irrational : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ∀ q : ℚ, (α₂ : ℚ_[2]) ≠ q := sorry
  def S (p n : ℕ) : ℤ := ∑ t ∈ Finset.range n, (if Rule30Prize.center t then 1 else 0) * (p : ℤ) ^ t
  theorem problem1_iff_padic_int (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ a b : ℤ, b ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ n, (p : ℤ) ^ n ∣ b * S p n - a := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.*
  - Has: `PadicInt` (notation ℤ_[p], NumberTheory/Padics/PadicIntegers.lean), `Padic`, `PadicInt.toZModPow` and `PadicInt.appr` (Padics/RingHoms.lean), and the instance `fact_prime_two`. Summability comes from the to_additive form of `NonarchimedeanGroup.multipliable_of_tendsto_cofinite_one` (Topology/Algebra/InfiniteSum/Nonarchimedean.lean).
  - Missing: digit expansions in ℤ_[p], and "rational ⟺ EP digits".
- *Sources:* [Gou97], [Kob], [KG97].

**[30] fcsr-complexity: 2-adic complexity.**
- *Statement.* For every bound B there is an n with no pair a, b (b ≠ 0, abs(a), abs(b) ≤ B) such that 2ⁿ divides b·S_2(n) − a. Equivalently, no feedback-with-carry shift register generates c.
- *Route.* Only finitely many pairs satisfy the bound. If each n had one, a single pair would work for infinitely many n, hence for all n, since the congruences descend to smaller n. Then apply [15]. Klapper–Goresky's rational approximation algorithm is the 2-adic analogue of Berlekamp–Massey.

  ```lean

      ∀ B : ℕ, ∃ n, ¬ ∃ a b : ℤ, b ≠ 0 ∧ |a| ≤ B ∧ |b| ≤ B ∧ (2 : ℤ) ^ n ∣ b * S 2 n - a := sorry
  ```

- *Data.* In the algebra survey's computation, the log₂ of the 2-adic complexity stays within 3.6 bits of n/2 for n ≤ 65536, as for a random sequence.

### 3.4 Algebra: power series, recurrences, coding theory

**[5] series-f2-lfsr: rational over F₂, LFSRs, linear complexity.**
- *Statement.* The following are equivalent to Problem 1:
  - C(X) = Σ c(t)·Xᵗ ∈ F₂[[X]] is not rational: there is no Q ≠ 0 with Q·C a polynomial, or equivalently C ≠ P·Q⁻¹ with Q(0) ≠ 0;
  - c satisfies no eventual linear recurrence over F₂;
  - no LFSR (run from time 0, singular feedback allowed) generates c;
  - the linear complexity profile of c is unbounded.

  Function-field form: ξ = Σ c(t)·X^−(t+1) ∈ F₂((1/X)) is irrational, i.e. its continued fraction over F₂[X] is infinite. Berlekamp–Massey is Euclid's algorithm on ξ, and the jumps of the profile are the degrees of the partial quotients.
- *Route.* If c is EP, (1 − X^P)·C is a polynomial. Conversely, Q·C = P gives a recurrence starting from the lowest coefficient of Q, and pigeonhole on windows gives periodicity [LN97] ch. 8, [Mas69].
- *Lean* (Library, 6 theorems):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_series_not_rational_F2 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ P Q : Polynomial (ZMod 2), Q ≠ 0 ∧
        (Q : PowerSeries (ZMod 2)) * Rule30Equivalents.PowerSeriesF2.series Rule30Prize.center =
          (P : PowerSeries (ZMod 2)) :=
    Rule30Equivalents.PowerSeriesF2.problem1_iff_series_not_rational
  -- also: problem1_iff_series_not_rational_coeff_zero, problem1_iff_series_ne_mul_inv,
  --   problem1_iff_no_eventual_linear_recurrence, problem1_iff_no_lfsr,
  --   problem1_iff_linear_complexity_unbounded
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Has `PowerSeries.mk`, `PowerSeries.coeff`, the Polynomial-to-PowerSeries coercion, `PowerSeries.eq_mul_inv_iff_mul_eq` and `Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite`. Missing: Berlekamp–Massey, and continued fractions over F_q((1/X)); `GenContFract` needs an ordered field.
- *Data.* L(c↾10^6) = 499,998, and abs(L_n − n/2) ≤ 9.5 for all n ≤ 10^6. Two independent runs agree. This is the profile of a random sequence. Since L_n ≤ T+P, it implies T + P ≥ 499,998 (data, not kernel-checked).
- *Caveat.* A profile near n/2 does not separate random from automatic sequences: Thue–Morse also deviates by at most 1.
- *Sources:* [LN97], [Mas69], [Mil75], [WS79], [Dor87], [Nie88].

- *Statement.* Let K be any field and read c in {0,1} ⊆ K. Then Problem 1 ⟺ C(X) ∉ K(X), i.e. there is no Q ≠ 0 in K[X] with Q·C ∈ K[X]. It is also ⟺ c satisfies no constant-coefficient linear recurrence over K (Mathlib's `LinearRecurrence`, valid from n = 0).

**[31] p-recursive: polynomial-coefficient recurrences and D-finiteness.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ there is no recurrence Σ_{i≤d} p_i(n)·c(n+i) = 0 for n ≥ N with p_i ∈ ℤ[n] not all zero ⟺ C(X) is not D-finite over ℚ(X).
- *Route (elementary).* Let D = max deg p_i and let a_i be the n^D coefficients. The sum Σ a_i·c(n+i) takes finitely many values and is O(1/n), so it is eventually 0. That is a constant-coefficient recurrence; apply [17].
- *Classical results.* [vdPS96]: a finite-valued P-recursive sequence has a rational generating function. [Sta80]: P-recursive ⟺ D-finite.
- *Consequence* (number-theory survey). If Problem 1 holds, methods that need a linear ODE have nothing to work with. This covers Siegel–Shidlovskii and Apéry- or Beukers-type Padé approximations.
- *Lean* (stated):

**[28] nlfsr: nonlinear feedback shift registers and maximum-order complexity.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ each of:
  - there are no m and F : {0,1}^m → {0,1} with c(i+m) = F(c(i), …, c(i+m−1)) for all i;
  - the maximum-order complexity M_n(c) tends to ∞;
  - for every m, two equal length-m windows of c have different successors.

  The same holds for the k-th order complexity (feedback of algebraic degree ≤ k), for each fixed k.
- *Route.* If c is EP with (T, P), windows of length T+P determine the next bit: both successors lie in the periodic part at the same phase. Conversely, a feedback function makes the dynamics finite and deterministic. Each lower bound M_n ≥ m+1 has a two-position certificate that `decide` can check.

  ```lean
        ∀ i, Rule30Prize.center (i + m) = F (fun k => Rule30Prize.center (i + k)) := sorry
  ```

- *Data* (algebra survey). M_n = 37 at n = 10^6 and 44 at 10^7; for random bits, 2·log₂ n ≈ 40 and 46.5.
