### 3.5 Complex analysis

**[41] natural-boundary: Szegő and Pólya–Carlson.**
- *Statement.* f(z) = Σ c(t)zᵗ has radius of convergence exactly 1, since c is bounded and not eventually 0. Problem 1 ⟺ f has no analytic continuation across any arc of abs(z) = 1.
- *Route.* Szegő 1922: a power series with finitely many distinct coefficients that continues across some arc equals P(z)/(1 − z^m). Pólya–Carlson (Carlson 1921): integer coefficients and radius 1 give either a rational function or the unit circle as natural boundary. Conversely, an EP sequence gives P(z)/(1 − z^P), which is meromorphic with poles only at roots of unity. Then apply [17] over ℂ.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  noncomputable def genFun (z : ℂ) : ℂ := ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℂ) else 0) * z ^ t
  theorem problem1_iff_natural_boundary : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ z₀ : ℂ, ‖z₀‖ = 1 → ∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → ¬ ∃ g : ℂ → ℂ,
        AnalyticOnNhd ℂ g (Metric.ball z₀ r) ∧
          ∀ z ∈ Metric.ball z₀ r, ‖z‖ < 1 → g z = genFun z := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Has `AnalyticOnNhd`, `AnalyticOnNhd.eqOn_of_preconnected_of_eventuallyEq` and `FormalMultilinearSeries.radius`. Missing: natural boundaries, Szegő's theorem, Pólya–Carlson.
- *Sources:* [Sze22], [Car21], [Pol16], [BC17] (Thm 1.1 states Szegő's theorem in this form).

### 3.6 Combinatorics on words and symbolic dynamics

**[3] shift-orbit.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ the shifts σⁿc = (c(n+t))_t are pairwise distinct ⟺ there are infinitely many of them ⟺ c is not a preperiodic point of the shift (no iterate is a periodic point).
- *Route.* σ^(T+P)c = σ^T c says exactly "period P from time T". Then pigeonhole.
- *Lean* (Library, plus a one-line scratch bridge to Mathlib's `FullShift.shift`, which is definitional):

  ```lean
    Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_infinite_shifts
  theorem problem1_iff_not_preperiodic : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ m, Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.shift^[m] Rule30Prize.center ∉
        Function.periodicPts Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.shift :=
    Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_not_preperiodic

      Function.Injective (fun n : ℕ => SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.shift n Rule30Prize.center) :=
    Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_injective_shifts
  ```

- *Known.* Kernel-checked: σ⁰c, …, σ^16358 c are pairwise distinct (`Rule30FactorWindow`).

**[4] morse-hedlund.**
- *Statement.* Let p_c(n) be the number of distinct length-n factors of c. Problem 1 ⟺ p_c(n) ≥ n+1 for all n ⟺ p_c is strictly increasing ⟺ p_c is unbounded.
- *Route.* Morse–Hedlund 1938, in the one-sided form of Coven–Hedlund 1973. If p(m+1) = p(m), every length-m factor has a unique right extension, so the window dynamics is a self-map of a finite set.
- *Lean* (Library):

  ```lean

  theorem problem1_iff_ncard_factors : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ n, n + 1 ≤ (Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.factors Rule30Prize.center n).ncard :=
    Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_ncard_factors
  -- also problem1_iff_ncard_factors_lt_succ, problem1_iff_strictMono_ncard_factors,
  --   problem1_iff_ncard_factors_unbounded
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Has `Set.ncard`, `Set.Finite`, and `Pattern` and `LanguageOn` in Dynamics/SymbolicDynamics/Basic.lean. It has no factor complexity and no Morse–Hedlund.
- *Data.* Kernel-checked: p_c(26) ≥ 16359. In the first 10^7 bits, p_c(n) = 2ⁿ for n ≤ 19, and 96 of the 2^20 words of length 20 are absent (a random model predicts about 76).
- *Sources:* [MH38] Thms 7.3–7.4, [CH73], [CN].

**[23] special-factors.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ for every n some word w of length n is right-special, meaning both w0 and w1 occur in c. By König's lemma this is also ⟺ there is a left-infinite word all of whose suffixes are right-special.
- *Route.* For a one-sided binary word, p(n+1) − p(n) is the number of right-special factors of length n; then apply [4]. For König, the right-special factors form a finitely branching tree under extension to the left.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  def OccursThen (w : List Bool) (a : Bool) : Prop :=
    ∃ i : ℕ, (∀ j : Fin w.length, Rule30Prize.center (i + (j : ℕ)) = w.get j) ∧
      Rule30Prize.center (i + w.length) = a
  theorem problem1_iff_right_special : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ n, ∃ w : List Bool, w.length = n ∧ OccursThen w false ∧ OccursThen w true := sorry
  ```

- *Data.* Every word of length ≤ 18 is right-special in the first 10^7 bits.
- *Sources:* [Cas97], [CN].

**[24] finite-certificates.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ for every N there are n and M such that more than N distinct length-n factors start below position M.
- *Why it is useful.* For fixed N, the inner statement is Σ⁰₁. It is equivalent to "no eventual period with T + P ≤ N": for an EP c, sup_n p_c(n) = T_min + P_min, because those T_min + P_min shifts are distinct and eventually separated by their prefixes. `Rule30FactorWindow` is the kernel-checked instance N = 16358 (W = 26, M = 16384). The 10^7-bit file gives N = 9,999,956 as data.
- *Route.* Apply [4], noting that every factor occurs in some finite prefix. For a concrete N the inner bound can be checked by `decide`.

  ```lean
      ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n M : ℕ, N < ((Finset.range M).image
        fun i => List.ofFn fun j : Fin n => Rule30Prize.center (i + j)).card := sorry
  ```

**[13] orbit-closure.**
- *Statement.* The closure of {σⁿc} in {0,1}^ℕ (product topology) is infinite; equivalently, it has an accumulation point.
- *Route.* Apply [3]; finite sets are closed in a T1 space.
- *Lean* (scratch proof):

  ```lean

      (closure (Set.range fun n : ℕ => fun t => Rule30Prize.center (n + t))).Infinite := by
    rw [Rule30Equivalents.ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_infinite_shifts]
    constructor
    · exact fun h => h.mono subset_closure
    · intro h hfin
      exact h (by rw [hfin.isClosed.closure_eq]; exact hfin)
  ```

- *Known.* By the kernel results, the closure has at least 16359 points.

**[34] omega-limit.**
- *Statement.* The ω-limit set ω(c) of c under the shift is infinite; equivalently, it contains a non-periodic point.
- *Width-1 trace view.* Let F be rule 30 on {0,1}^ℤ and Tr₀(x) = ((Fᵗx)₀)_t. Tr₀ is a factor map, and ω_σ(c) = Tr₀(ω_F(δ₀)), where δ₀ is the single seed.
- *Route.*
  - If c is EP, ω(c) is one periodic orbit.
  - Conversely, a finite ω(c) is invariant, so it consists of periodic points. Choose L so that length-(L−1) prefixes separate those points. Eventually σᵗc shares its length-L prefix with some z_t ∈ ω(c), and this forces z_{t+1} = σz_t. So c is eventually a shifted periodic point.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_omegaLimit_infinite : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      (omegaLimit Filter.atTop (fun (n : ℕ) (x : ℕ → Bool) => fun t => x (n + t))
        {Rule30Prize.center}).Infinite := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.* `omegaLimit`, `mem_omegaLimit_iff_frequently`, `isInvariant_omegaLimit` and `nonempty_omegaLimit` (Dynamics/OmegaLimit.lean).
- *Sources:* [Kop23], [CFG10], [LM95].

**[35] tail-language.**
- *Statement.* Let L∞(c) be the set of words that occur infinitely often, and p∞(n) the number of them of length n. Problem 1 ⟺ each of:
  - p∞(n) ≥ n+1 for all n;
  - the two-sided subshift Ω(c) with language L∞(c) is infinite;
  - no Rauzy graph Γ_n of L∞(c) is a single cycle. (The Γ_n are strongly connected.)
- *Route.* L∞ is factorial and extendable on both sides. A flat step p∞(m+1) = p∞(m) gives unique right extensions inside L∞. Only finitely many words of length m+1 occur finitely often; after the last such occurrence, c follows the extension map. If c is EP with least period P, then p∞(n) = P for n ≥ P−1.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  def tailFactors (n : ℕ) : Set (Fin n → Bool) :=
    {w | ∀ N, ∃ i : ℕ, N ≤ i ∧ ∀ j : Fin n, Rule30Prize.center (i + (j : ℕ)) = w j}
  theorem problem1_iff_tail_complexity : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ n, n + 1 ≤ (tailFactors n).ncard := sorry
  ```

- *Note.* No finite computation constrains L∞(c), and every complexity reformulation is decided by this tail language alone.
- *Sources:* [CN], [Rau83], [MeSa17].

**[19] simple-transforms.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ each of the following is not EP:
  - ¬c (A226474; the center column of rules 135 and 149 from a white cell);
  - c(· + k) for any fixed k;
  - the XOR derivative c(t) XOR c(t+1) (A327974);
  - the running parity c(0) XOR … XOR c(t) (the parity of A327982);
  - any right-permutive sliding block code f(c(t), …, c(t+r)), with f bijective in its last argument.
- *Route.* Sliding block codes preserve EP. If the derivative has period P from T, then c(t+P) XOR c(t) is constant, so c has period P or 2P. For permutive codes, the pair (window, phase) is finite-state.

**[20] decimations.**
- *Statement.*
  - (a) For each fixed k ≥ 1, Problem 1 ⟺ some decimation n ↦ c(kn + r) with r < k is not EP. For example: c at even times or c at odd times is not EP.
  - (b) Problem 1 ⟺ for every P ≥ 1 some residue class k ↦ c(r + kP) is not eventually constant. The case P = 1 is the proved `center_not_eventually_constant`.
- *Route.*
  - (a) If decimation r has period P_r from T_r, then c has period k·lcm(P_r) from k·max T_r + k.
  - (b) c has period P ⟺ every residue class mod P is eventually constant.
- *Lean:*

  ```lean

      ∃ r < k, ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun n => Rule30Prize.center (k * n + r)) := sorry
  theorem problem1_iff_nonconstant_class : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ P, 0 < P → ∃ r < P, ¬ ∃ K b, ∀ k, K ≤ k → Rule30Prize.center (r + k * P) = b  -- scratch proof
  ```

- *Note.* Read the right half of row t as y_t = Σ_{p≥0} cell(t,p)·2^−(p+1). Then c(t) = [y_t ≥ 1/2] exactly. So Wolfram's suggestion, that [y_{Pk+r} ≥ 1/2] is not eventually constant for some r, is (b) again [W19].

**[29] return-words: gaps and run lengths.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ each of the following is not EP:
  - the gaps between consecutive black cells (first differences of A327984);
  - the gaps between consecutive white cells (A327985);
  - the run lengths (A327983);
  - for some recurrent word u (equivalently, for every one), the derived sequence of return words to u [Dur98].
- *Route.* There are infinitely many black and white cells (`center_not_eventually_constant`), so each of these sequences and c determine each other up to eventual periodicity. Since colors alternate, an odd period of the run lengths doubles in c.

  ```lean
    Nat.nth (fun t => Rule30Prize.center t = true) (n + 1) -
  ```

### 3.7 Cellular-automaton structure

**[6] symmetric-rules.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ each of the following center columns is not EP:
  - rule 86 (the mirror image of rule 30) from a single black cell; its center column is c;
  - rule 135 (the complement) from a single white cell on black; its center column is ¬c;
  - rule 149 (the mirror complement) from a single white cell; its center column is ¬c.
- *Route.* Reflection and conjugation are symmetries of elementary CA. The black seed is mirror-symmetric, the white seed is its complement, and EP is invariant under complement. The library computes the class {30, 86, 135, 149}, and the classical count of 88 classes, by `decide`.
- *Caveat.* Rule 135 from a single *black* cell has center column ¬cell(t−1, −1). That is the column −1 problem, which is related but not equivalent (Section 6).
- *Lean* (Library):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_rule86 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ¬ Rule30Equivalents.EventuallyPeriodic
      (fun t => Rule30Equivalents.Symmetry.evolve 86 Rule30Equivalents.Symmetry.blackSeed t 0) :=
    Rule30Equivalents.Symmetry.problem1_iff_rule86
  -- likewise Symmetry.problem1_iff_rule135 and problem1_iff_rule149, with Symmetry.whiteSeed
  ```

- *Sources:* [LP90], [MW], OEIS A051023 (rule 86), A226474 (rules 135 and 149).

**[21] stripe-seeds: finite seeds with exactly the seed's center column.**
- *Statement.* For n ≥ 0 let s_n be the row that is black exactly at the even positions of [0, n) and at n: 1, 11, 101, 1011, 10101, …. Rule 30 from s_n has this pattern:
  - it agrees with the single-seed pattern at every (t, p) with p < t;
  - it is the fixed stripe (black at even p) on [t, t+n);
  - its right edge is at t+n.

  So its center column is exactly c, and Problem 1 ⟺ the center column of rule 30 from s_n is not EP, for any n.
- *Route.* Induction on t with the explicit pattern. The stripe …1010… is a fixed point that always shows x_p OR x_{p+1} = 1 to its left neighbour (the "OR latch"), so the light cone left of p = t never sees it. Changes on the left side never preserve c: flipping cell −m flips c(m).
- *Checks.* Checked numerically for n ≤ 11 and t < 400 in this merge, and for n ≤ 51 and t ≤ 2500 by the CA-structure survey. That survey also searched exhaustively: among the 1023 nonzero rows supported in [0, 9], exactly s_0, …, s_9 give c. The surveys found no literature for this observation.
- *Lean* (scratch proof, ca-structure/lean/SymSeeds.lean):

  ```lean
  def stripeSeed (n : ℕ) (p : ℤ) : Bool := decide (0 ≤ p ∧ p < n ∧ p % 2 = 0) || decide (p = n)
  theorem problem1_iff_stripeSeed (n : ℕ) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => Rule30Realization.evol (stripeSeed n) t 0)
  ```

- *Sources:* CA-structure survey; [Con26] (the OR latch and triangular uniqueness).

**[22] realization: the inverse problem.**
- *Statement.* Keep the right half white. Every column u : ℕ → Bool is then the center column of exactly one row Λ(u). This follows from left-permutivity: rule 30 is affine in its left cell. Λ(c) is the single seed, and Λ(u)(−m) depends only on u(0..m) and flips when u(m) flips. Problem 1 ⟺ no EP column u has Λ(u) equal to the single seed.
- *2-adic reading* (the CA-structure survey's own reformulation). For a fixed right half, the trace map Σ x_{−m}·2^m ↦ Σ c_t·2ᵗ is an isometry of ℤ₂. The seed is the 2-adic integer 1, and Problem 1 says its image is not rational.
- *Lean* (scratch proof, ca-structure/lean/SymSeeds.lean):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_realization : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ u : ℕ → Bool, Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic u →
        Rule30Realization.conf Rule30Realization.seed u ≠ Rule30Realization.seed
  ```

- *Catalog lemmas.* `Rule30Realization.column_realizable_unique`, `realize`, `unique`, `evol_seed`, and `seed_perturbation`. The last is a barrier: for every n, some row that agrees with the seed on [−n, ∞) has column c up to time n and white after it.
- *Sources:* [W86] §§3–4 and 7, [NKS] p. 1087, [MS91], [Con26] (Theorems 2–3 compute Λ of the two constant columns).

**[33] coupled-halves: a causal fixed point.**
- *Statement.* Let L_u be rule 30 on p ≤ −1, started white and driven at p = 0 by the column u. Let R_u be rule 30 on p ≥ 1, started white and driven by u. The system u(0) = 1, u(t+1) = rule(L_u(t, −1), u(t), R_u(t, 1)) is causal, and its unique solution is c. Problem 1 ⟺ no solution of this system is EP.
- *Route.* L_u(t) and R_u(t) depend only on u(0..t). The catalog lemmas `Rule30DrivenLeft.cell_eq_L` and `Rule30Ether.cell_eq_drv` (with T = 0) identify the solution with c. The left half sees the center only through c(t) AND c(t+1) (`Rule30MaskedJen.effective_step`).
- *Context.* The project's period-specific reductions are relaxations that drop one half: Q01, Q001, C3, C3w and C3s001 keep the left half; Absorption and AbsorptionT keep the right.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean

      ∀ u : ℕ → Bool, u 0 = true →
        (∀ t, u (t + 1) = Rule30Jen.rule (Rule30DrivenLeft.L u (fun _ => false) t (-1)) (u t)
          (Rule30Ether.drv u (fun _ => false) t 1)) →
        ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic u := sorry
  ```

### 3.8 Logic, automata and computation

**[9] presburger.**
- *Statement.* Let S = {t : c(t) = 1} (A327984). Problem 1 ⟺ S is not definable in Presburger arithmetic (ℕ, 0, 1, +), with any set of parameters ⟺ S is not semilinear.
- *A further classical equivalent* (no Lean statement here): (ℕ, +, S) defines an infinite set with unbounded gaps, and one formula works uniformly [MV96], [Mil16].
- *Route.* By Presburger's quantifier elimination, or Ginsburg–Spanier, the definable subsets of ℕ are exactly the ultimately periodic sets. Mathlib proves this.
- *Lean* (scratch proofs):

  ```lean
  theorem ep_iff (f : ℕ → Bool) : Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic f ↔
      ∃ k, ∃ p > 0, ∀ x ≥ k, x ∈ {t | f t = true} ↔ x + p ∈ {t | f t = true} := by
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨T, P, hP, h⟩
      exact ⟨T, P, hP, fun x hx => by simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, h x hx]⟩
    · rintro ⟨k, p, hp, h⟩
      refine ⟨k, p, hp, fun t ht => ?_⟩
      have := h t ht
      simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at this
      cases h1 : f t <;> cases h2 : f (t + p) <;> simp_all
  theorem problem1_iff_not_presburger (A : Set ℕ) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ A.Definable₁ FirstOrder.Language.presburger {t | Rule30Prize.center t = true} := by
    rw [FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic, ← ep_iff]; rfl
  theorem problem1_iff_not_semilinear : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ IsSemilinearSet {t : ℕ | Rule30Prize.center t = true} := by
    rw [Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic, ← ep_iff]; rfl
  ```

- *Mathlib.*
  - Has: `FirstOrder.Language.presburger`; `presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic` and `presburger.definable_iff_isSemilinearSet` (ModelTheory/Arithmetic/Presburger/Definability.lean); `Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic` and `IsSemilinearSet` (…/Semilinear/Defs.lean); `Set.Definable₁`.

**[18] regular-languages.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ L₁ = {1ⁿ : c(n) = 1} is not regular (⟺ no unary DFA with output computes c) ⟺ the prefix language {c(0)…c(n−1)} ⊆ {0,1}* is not regular.
- *Route.* By Myhill–Nerode, the left quotient of L₁ by 1ⁿ is the language of the shift σⁿc, and distinct sequences give distinct languages. So L₁ is regular ⟺ c has finitely many shifts ⟺ c is EP. The prefix language works the same way.
- *Lean* (scratch proofs, logic-computation/lean/RegularTest.lean and PrefixTest.lean):

  ```lean
  def unaryLang : Language Unit := {l | Rule30Prize.center l.length = true}
  theorem problem1_iff_unary_not_regular : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ¬ unaryLang.IsRegular
  def prefixLang : Language Bool := {l | l = (List.range l.length).map Rule30Prize.center}
  theorem problem1_iff_prefixes_not_regular : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ¬ prefixLang.IsRegular
  ```

- *Mathlib.* `Language.IsRegular` (Computability/DFA.lean); `Language.leftQuotient` and `Language.isRegular_iff_finite_range_leftQuotient` (Computability/MyhillNerode.lean).
- *Kernel consequence.* A unary DFA that computes c needs at least 16359 states.

**[40] context-free.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ L₁ is not context-free ⟺ the prefix language is not context-free.
- *Route.* Unary context-free languages are regular [GR62], [Par66]. An infinite context-free language made of prefixes of a single infinite word forces that word to be ultimately periodic [Boo77]; Book's proof uses the context-free pumping lemma. Then apply [18].
- *Lean* (stated; `unaryLang` and `prefixLang` as in [18]):

  ```lean
  theorem problem1_iff_unary_not_contextFree : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ¬ unaryLang.IsContextFree := sorry
  theorem problem1_iff_prefixes_not_contextFree : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ¬ prefixLang.IsContextFree := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.* Has `Language.IsContextFree` and `ContextFreeGrammar`, and the regular pumping lemmas `DFA.pumping_lemma` and `NFA.pumping_lemma`. Missing: the context-free pumping lemma and Parikh's theorem.
- *A stronger relative.* "c is not morphic", equivalently "c is determined by no indexed language" [Smi14]; see Section 4.

**[36] omega-regular.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ the singleton {c} ⊆ {0,1}^ω is not ω-regular (no Büchi automaton accepts exactly c) ⟺ S is not definable in MSO(ℕ, <), by Büchi's theorem.
- *Route.*
  - (⇐) If c = u v^ω, a deterministic lasso automaton accepts exactly c.
  - (⇒) An accepting run on c visits some accepting state twice. Pumping that loop gives an accepted ultimately periodic word, which must be c.
- *Lean* (stated, with the definitions):

  ```lean
  structure Buchi (α : Type) where
    Q : Type
    [fin : Finite Q]
    init : Q
    step : Q → α → Q → Prop
    acc : Set Q
  def Buchi.Accepts {α : Type} (B : Buchi α) (w : ℕ → α) : Prop :=
    ∃ r : ℕ → B.Q, r 0 = B.init ∧ (∀ n, B.step (r n) (w n) (r (n + 1))) ∧
      ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ r n ∈ B.acc
  theorem problem1_iff_not_omega_regular : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ B : Buchi Bool, ∀ w, B.Accepts w ↔ w = Rule30Prize.center := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.* No ω-automata and no MSO. Externally, the logic survey reports ctchou/AutomataTheory, a Lean 4 library with Büchi automata that is being ported to CSLib (not verified here).
- *Sources:* [Bue62], [Tho90].

**[27] finite-state-machines: prediction and generation.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ either of:
  - every finite-state predictor errs infinitely often. A predictor has a finite state set; it reads c(0), …, c(n−1), and guesses g(state) for c(n).
  - no finite autonomous machine (F : σ → σ with output g) has c(t) = g(Fᵗ s₀) for all large t. So no LFSR, NLFSR, FCSR or finite cyclic rule-30 register produces c from some time on.
- *Route.* If c is EP, a counter predictor works. Conversely, an eventually-correct predictor effectively reads its own guesses, so it runs autonomously on a finite set and is eventually periodic.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  def readState {σ : Type} (s₀ : σ) (δ : σ → Bool → σ) : ℕ → σ
    | 0 => s₀
    | n + 1 => δ (readState s₀ δ n) (Rule30Prize.center n)
  theorem problem1_iff_unpredictable : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ∀ (σ : Type) [Finite σ] (s₀ : σ) (δ : σ → Bool → σ) (g : σ → Bool),
        ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ g (readState s₀ δ n) ≠ Rule30Prize.center n := sorry
  theorem problem1_iff_no_finite_generator : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ ∃ (σ : Type) (_ : Finite σ) (s₀ : σ) (F : σ → σ) (g : σ → Bool) (T : ℕ),
        ∀ t, T ≤ t → Rule30Prize.center t = g (F^[t] s₀) := sorry
  ```

- *Stronger relative.* Finite-state unpredictability at error rate 1/2 implies both Problem 1 and Problem 2.
- *Sources:* [FMG92], [SS72], [W19] (on "predictable regularities").

**[37] lz76.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ the Lempel–Ziv (1976) complexity of the prefixes c(0…n−1) is unbounded.
- *Route.*
  - If c is EP, the last component of the exhaustive history copies (with overlap) forever, so the complexity is bounded.
  - Conversely, the exhaustive histories of longer prefixes extend those of shorter ones. If the complexity is bounded, the last component is therefore infinite. Its copy source s ≤ h works for infinitely many n, hence for all n, which gives period h + 1 − s.
  - With the "fewest components" definition below, use Lempel–Ziv's theorem that the exhaustive history is optimal.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean
  def IsLZHistory (n : ℕ) (b : List ℕ) : Prop :=
    b.head? = some 0 ∧ b.getLast? = some n ∧ List.IsChain (· < ·) b ∧
      ∀ p ∈ b.zip b.tail, p.2 = p.1 + 1 ∨ ∃ s < p.1, ∀ j, p.1 + j + 1 < p.2 →
        Rule30Prize.center (s + j) = Rule30Prize.center (p.1 + j)
  noncomputable def lzComplexity (n : ℕ) : ℕ := sInf {k | ∃ b, IsLZHistory n b ∧ b.length = k + 1}
  theorem problem1_iff_lz_unbounded : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ∀ K, ∃ n, K < lzComplexity n := sorry
  ```

- *Data* (logic survey). C_LZ(c↾20000) = 1433, against 1437 for pseudorandom bits.
- *Sources:* [LZ76].

**[42] cobham-christol.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ each of:
  - c is not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic (any multiplicatively independent pair of bases works);
  - C(X) is transcendental over F₂(X) or over F₃(X), reading the 0/1 values in F₂ and in F₃;
  - S is not definable in both Büchi arithmetics (ℕ, +, V₂) and (ℕ, +, V₃);
  - c is not k-automatic for some k ≥ 2.
- *Route.*
  - EP ⟹ the k-kernel is finite for every k ⟹ k-automatic (Eilenberg's criterion).
  - Cobham 1969: a sequence that is k- and l-automatic, with k and l multiplicatively independent, is EP.
  - Christol 1979 and [CKMR80]: over F_p, p-automatic ⟺ algebraic over F_p(X).
  - Büchi–Bruyère: k-automatic ⟺ definable in (ℕ, +, V_k). Cobham–Semenov gives the two-base version.
- *Lean* (stated):

  ```lean

    {g | ∃ e r, r < k ^ e ∧ g = fun n => f (k ^ e * n + r)}
  def IsAutomatic (k : ℕ) (f : ℕ → Bool) : Prop := (kernel k f).Finite
  theorem problem1_iff_not_two_three_automatic : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      ¬ (IsAutomatic 2 Rule30Prize.center ∧ IsAutomatic 3 Rule30Prize.center) := sorry
  open scoped RatFunc in
  theorem problem1_iff_transcendental_F2_or_F3 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
      Transcendental (RatFunc (ZMod 2)) ((series (ZMod 2) : PowerSeries (ZMod 2)) : LaurentSeries (ZMod 2)) ∨
      Transcendental (RatFunc (ZMod 3)) ((series (ZMod 3) : PowerSeries (ZMod 3)) : LaurentSeries (ZMod 3)) := sorry
  ```

- *Mathlib.*
  - Has: `DFA`, `Language`, `RatFunc`, `LaurentSeries`, `Transcendental`, `ZMod`, and the instances `fact_prime_two` and `fact_prime_three`.

**[43] gap-theorems.**
- *Statement.* Problem 1 ⟺ no one-tape deterministic Turing machine decides L₁ = {1ⁿ : c(n) = 1} in time o(n log n) ⟺ no DTM with a read-only input tape decides L₁ in space o(log log n). So Problem 1 is exactly an effort lower bound for *unary* input; Problem 3 asks for one with binary input.

- c is uniformly recurrent.
- The orbit closure of c is not sofic.
- c is a Toeplitz sequence.
- Ω(c) is minimal.
- The defect bound with coefficient 2.

## 5. Weaker statements (implied by Problem 1)

- **NoPer(P) for a fixed P.** Status of each case:
  - P = 1 is proved, for every column (`Rule30Prize.no_column_eventually_constant`).
  - Every P ≤ 4096 with transient ≤ 8192 is excluded (`Rule30Window.no_small_eventual_period`).
  - Any eventual period has T + P ≥ 16359 (`Rule30FactorWindow.transient_add_period_ge`).
  - P = 2 is reduced to Q01 (`not_eventually_period_two_of_Q01`) and to CQ01. Q01 is proved for starts of width ≤ 52 (`q01_width_le_52`).
  - Least period 3 is reduced: for the word 001 to AbsorptionT t001, Q001 or C3s001; for 011 to C3w.
  - Least period 4 is reduced to Absorption (`least_period_four_of_absorption`).
  - Strip certificates exclude 30 words of length 8–13, and long black runs exclude many periods (`Rule30BlackRuns`).
  - The 10^9-bit data excludes P ≤ 2.5·10^8 with T ≤ 5·10^8 (data only).
  - Problem 1 is the conjunction of NoPer(k!) over all k, by [14].
- **Not purely periodic** (the case T = 0). The kernel gives P ≥ 16359. This statement is equivalent to Problem 1 if c is recurrent.
- **No eventual period 2^k.** Equivalent forms: no tail extends to a continuous function ℤ₂ → F₂; the F₂ Mahler (binomial) coefficients of every tail are not eventually 0 (via Lucas' theorem). This is open, because it includes periods 2 and 4. Replacing ℤ₂ by the profinite integers gives back Problem 1. Mathlib has `PadicInt.mahler`, `PadicInt.mahlerEquiv` and `PadicInt.hasSum_mahler`.
- **Jen's pairs and masked Jen** (proved):
  - c and column j ≠ 0 are not both EP (`Rule30Jen.jen`);
  - c and c OR column 1 are not both EP;
  - c and column 1 restricted to the white times of c are not both EP (`Rule30MaskedJen.masked_jen`, `orCol_not_eventuallyPeriodic`, `window_jen`, `finitary_jen`).

  Barrier: rules 90, 150 and 210 satisfy all of these, yet their center columns are eventually constant (`Rule30Realization.barrier`).
- **Number-theoretic shadows of the kernel bounds:** x₂ ≠ p/q for every q ≤ 16359.

## 6. Related statements with no known implication

- **Column j ≠ 0, and the white seed (column −1).** Problem 1 ∨ CP(j) is proved (Jen). So proving "Problem 1 ⟺ CP(j)" is the same as proving "Problem 1 ∧ CP(j)" (scratch: `problem1_iff_column_iff_both`). No other column can be shown equivalent to Problem 1 without solving both problems. See also `Rule30WhiteSeed.problem1_black_or_white` and `problem1_30_or_135`.
- **Diagonals (solved).** Right diagonals are purely 2^j-periodic and left diagonals are eventually periodic (`Rule30Diagonals.R_periodic`, `D_periodic`; Jen 1986 Thm 4; Rowland 2006). Records of the left periods occur at 1, 4, 9, 30, 401, 87868 (A364239).
- **Lines of a single slope** p/q ∉ {0, ±1}: open, and numerically aperiodic.
- **The project's period reductions**: Q01, CQ01, Q001, C3, C3w, C3s001, Absorption, AbsorptionT. Each is uniform over finite rows, and each is used to exclude one period or word. None is implied by Problem 1.
- **Finite rings.** Rule 30 on n cells has periods of about 2^(0.61n) to 2^(0.63n). The ring's center agrees with c for t ≤ (n−1)/2. No implication is known; Wolfram (2019): "I, at least, don't immediately see."
- **Other rules.** Rule 45, code 10, rule 22 with two seeds, and the 4-color code 150898 (which has a long transient). Rules 161 and 69540422 have non-periodic automatic center columns. Rules 90, 150 and 210 are barrier rules with eventually constant centers. NKS p. 956 notes that rule 30 is the square of the 3-color radius-1/2 rules 11736, 11739 and 11742; this was not checked here.
- **Other seeds and backgrounds.** A white seed; defects in periodic backgrounds; random initial conditions. Under the Bernoulli measure every block occurs in every column with equal frequency, but that says nothing about the single seed.
- **Mahler's 3/2 problem, Z-numbers, and Kopra's ×p/q automata.** Rule 30 and ×p/q automata are both rapidly left expansive. Width-1 aperiodicity is solved for ×p/q [Kop21] but open for rule 30; Kopra's Problem 4.8 is Problem 1.
- **Recurrence and uniform recurrence of c.** As properties of sequences these are independent of Problem 1. A normal sequence is recurrent but not uniformly recurrent.
- **Kolmogorov complexity.** K(c↾n) = K(n) + O(1), as for every computable sequence, so it cannot see Problem 1. The resource-bounded measures in [5], [27], [28] and [37] can.
- **The ANF degree of the t-step map** is 2t − 1 (a round-1 paper proof, checked numerically for t ≤ 10). It concerns all seeds jointly, and rules of maximal degree with EP centers show it cannot decide Problem 1.
- **Rowland's Conjecture 1** (rigidity of the right edge) has no known relation. The stripe seeds show that the center column does not determine the right edge.

## 7. Problems 2 and 3

**Problem 2** (density 1/2).

Forms:
- Ours: `Rule30Prize.Problem2`, stated with integers: for all k > 0, eventually k·abs(2·blackCount n − n) ≤ n.
- formal-conjectures: `{t | centerColumn t}.HasDensity (1/2)`, where `Set.HasDensity` comes from its own ForMathlib layer.
- Wolfram: `DiscreteLimit[Total[c[t]]/t, t -> Infinity] == 1/2`.
- Equivalently, x₂ is simply normal in base 2. This uses that c is not eventually constant, so it is the unique expansion of x₂.
- Equivalently, lim_{x→1⁻} (1 − x)·Σ c(t)xᵗ = 1/2. The Abelian direction is elementary; the converse is the Hardy–Littlewood–Karamata Tauberian theorem, valid since the coefficients are nonnegative.

Problem 2 transfers verbatim to rule 86 and the stripe seeds (same column) and to rules 135 and 149 (complemented column; density 1/2 is preserved).

Two Lean forms typecheck (stated):

```lean
theorem problem2_iff_tendsto : Rule30Prize.Problem2 ↔
    Filter.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (Rule30Prize.blackCount n : ℝ) / n) Filter.atTop (nhds (1 / 2)) := sorry
theorem problem2_iff_abel : Rule30Prize.Problem2 ↔
    Filter.Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => (1 - x) * ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℝ) else 0) * x ^ t)
      (nhdsWithin 1 (Set.Iio 1)) (nhds (1 / 2)) := sorry
```

Mathlib has Abel's theorem (`Complex.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_stolzSet`, `Real.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_lt`, Analysis/Complex/AbelLimit.lean). It has no Tauberian theorem, no natural-density predicate and no normal numbers.

Relation to Problem 1:
- As properties of sequences the two are independent: (01)^∞ has density 1/2 and is periodic; aperiodic sequences of density 1/3 exist.
- Normality implies both.
- Density 1/2 along every arithmetic progression implies the anti-Toeplitz statement, which implies Problem 1.
- An explicit periodic tail would decide Problem 2 [W19].

Problem 2 is Π⁰₃. Data: 500,025,038 ones in the first 10^9 bits, about 1.6 standard deviations from half [W19].

**Problem 3** (effort Ω(n)).

Wolfram's formal statement is `NotExists[m, ForAll[n, machine[m][n][[1]] == Last[c[n]]] && MaxLimit[machine[m][n][[2]]/n, n -> Infinity] < Infinity]`, with Turing machines reading n. Notes:
- Read literally, it forbids even O(n) algorithms, which is stronger than the verbal "at least O(n)".
- The machine model matters. On a unit-cost RAM with bitwise operations on unbounded integers, [25] computes c(n) in O(n) operations, so the literal statement is false in that model.
- Implication chain: Problem 3 ⟹ no polylog-time digit extraction ⟹ c is not automatic ⟹ Problem 1. Wolfram notes that Problem 3 implies Problem 1.
- Problem 1 itself is exactly the analogous statement for *unary* input [43].
- The literal statement is Π⁰₂.
- It is formalized nowhere; formal-conjectures omits it as model-relative. Mathlib's `Turing.TM2ComputableInTime` measures time in input length, so "O(n)" corresponds to O(2^len).
- Its circuit-complexity strengthenings are beyond current lower-bound techniques [LY22], and natural proofs are a barrier [RR97].
- Problem 3 also transfers to rules 86, 135 and 149 and to the stripe seeds (identical or complemented columns, an O(1) difference).

## 8. Perspectives

1. **Hubs.** A handful of general lemmas about 0/1 sequences generate the whole equivalent catalog:
   - "rational ⟺ EP digits", for real, p-adic and function-field expansions;
   - "finitely many shifts ⟺ EP", which gives regular languages, the orbit closure, the ω-limit and Myhill–Nerode;
   - "a finite-state deterministic system has EP output", which gives recurrences, LFSRs, NLFSRs, FCSRs, predictors, Büchi lassos and LZ76;
   - "ultimately periodic sets are the Presburger/semilinear sets".

   Formalizing these hubs once in Mathlib form gives most of the entries cheaply.
2. **A ladder of randomness criteria** [W19]. Each implies the next: Problem 3 ⟹ no polylog extraction ⟹ not automatic ⟹ Problem 1. Normal ⟹ disjunctive ⟹ positive entropy ⟹ Problem 1, and normal ⟹ Problem 2. Problems 1 and 2 are independent of each other.
3. **The digits-of-π analogy** [W19]. Problem 1 is irrationality, Problem 2 is simple normality, the block version is normality, and Problem 3 is the absence of BBP-type digit extraction. For naturally constructed constants, irrationality has only been proved through explicit rational approximations of arithmetic origin (Hermite, Apéry, Beukers), and x₂ has no such origin.
4. **A number-theoretic barrier** (number-theory survey). Classical irrationality and transcendence methods need a functional equation or repetitions:
   - D-finite ⟺ EP for 0/1 sequences [vdPS96];
   - Mahler functions ⟺ automatic sequences for 0/1 coefficients [ABS23];
   - criteria based on the subspace theorem need sublinear complexity or early repetitions [AB07].

   Problem 1, or the data, rules each of these out. A proof must build arithmetic structure out of the CA dynamics.
5. **Left-permutivity and sideways evolution.** Rule 30 is affine in its left cell. Two adjacent columns, or one column plus the neighbouring column where the first is white, determine everything to the left, and every single column is realizable. This drives Jen's theorem and the realization form [22]. Rules 90, 150 and 210 share all of this but have periodic centers, so a proof must use the nonlinear OR, i.e. the qr term.
6. **Jen's dichotomy blocks equivalences.** If A ∨ B is a theorem, proving A ⟺ B is as hard as proving A ∧ B. So no other column, and not the white seed, can be proved equivalent to Problem 1.
7. **A uniformity hierarchy.** Problem 1 ⊂ FinConf ⊂ NumberLike ⊂ LHC, each stronger than the one before. Every classical partial result (Jen; Kopra width 2; Condrey period 1) and every project reduction is uniform over finite rows. A proof of Problem 1 that does not also prove FinConf must use something specific to the seed's orbit, such as the odometer structure of its right edge.
8. **Odometer and diagonals.** The right diagonals are 2^j-periodic, and the orbit closure in the right-edge frame is the 2-adic odometer [CPY07]. c is a moving diagonal that, for each t, reads the diagonal of depth t inside its first period (right diagonals) or inside its transient (left diagonals). This is why diagonal periodicity does not reach c.
9. **Distribution mod 1 and Mahler.** Rows of rule 30 are dyadic numbers, and c(t) is the first digit of the fractional part of row t read from the left. Kopra puts rule 30 and the ×p/q automata in one class. The analogues of Dubickas, and of Pisot–Vijayaraghavan, are proved for rule 30; Mahler's Z-number problem and the equidistribution of (3/2)ⁿ remain the open counterparts.
10. **Generic versus special points.** For μ-almost every configuration, and for a comeager set of them, the center trace is normal. The single seed lies in the countable, null, meager set of finite configurations. Ergodicity of the doubling map (`AddCircle.ergodic_nsmul`) likewise says nothing about one specific number.
11. **Proof theory.** Problem 1 is Π⁰₂ and its negation Σ⁰₂, so finite computation settles neither. Independence from PA or ZFC is conceivable [W19]. A proof in PA would yield, by proof mining, a provably total bound on defects, which is a Π⁰₁ strengthening like the defect bound of Section 4.
12. **Complexity profiles from cryptography.** For any finite alphabet, each finite-register model has "profile bounded ⟺ EP". This holds for LFSR linear complexity, FCSR 2-adic complexity, maximum-order and k-th order complexity, and finite-state generation. For c every one of these profiles looks random. As numeric certificates they are weaker per bit than the kernel factor count (T+P ≥ about n/2 from n bits, against about n).
13. **Missing Mathlib infrastructure.**
    - Mathlib already has: Presburger definability, Myhill–Nerode, `LinearRecurrence`, AddCircle torsion and density, continued fractions over ordered fields, p-adics, PowerSeries/RatFunc/LaurentSeries, `omegaLimit`, `SymbolicDynamics`, König's lemma, `Dioph`.
    - Missing: an eventually-periodic predicate, the digits-rationality lemma, Morse–Hedlund, Kronecker, Fatou, Szegő, Pólya–Carlson, Lagrange, Christol, Cobham, automatic sequences, Büchi and MSO, Parikh, the context-free pumping lemma, the gap theorems, normal numbers, natural density, the pointwise ergodic theorem, and cellular automata.

---

## 9. Classification checks and corrections to the surveys

1. **All 43 equivalences were re-derived.** No survey's "equivalent" had to be downgraded, but several needed sharper statements:
   - Only positional readings in an integer base are equivalent. Non-positional readings, such as Σ c(t)/t! and Σ c(t)·2^−t!, are irrational or Liouville unconditionally.
   - integer-digits and return-words need the proved fact that c is not eventually constant. They are not facts about every sequence.
   - In the p-adic congruence form, when p divides b, the p-power must be divided out first; it then divides a. The survey's sketch assumed b coprime to p.
   - In LZ76, the first component has no earlier source, so a definition must allow one-letter "innovation" components. The "fewest components" definition also needs Lempel–Ziv's optimality theorem.
   - Hankel: "H_n odd infinitely often" is equivalent, but "H_n odd for all n" (a perfect linear complexity profile) is false: H_3 = −2, and the Wang–Massey criterion fails at i = 2.
   - Wolfram's printed formal statement of Problem 1 is degenerate as printed (Section 3.1, [8]).
2. **Stronger, not equivalent.**
   - Transcendence over F₂(X) (⟺ not 2-automatic) is strictly stronger, while transcendence over ℚ(X) is equivalent, by Fatou.
   - Unbounded expansion complexity, normality, disjunctiveness, μ(x₂) = 2, transcendence of x₂, and every Problem-3-type lower bound are strictly stronger.
   - LHC, FinConf, NumberLike and "no column EP" are stronger. Q01 and CQ01 are not implied by Problem 1.
3. **Probably false strengthenings** are flagged in Section 4.
4. **Cannot be proved equivalent without solving the problem:** column j ≠ 0 and the white seed (Section 6).
5. **A citation correction.** The Pólya–Carlson theorem is F. Carlson, *Über Potenzreihen mit ganzzahligen Koeffizienten*, Math. Z. 9 (1921) 1–13. The Wolfram-writings survey cited Carlson's different paper *Über ganzwertige Funktionen*, Math. Z. 11 (1921).
6. **Status updates relative to the surveys:**
   - Morse–Hedlund is now in the library; the words survey had listed it as missing.
   - The `Real.ofDigits` form now has a 15-line bridge; the surveys said it needed a missing lemma.
   - Ten further corollaries were proved in this merge.
7. **Unverified claims, kept with flags:**
   - Condrey 2026 and Nersissian 2026 are unrefereed and were read through the project's literature notes.
   - "Period 1 holds for number-like rows" is the CA-structure survey's own derivation.
   - "Absorption also excludes w^∞ for every finite row" is the CA survey's reading of the proofs.
   - The contents of ctchou/AutomataTheory.
   - Rule 30 as the square of 3-color rules (NKS p. 956).
   - The OEIS numbers A327980 and A327981 cited by one survey were not checked; this catalog uses A327984 and A327985 (positions of the 1s and 0s), whose titles were checked.

equivalents.name: Irrationality of the binary number 0.c(0)c(1)c(2)... (the user's example)
equivalents.proof_route: Status: DONE in the untracked library (Rule30Equivalents.BinaryIrrational.problem1_iff_irrational_binary; generic lemma eventuallyPeriodic_iff_not_irrational for every base B >= 2); commit it. Route: classical 'rational iff eventually periodic expansion' (Wallis, Euler, Gauss Disq. art. 312ff; Hardy-Wright ch. IX). EP implies rational by the geometric series x2 = (N_T + N/(2^P-1))/2^T. Rational x2 = p/q: the tail values x_t = 2^t x2 - N_t lie in (1/q)Z intersected with [0,1], so x_i = x_j for some i < j by pigeonhole. If c has infinitely many 1s, c(t) = [2 x_t > 1] and x_{t+1} = 2 x_t - c(t) are functions of x_t, giving period j-i from i. Otherwise c is eventually 0, which also handles double expansions. Consequence of the kernel bound T+P >= 16359: x2 != p/q for every q <= 16359.

equivalents.name: Irrationality in every integer base b >= 2 (tsum, Real.ofDigits, Cantor function)
equivalents.statement: For each integer b >= 2, Problem 1 holds iff x_b = sum c(t) b^-(t+1) is irrational. Examples: the decimal 0.1101110011..._10 and x3 = 0.4623450726095034173712.... Equivalently, in Mathlib vocabulary, Real.ofDigits of the digit sequence c is irrational, and Cardinal.cantorFunction (1/b) c = b * x_b is irrational. Caution: only positional integer-base readings are equivalent. Sum c(t)/t! is irrational and sum c(t) 2^-t! is Liouville for ANY sequence with infinitely many 1s.

theorem problem1_iff_irrational_base {B : ℕ} (hB : 2 ≤ B) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    Irrational (∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℝ) else 0) / (B : ℝ) ^ (t + 1)) :=
  Rule30Equivalents.BinaryIrrational.problem1_iff_irrational_base hB
theorem ofDigits_eq (b : ℕ) [NeZero b] (hb : 2 ≤ b) :
    Real.ofDigits (b := b) (fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then 1 else 0) =
      ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℝ) else 0) / (b : ℝ) ^ (t + 1) := by
  unfold Real.ofDigits Real.ofDigitsTerm
  congr 1
  funext t
  have h1 : 1 % b = 1 := Nat.one_mod_eq_one.mpr (by omega)
  cases hc : Rule30Prize.center t
  · simp [hc]
  · simp [hc, h1, div_eq_mul_inv]
theorem problem1_iff_irrational_ofDigits (b : ℕ) [NeZero b] (hb : 2 ≤ b) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    Irrational (Real.ofDigits (b := b) fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then 1 else 0) := by
  rw [ofDigits_eq b hb]

equivalents.name: Morse-Hedlund factor complexity
equivalents.statement: Let p_c(n) be the number of distinct length-n factors of c. Problem 1 holds iff p_c(n) >= n+1 for all n, iff p_c is strictly increasing, iff p_c is unbounded.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: DONE in the library (ShiftOrbit.problem1_iff_ncard_factors, _ncard_factors_lt_succ, _strictMono_ncard_factors, _ncard_factors_unbounded). Route: Morse-Hedlund 1938 (Thms 7.3-7.4), in the one-sided form of Coven-Hedlund 1973. If p(m+1) = p(m), every length-m factor has a unique right extension, so the window dynamics is a self-map of a finite set. Kernel-checked consequence: p_c(26) >= 16359 (Rule30FactorWindow).

equivalents.name: Generating series not rational over F2; no LFSR; linear complexity unbounded
equivalents.statement: C(X) = sum c(t) X^t in F2[[X]] is not rational: no Q != 0 with Q*C a polynomial, equivalently C != P*Q^-1 with Q(0) != 0. Equivalently: c satisfies no eventual linear recurrence over F2; no LFSR generates c; the linear complexity profile (Berlekamp-Massey) is unbounded. Function-field form: xi = sum c(t) X^-(t+1) in F2((1/X)) is irrational, so its continued fraction is infinite.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: DONE in the library (PowerSeriesF2.problem1_iff_series_not_rational, _coeff_zero, _ne_mul_inv, problem1_iff_no_eventual_linear_recurrence, problem1_iff_no_lfsr, problem1_iff_linear_complexity_unbounded). Route: if c is EP, (1-X^P)C is a polynomial. Q*C = P gives a recurrence from the lowest coefficient of Q; pigeonhole on windows (Lidl-Niederreiter ch. 8). Bounded profile: finitely many registers of length d. Berlekamp-Massey equals Euclid on xi (Mills 1975, Welch-Scholtz 1979, Dornstetter 1987, Niederreiter 1988). Data: L(c|10^6) = 499,998.

equivalents.name: The formal-conjectures statement and Wolfram's formal statement
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff google-deepmind/formal-conjectures' Rule30.centerColumn_not_eventually_periodic holds: not (exists p > 0, exists N, for all t >= N, centerColumn (t+p) = centerColumn t), with state t = cell t. It also holds iff Wolfram's 2019 formal statement holds in its intended reading: no p >= 1 and i with c(t+p) = c(t) for all t > i. As printed, Wolfram's formula is degenerate: p = 0 is allowed, and c[t] is a list.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: the FC form is proved in scratch (merge/QuickProofs.lean, axiom Quot.sound only). The t > i form is stated (trivial). Route: state t = fun i => cell t i by induction (each step rfl); swap the quantifiers; t > i iff t >= i+1.
equivalents.lean_statement:
namespace FC
def step (row : ℤ → Bool) : ℤ → Bool := fun i => xor (row (i - 1)) (row i || row (i + 1))
def state : ℕ → ℤ → Bool
  | 0 => fun i => decide (i = 0)
  | t + 1 => step (state t)
def centerColumn (t : ℕ) : Bool := state t 0
theorem state_eq : ∀ t, state t = fun i => Rule30Jen.cell t i
  | 0 => rfl
  | t + 1 => by rw [state, state_eq t]; rfl
theorem problem1_iff_fc : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ t : ℕ, N ≤ t → centerColumn (t + p) = centerColumn t := by
  have hc : centerColumn = Rule30Prize.center := funext fun t => by
    rw [centerColumn, state_eq]; rfl
  rw [hc]
  constructor
  · rintro h ⟨p, hp, N, hN⟩; exact h ⟨N, p, hp, hN⟩
  · rintro h ⟨N, p, hp, hN⟩; exact h ⟨p, hp, N, hN⟩
end FC
theorem problem1_iff_wolfram : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ p i : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ t, i < t → Rule30Prize.center (t + p) = Rule30Prize.center t := sorry

equivalents.name: Black times are not Presburger-definable (not semilinear)
equivalents.statement: Let S = {t : c(t) = 1} (OEIS A327984). Problem 1 holds iff S is not definable in Presburger arithmetic (ℕ,0,1,+) with any set of parameters, iff S is not a semilinear set. A further classical equivalent (Michaux-Villemaire 1996, Milchior): (ℕ,+,S) defines an infinite set with unbounded gaps.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: proved in scratch (merge/QuickProofs.lean, about 3 lines each; also logic-computation/lean/PresburgerTest.lean and words-dynamics/PresburgerCheck.lean). Route: Presburger quantifier elimination / Ginsburg-Spanier: the definable subsets of ℕ are exactly the ultimately periodic sets. Mathlib proves this; only the Bool-to-Set bookkeeping (ep_iff) remains.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem ep_iff (f : ℕ → Bool) : Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic f ↔
    ∃ k, ∃ p > 0, ∀ x ≥ k, x ∈ {t | f t = true} ↔ x + p ∈ {t | f t = true} := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨T, P, hP, h⟩
    exact ⟨T, P, hP, fun x hx => by simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, h x hx]⟩
  · rintro ⟨k, p, hp, h⟩
    refine ⟨k, p, hp, fun t ht => ?_⟩
    have := h t ht
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at this
    cases h1 : f t <;> cases h2 : f (t + p) <;> simp_all
theorem problem1_iff_not_presburger (A : Set ℕ) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ A.Definable₁ FirstOrder.Language.presburger {t | Rule30Prize.center t = true} := by
  rw [FirstOrder.Language.presburger.definable₁_iff_ultimately_periodic, ← ep_iff]; rfl
theorem problem1_iff_not_semilinear : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ IsSemilinearSet {t : ℕ | Rule30Prize.center t = true} := by
  rw [Nat.isSemilinearSet_iff_ultimately_periodic, ← ep_iff]; rfl

equivalents.name: The 2-adic (p-adic) number sum c(t) 2^t is irrational
equivalents.statement: alpha = sum c(t) 2^t in ℤ_2 is not in ℚ. Integer form, for any prime p (reading 0/1 digits p-adically): there are no a, b in ℤ with b != 0 and p^n dividing b*S_p(n) - a for all n, where S_p(n) = sum_{t<n} c(t) p^t.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: a p-adic integer is rational iff its digits are eventually periodic (Gouvea; Koblitz ch. I). EP gives alpha = A + p^T B/(1-p^P). Conversely, the congruences say b*alpha = a in ℤ_p. Divide out the p-power of b (it must divide a). The remainders a_n = (a - b S_n)/p^n are integers with a_{n+1} = (a_n - b c(n))/p and |a_{n+1}| <= (|a_n|+|b|)/2, so eventually |a_n| <= |b|. With p not dividing b, c(n) = a_n b^-1 mod p: a finite deterministic system.
equivalents.difficulty: easy for the integer congruence form; moderate for the PadicInt form
