equivalents.name: The user's example without real numbers (core Lean)
equivalents.statement: There are no natural numbers p and q > 0 with c(t) = floor(2^(t+1) p / q) mod 2 for all t. That is, c is not the binary expansion of a rational number.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: with r_t = 2^t p mod q, floor(2^(t+1) p/q) mod 2 = floor(2 r_t / q) and r_{t+1} = 2 r_t mod q. That is a finite deterministic system, so such digit sequences are eventually periodic. Conversely, if c is EP it is the greedy expansion of its rational value, because c is not eventually 1 (Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant). This fits the Mathlib-free core catalog.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_not_rational_digits : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ p q : ℕ, 0 < q ∧ ∀ t, Rule30Prize.center t = decide (2 ^ (t + 1) * p / q % 2 = 1) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Nat arithmetic). Uses the catalog's Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant.

equivalents.name: Rational generating function over any field; constant-coefficient recurrences
equivalents.statement: For every field K (ℚ, ℝ, ℂ, F_p, ...), reading c(t) in {0,1} ⊆ K: Problem 1 holds iff C(X) = sum c(t) X^t is not in K(X) (no Q != 0 in K[X] with Q*C in K[X]), iff c satisfies no linear recurrence with constant coefficients in K (Mathlib's LinearRecurrence, valid from n = 0).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: the LinearRecurrence form is proved in scratch for every field (logic-computation/lean/LinRecTest.lean, R30Test.problem1_iff_no_recurrence). The power-series form is stated; it generalizes the library's PowerSeriesF2 proof. Route: (1-X^P)C is a polynomial. Q*C = P gives a recurrence whose first nonzero coefficient is invertible. Values in {0,1} (and 0 != 1 in K) make the window finite-state. Fatou is not needed.
equivalents.lean_statement:
noncomputable def series (K : Type*) [Field K] : PowerSeries K :=
  PowerSeries.mk fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : K) else 0
theorem problem1_iff_series_not_rational (K : Type*) [Field K] : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ P Q : Polynomial K, Q ≠ 0 ∧ (Q : PowerSeries K) * series K = (P : PowerSeries K) := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_no_linearRecurrence (K : Type*) [Field K] : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ E : LinearRecurrence K, ¬ E.IsSolution (fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : K) else 0) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: LinearRecurrence, LinearRecurrence.IsSolution, LinearRecurrence.mkSol, LinearRecurrence.charPoly (Mathlib/Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean); PowerSeries.mk, PowerSeries.coeff, the Polynomial→PowerSeries coercion; Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite.

equivalents.name: The unary language and the prefix language of c are not regular
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff L1 = {1^n : c(n) = 1} over a one-letter alphabet is not regular (equivalently, no unary DFA with output computes c), iff the prefix language {c(0)...c(n-1)} ⊆ {0,1}* is not regular.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: proved in scratch (logic-computation/lean/RegularTest.lean, R30Test.problem1_iff_not_regular; PrefixTest.lean, R30Test.problem1_iff_prefixes_not_regular). Route: Myhill-Nerode. The left quotient of L1 by 1^n is the language of the shift sigma^n c, and distinct sequences give distinct languages, so L1 is regular iff c has finitely many shifts iff c is EP. Kernel consequence: a unary DFA computing c needs at least 16359 states.
equivalents.mathlib_support: Language.IsRegular (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean), Language.leftQuotient, Language.isRegular_iff_finite_range_leftQuotient (Mathlib/Computability/MyhillNerode.lean).

equivalents.name: Complement, index shift, XOR derivative, running parity, permutive codes
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff each of the following is not EP: not c (OEIS A226474, the center of rules 135 and 149 from a white cell); c(.+k) for any fixed k; the XOR derivative c(t) xor c(t+1) (A327974); the running parity c(0) xor ... xor c(t); any right-permutive sliding block code f(c(t),...,c(t+r)).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: the complement is DONE in the library (Symmetry.problem1_iff_complement); the XOR derivative is proved in scratch (words-dynamics/CoreEquiv.lean, Scratch2.problem1_iff_deriv); the shift and parity forms are stated. Route: sliding block codes preserve EP. If the derivative has period P from T, then c(t+P) xor c(t) is constant, so c has period P or 2P. The parity is the prefix XOR, so the same argument applies. For permutive codes, the pair (window, phase) is finite-state.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_complement : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Equivalents.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => !Rule30Prize.center t) :=
  Rule30Equivalents.Symmetry.problem1_iff_complement
theorem problem1_iff_shifted (k : ℕ) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => Rule30Prize.center (t + k)) := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_xor_derivative : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => xor (Rule30Prize.center t) (Rule30Prize.center (t + 1))) := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_running_parity : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => ((List.range (t + 1)).map Rule30Prize.center).foldl xor false) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean). Mathlib has no sliding block codes.

equivalents.name: Decimations and residue classes
equivalents.statement: (a) For each fixed k >= 1, Problem 1 holds iff some decimation n ↦ c(kn+r) with r < k is not EP; for example, c at even times or c at odd times is not EP. (b) Problem 1 holds iff for every P >= 1 some residue class k ↦ c(r+kP) is not eventually constant. P = 1 is the proved center_not_eventually_constant.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: (b) is proved in scratch (words-dynamics/CoreEquiv.lean, Scratch2.problem1_iff_decimations); (a) is stated. Route: (a) decimation periods P_r from T_r combine into period k*lcm(P_r) from k*max T_r + k. (b) c has period P iff every residue class mod P is eventually constant. Since c(t) = [y_t >= 1/2] for the right-half row reading y_t, Wolfram's progression question is (b).
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_decimation (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∃ r < k, ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun n => Rule30Prize.center (k * n + r)) := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_nonconstant_class : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ P, 0 < P → ∃ r < P, ¬ ∃ K b, ∀ k, K ≤ k → Rule30Prize.center (r + k * P) = b := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean; Nat.lcm for (a)).

equivalents.name: Stripe seeds 1, 11, 101, 1011, 10101, ... have exactly the center column c
equivalents.statement: For n >= 0 let s_n be black exactly at the even positions of [0,n) and at n. Rule 30 from s_n agrees with the single-seed pattern left of the diagonal p = t, is the fixed stripe on [t, t+n), and has its right edge at t+n. So its center column is exactly c, and Problem 1 holds iff the center column of rule 30 from s_n is not EP, for any n.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: proved in scratch (ca-structure/lean/SymSeeds.lean, R30EquivScratch.problem1_iff_stripeSeed via evol_stripeSeed). Route: induction on t with the explicit pattern. The stripe ...1010... is a fixed point that always shows x_p OR x_{p+1} = 1 to its left neighbour (the OR latch), so the light cone left of p = t never sees it. Checked numerically for n <= 11, t < 400 (this merge) and n <= 51, t <= 2500 (survey). An exhaustive search found exactly s_0..s_9 among the rows supported in [0,9]. The surveys found no literature for this.
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean; the catalog's Rule30Realization.evol, Rule30Diagonals.R_zero and R_one_succ).

equivalents.name: Inverse problem: no eventually periodic column is realized by the single seed
equivalents.statement: With the right half white, every column u : ℕ → Bool is the center column of exactly one row Lambda(u), by left-permutivity. Lambda(c) is the single seed. Problem 1 holds iff no eventually periodic u has Lambda(u) equal to the single seed. 2-adic reading: for a fixed right half the trace map is an isometry of ℤ_2, the seed is 1, and Problem 1 says its image is irrational.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: proved in scratch (ca-structure/lean/SymSeeds.lean, R30EquivScratch.problem1_iff_realization; axioms propext and Quot.sound). Route: Rule30Realization.realize and unique (column_realizable_unique) together with evol_seed.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_realization : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ u : ℕ → Bool, Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic u →
      Rule30Realization.conf Rule30Realization.seed u ≠ Rule30Realization.seed := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean; the catalog's Rule30Realization.conf, realize, unique, evol_seed, seed_perturbation).

equivalents.name: A right-special factor of every length
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff for every n some word w of length n is right-special, meaning both w0 and w1 occur in c. By König's lemma this holds iff there is a left-infinite word all of whose suffixes are right-special.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: for a one-sided binary word, p(n+1) - p(n) is the number of right-special factors of length n. Then apply the library's problem1_iff_ncard_factors_lt_succ. The König form uses the finitely branching tree of right-special factors under left extension.
equivalents.lean_statement:
def OccursThen (w : List Bool) (a : Bool) : Prop :=
  ∃ i : ℕ, (∀ j : Fin w.length, Rule30Prize.center (i + (j : ℕ)) = w.get j) ∧
    Rule30Prize.center (i + w.length) = a
theorem problem1_iff_right_special : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ n, ∃ w : List Bool, w.length = n ∧ OccursThen w false ∧ OccursThen w true := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: exists_seq_covby_of_forall_covby_finite (König, Mathlib/Order/KonigLemma.lean); Set.ncard. No special-factor API.

equivalents.name: Finite certificates: prefixes with many distinct factors
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff for every N there are n and M such that more than N distinct length-n factors start below M. For fixed N the inner statement is Sigma-0-1. It is equivalent to 'no eventual period with T+P <= N', because sup_n p_c(n) = T_min + P_min for an EP c. Rule30FactorWindow is the kernel instance N = 16358.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: Morse-Hedlund (library). Every factor occurs in a finite prefix, and an EP c has at most T+P factors of each length. For concrete N, decide can check the inner statement.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_prefix_certificates : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n M : ℕ, N < ((Finset.range M).image
      fun i => List.ofFn fun j : Fin n => Rule30Prize.center (i + j)).card := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Finset.image, Finset.card, List.ofFn; the library's ShiftOrbit.factors.

equivalents.name: Rows as integers (NKS p. 871): c(t) is bit t of a(t)
equivalents.statement: a(0) = 1, a(t+1) = a(t) XOR (2a(t) OR 4a(t)) (OEIS A110240; one step is A269160). Then cell(t,p) = bit (t-p) of a(t), so c(t) = bit t of a(t). Problem 1 holds iff t ↦ testBit(a(t), t) is not EP.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. A Lean #eval agrees with A051023 for 60 bits, and Python agrees for 400 bits. Route: induction on t with the core lemmas Nat.testBit_xor, Nat.testBit_or, Nat.testBit_shiftLeft. The catalog's Rule30Window.stepRow and row_testBit use the opposite bit order.
equivalents.lean_statement:
def nksRow : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 1
  | t + 1 => let a := nksRow t; a ^^^ (2 * a ||| 4 * a)
theorem problem1_iff_nksRow : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => (nksRow t).testBit t) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Init/Data/Nat/Bitwise lemmas).

equivalents.name: Main diagonal of the 2-adic right-diagonal array
equivalents.statement: A(j,t) = cell(t, t-j) satisfies A(0,t) = 1, A(1,t) = [t odd], A(j+2,0) = 0, A(j+2,t+1) = A(j+2,t) XOR (A(j+1,t) OR A(j,t)). Every row j is purely 2^j-periodic, and c(t) = A(t,t) (OEIS A363343). Problem 1 holds iff the main diagonal of this array is not EP. In the right-edge frame the orbit closure is the 2-adic odometer (Coven-Pivato-Yassawi).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated; #eval agrees for 13 terms. Route: diagArray = Rule30Diagonals.R by induction (R_zero, R_one_succ, R_step), then center_eq_R.
equivalents.lean_statement:
def diagArray : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, _ => true
  | 1, t => decide (t % 2 = 1)
  | _ + 2, 0 => false
  | j + 2, t + 1 => xor (diagArray (j + 2) t) (diagArray (j + 1) t || diagArray j t)
theorem problem1_iff_diagArray : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic (fun t => diagArray t t) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean; the catalog's Rule30Diagonals). Mathlib has no odometer.

equivalents.name: Finite-state prediction and generation
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff every finite-state predictor (finite states, transitions reading c(0..n-1), a guess g(state) for c(n)) errs infinitely often, iff no finite autonomous machine (F : sigma → sigma, output g) has c(t) = g(F^t s0) for all large t. So no LFSR, NLFSR, FCSR or finite cyclic rule-30 register produces c from some time on.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: an EP c is predicted by a counter. An eventually-correct predictor effectively reads its own guesses, so it runs autonomously on a finite set and is eventually periodic. Finite-state unpredictability at error rate 1/2 is stronger and implies Problem 2 as well (Feder-Merhav-Gutman; Schnorr-Stimm).
equivalents.lean_statement:
def readState {σ : Type} (s₀ : σ) (δ : σ → Bool → σ) : ℕ → σ
  | 0 => s₀
  | n + 1 => δ (readState s₀ δ n) (Rule30Prize.center n)
theorem problem1_iff_unpredictable : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ (σ : Type) [Finite σ] (s₀ : σ) (δ : σ → Bool → σ) (g : σ → Bool),
      ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ g (readState s₀ δ n) ≠ Rule30Prize.center n := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_no_finite_generator : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ (σ : Type) (_ : Finite σ) (s₀ : σ) (F : σ → σ) (g : σ → Bool) (T : ℕ),
      ∀ t, T ≤ t → Rule30Prize.center t = g (F^[t] s₀) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite, Function.IsPeriodicPt; DFA (Mathlib/Computability/DFA.lean) has no output map.

equivalents.name: No nonlinear feedback shift register; maximum-order complexity unbounded
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff for no m and F : {0,1}^m → {0,1} is c(i+m) = F(c(i),...,c(i+m-1)) for all i, iff the maximum-order complexity M_n(c) → infinity (Jansen-Boekee), iff for each m two equal length-m windows have different successors. The same holds for the k-th order complexity, for each fixed k.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: for an EP c with (T,P), windows of length T+P determine the next bit (both successors lie in the periodic part at the same phase). Conversely, a feedback function makes the dynamics finite and deterministic. Each lower bound has a two-position certificate. Data: M_n = 37 at 10^6 and 44 at 10^7, close to 2 log2 n.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_no_nlfsr : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ m : ℕ, ¬ ∃ F : (Fin m → Bool) → Bool,
      ∀ i, Rule30Prize.center (i + m) = F (fun k => Rule30Prize.center (i + k)) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean plus pigeonhole). No feedback-shift-register API in Mathlib.

equivalents.name: Gaps between black cells, run lengths, return words
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff the gaps between consecutive black cells (first differences of OEIS A327984) are not EP, iff the same for white cells (A327985), iff the run lengths (A327983) are not EP, iff for some (every) recurrent word u the derived sequence of return words is not EP (Durand 1998).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: c has infinitely many black and white cells (center_not_eventually_constant), so each sequence and c determine each other up to eventual periodicity. Since colors alternate, an odd period of the run lengths doubles in c. The Nat.nth bookkeeping is the fiddly part.
equivalents.lean_statement:
noncomputable def blackGap (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.nth (fun t => Rule30Prize.center t = true) (n + 1) -
    Nat.nth (fun t => Rule30Prize.center t = true) n
theorem problem1_iff_black_gaps : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ T P, 0 < P ∧ ∀ n, T ≤ n → blackGap (n + P) = blackGap n := sorry
noncomputable def runLength (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.nth (fun t => Rule30Prize.center t ≠ Rule30Prize.center (t + 1)) (k + 1) -
    Nat.nth (fun t => Rule30Prize.center t ≠ Rule30Prize.center (t + 1)) k
theorem problem1_iff_run_lengths : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ T P, 0 < P ∧ ∀ k, T ≤ k → runLength (k + P) = runLength k := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Nat.nth (Mathlib/Data/Nat/Nth.lean). No return-word or run-length API.

equivalents.name: 2-adic (FCSR) complexity unbounded
equivalents.statement: For every bound B there is n such that no a, b (b != 0, |a|, |b| <= B) satisfy 2^n | b*S_2(n) - a, where S_2(n) = sum_{t<n} c(t) 2^t. Equivalently, no feedback-with-carry shift register generates c (Klapper-Goresky).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: only finitely many pairs (a,b) satisfy the bound. If each n had one, a single pair would work for infinitely many n, hence for all n (the congruences descend); then apply two-adic. Data: the 2-adic complexity stays within 3.6 bits of n/2 for n <= 65536.
equivalents.lean_statement:
def S (p n : ℕ) : ℤ := ∑ t ∈ Finset.range n, (if Rule30Prize.center t then 1 else 0) * (p : ℤ) ^ t
theorem problem1_iff_two_adic_complexity : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ B : ℕ, ∃ n, ¬ ∃ a b : ℤ, b ≠ 0 ∧ |a| ≤ B ∧ |b| ≤ B ∧ (2 : ℤ) ^ n ∣ b * S 2 n - a := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Int divisibility and Finset.sum only; no FCSR API.

equivalents.name: No polynomial-coefficient recurrence; the generating function is not D-finite
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff there are no d, N and polynomials p_0..p_d in ℤ[n], not all zero, with sum_i p_i(n) c(n+i) = 0 for all n >= N, iff sum c(t) X^t is not D-finite over ℚ(X).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Elementary route: let D = max deg p_i and a_i the n^D coefficients. Then sum a_i c(n+i) takes finitely many values and is O(1/n), so it is eventually 0. That is a constant-coefficient recurrence; apply rational-any-field. Classical: van der Poorten-Shparlinski 1996 (finite-valued P-recursive implies rational); Stanley 1980 (P-recursive iff D-finite).
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_not_pRecursive : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ (d N : ℕ) (p : Fin (d + 1) → Polynomial ℤ), (∃ i, p i ≠ 0) ∧
      ∀ n, N ≤ n → ∑ i : Fin (d + 1),
        (p i).eval (n : ℤ) * (if Rule30Prize.center (n + i) then 1 else 0) = 0 := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Polynomial.eval, Polynomial.natDegree, Polynomial.leadingCoeff. Missing: D-finite/holonomic notions and van der Poorten-Shparlinski.

equivalents.name: Hankel determinants infinitely often nonzero (Kronecker)
equivalents.statement: Let H_n = det(c(i+j))_{0<=i,j<n}. Problem 1 holds iff H_n != 0 for infinitely many n over ℤ, iff H_n is odd for infinitely many n (over F2). H_1..H_12 = 1, -1, -2, 3, 2, -1, 0, 0, -1, -10, 4, 378. 'H_m != 0 for all m >= 9' is a stronger open statement. 'H_n odd for all n' is false.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Easy half: an eventual period (T,P) makes rows T and T+P of the n×n Hankel matrix equal once n > T+P, so H_n = 0. Converse: Kronecker 1881 (a power series over a field is rational iff its Hankel determinants vanish from some n on), then rational-any-field / series-f2-lfsr. Over F2 the nonzero H_n are exactly the values of the Berlekamp-Massey profile (checked numerically for n < 600).
equivalents.difficulty: easy for the half 'infinitely many nonzero H_n implies Problem 1'; hard (classical theorem needed: Kronecker) for the converse
equivalents.lean_statement:
def hankel (R : Type*) [CommRing R] (n : ℕ) : R :=
  (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin n => if Rule30Prize.center ((i : ℕ) + (j : ℕ)) then (1 : R) else 0).det
theorem problem1_iff_hankel_int : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔ ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ hankel ℤ n ≠ 0 := sorry
theorem problem1_iff_hankel_F2 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ hankel (ZMod 2) n ≠ 0 := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Matrix.det, Matrix.of, Matrix.rank (Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Matrix/Rank.lean). Missing: Hankel matrices and Kronecker's rationality criterion.

equivalents.name: Coupled driven halves: a causal fixed point
equivalents.statement: Let L_u be rule 30 on p <= -1, started white and driven at p = 0 by the column u, and R_u rule 30 on p >= 1, started white and driven by u. The system u(0) = 1, u(t+1) = rule(L_u(t,-1), u(t), R_u(t,1)) is causal, and its unique solution is c. Problem 1 holds iff no solution is EP. The project's period reductions (Q01, Q001, C3 on the left; Absorption on the right) are relaxations that drop one half.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: L_u(t) and R_u(t) depend only on u(0..t). The catalog lemmas Rule30DrivenLeft.cell_eq_L and Rule30Ether.cell_eq_drv (T = 0) identify the solution with c. The left half sees the center only through c(t) AND c(t+1) (Rule30MaskedJen.effective_step).
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_coupled_halves : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ u : ℕ → Bool, u 0 = true →
      (∀ t, u (t + 1) = Rule30Jen.rule (Rule30DrivenLeft.L u (fun _ => false) t (-1)) (u t)
        (Rule30Ether.drv u (fun _ => false) t 1)) →
      ¬ Rule30Jen.EventuallyPeriodic u := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Not needed (core Lean; the catalog's Rule30DrivenLeft.L, Rule30Ether.drv, cell_eq_L, cell_eq_drv).

equivalents.name: The omega-limit set of c under the shift is infinite
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff omega(c) (the limit points of the shift orbit) is infinite, iff it contains a non-periodic point. Trace view: omega_sigma(c) = Tr_0(omega_F(delta_0)) for the width-1 trace factor map of rule 30.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: an EP c gives omega(c) = one periodic orbit. Conversely, a finite omega(c) is invariant, so it consists of periodic points. Choose L so that prefixes of length L-1 separate them. Eventually sigma^t c shares its length-L prefix with some z_t in omega(c), which forces z_{t+1} = sigma z_t, so c is eventually a shifted periodic point.
equivalents.lean_statement:
theorem problem1_iff_omegaLimit_infinite : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    (omegaLimit Filter.atTop (fun (n : ℕ) (x : ℕ → Bool) => fun t => x (n + t))
      {Rule30Prize.center}).Infinite := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: omegaLimit, mem_omegaLimit_iff_frequently, isInvariant_omegaLimit, nonempty_omegaLimit (Mathlib/Dynamics/OmegaLimit.lean); compactness of ℕ → Bool. Missing: CA traces.

equivalents.name: Tail language: p_inf(n) >= n+1; Omega(c) infinite; Rauzy graphs
equivalents.statement: Let L_inf(c) be the set of words occurring infinitely often, and p_inf(n) the number of them of length n. Problem 1 holds iff p_inf(n) >= n+1 for all n, iff the two-sided subshift Omega(c) with language L_inf(c) is infinite, iff no Rauzy graph Gamma_n of L_inf(c) is a single cycle.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: L_inf is factorial and extendable on both sides. A flat step p_inf(m+1) = p_inf(m) gives unique right extensions in L_inf. Only finitely many words of length m+1 occur finitely often; after their last occurrence, c follows the extension map. For an EP c with least period P, p_inf(n) = P for n >= P-1. No finite computation constrains L_inf.
equivalents.mathlib_support: Set.ncard; SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.Subshift (Mathlib/Dynamics/SymbolicDynamics/Basic.lean); Digraph/Quiver. Missing: subshift languages and Rauzy graphs.

equivalents.name: {c} is not omega-regular; the black times are not MSO(ℕ,<)-definable
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff no Büchi automaton accepts exactly the single word c, iff S = {t : c(t)=1} is not definable in monadic second-order logic over (ℕ,<) (Büchi's theorem).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: if c = u v^omega is EP, a deterministic lasso automaton accepts exactly c. Conversely, an accepting run on c revisits some accepting state; pumping that loop gives an accepted ultimately periodic word, which must equal c. The MSO form needs Büchi's theorem.
equivalents.difficulty: moderate for the Büchi form; hard (classical theorem needed: Büchi) for MSO
equivalents.lean_statement:
structure Buchi (α : Type) where
  Q : Type
  [fin : Finite Q]
  init : Q
  step : Q → α → Q → Prop
  acc : Set Q
def Buchi.Accepts {α : Type} (B : Buchi α) (w : ℕ → α) : Prop :=
  ∃ r : ℕ → B.Q, r 0 = B.init ∧ (∀ n, B.step (r n) (w n) (r (n + 1))) ∧
    ∀ N, ∃ n, N ≤ n ∧ r n ∈ B.acc
theorem problem1_iff_not_omega_regular : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ B : Buchi Bool, ∀ w, B.Accepts w ↔ w = Rule30Prize.center := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: None: Mathlib has no omega-automata and no MSO. The logic survey reports an external Lean 4 library, ctchou/AutomataTheory, with Büchi automata (not verified here).

equivalents.name: Lempel-Ziv (1976) complexity of the prefixes is unbounded
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff the LZ76 production complexity of c(0..n-1) is unbounded in n. Data: 1433 at n = 20000, against 1437 for pseudorandom bits.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: if c is EP, the last component of the exhaustive history copies with overlap forever. If the complexity is bounded, the exhaustive histories are prefix-consistent, so the last component is infinite; its copy source s <= h works for infinitely many n, hence for all n, giving period h+1-s. With the 'fewest components' definition below, use Lempel-Ziv's theorem that the exhaustive history is optimal. One-letter 'innovation' components must be allowed.
equivalents.mathlib_support: List.IsChain, List.zip, sInf on ℕ. No Lempel-Ziv theory.

equivalents.name: The generating function is transcendental over ℚ(z) (Fatou)
equivalents.statement: C(z) = sum c(t) z^t is transcendental over ℚ(z), equivalently over ℂ(z). Over F_p(z) the analogue is strictly stronger: algebraic iff p-automatic (Christol).
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: Fatou 1906: an integer-coefficient power series converging in |z| < 1 is rational or transcendental; then apply rational-any-field. Alternative: algebraic implies D-finite (Abel; Stanley 1980), then p-recursive.
equivalents.difficulty: hard (classical theorem needed: Fatou, or algebraic implies D-finite)
equivalents.lean_statement:
noncomputable def series (K : Type*) [Field K] : PowerSeries K :=
  PowerSeries.mk fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : K) else 0
open scoped RatFunc in
theorem problem1_iff_transcendental_Q : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    Transcendental (RatFunc ℚ) ((series ℚ : PowerSeries ℚ) : LaurentSeries ℚ) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Transcendental, IsAlgebraic (Mathlib/RingTheory/Algebraic/Defs.lean); RatFunc; LaurentSeries with the HahnSeries.ofPowerSeries coercion (Mathlib/RingTheory/LaurentSeries.lean); RatFunc.coeToLaurentSeries; scoped instance RatFunc.liftAlgebra (Mathlib/FieldTheory/RatFunc/Basic.lean). Missing: Fatou's theorem; algebraic implies D-finite.

equivalents.name: theta = [1+c(0); 1+c(1), 1+c(2), ...] is not a quadratic irrational
equivalents.statement: The continued fraction with partial quotients 1 + c(t), theta = 2.3693419984984465463470948954606643210774..., is not a root of any nonzero integer polynomial of degree <= 2. theta is irrational for every c.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: Euler-Lagrange: a real number has an eventually periodic regular continued fraction iff it is a quadratic irrational (Hardy-Wright §10.12, Theorem 177 for Lagrange's direction). The partial quotients 1 + c(t) are EP iff c is. Both directions are needed; neither is in Mathlib. 'theta transcendental' is conditional only (Bugeaud 2013, if c were automatic).
equivalents.lean_statement:
noncomputable def θ : ℝ :=
  Filter.limUnder Filter.atTop
    (GenContFract.mk (1 + if Rule30Prize.center 0 then (1 : ℝ) else 0)
      (Stream'.Seq.ofStream fun t => ⟨1, 1 + if Rule30Prize.center (t + 1) then (1 : ℝ) else 0⟩)).convs
theorem problem1_iff_not_quadratic : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ A B C : ℤ, (A, B, C) ≠ (0, 0, 0) ∧ (A : ℝ) * θ ^ 2 + B * θ + C = 0 := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: GenContFract, GenContFract.mk, GenContFract.convs, Stream'.Seq.ofStream, GenContFract.of_convergence. Missing: the periodic continued fraction / Euler-Lagrange theorem.

equivalents.name: The unary and prefix languages are not context-free
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff {1^n : c(n) = 1} is not context-free, iff the prefix language of c is not context-free.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: unary context-free languages are regular (Ginsburg-Rice 1962; Parikh 1966). An infinite context-free language of prefixes of one infinite word forces that word to be ultimately periodic (Book 1977, via the context-free pumping lemma). Then apply regular-languages.
equivalents.difficulty: hard (classical theorem needed: Parikh or Ginsburg-Rice; Book)
equivalents.mathlib_support: Language.IsContextFree, ContextFreeGrammar (Mathlib/Computability/ContextFreeGrammar.lean); DFA.pumping_lemma and NFA.pumping_lemma (regular only). Missing: the context-free pumping lemma and Parikh's theorem.

equivalents.name: The unit circle is a natural boundary of sum c(t) z^t (Szegő, Pólya-Carlson)
equivalents.statement: f(z) = sum c(t) z^t has radius of convergence exactly 1 and continues analytically across no arc of |z| = 1.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: Szegő 1922: a power series with finitely many distinct coefficients that continues across an arc equals P(z)/(1 - z^m). Pólya-Carlson (Carlson, Math. Z. 9 (1921) 1-13): integer coefficients and radius 1 give either a rational function or the unit circle as natural boundary. Then apply rational-any-field over ℂ. The radius is 1 because c is bounded and not eventually 0.
equivalents.difficulty: hard (classical theorem needed: Szegő or Pólya-Carlson)
equivalents.lean_statement:
noncomputable def genFun (z : ℂ) : ℂ := ∑' t, (if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : ℂ) else 0) * z ^ t
theorem problem1_iff_natural_boundary : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ∀ z₀ : ℂ, ‖z₀‖ = 1 → ∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → ¬ ∃ g : ℂ → ℂ,
      AnalyticOnNhd ℂ g (Metric.ball z₀ r) ∧
        ∀ z ∈ Metric.ball z₀ r, ‖z‖ < 1 → g z = genFun z := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: AnalyticOnNhd (Mathlib/Analysis/Analytic/Basic.lean), AnalyticOnNhd.eqOn_of_preconnected_of_eventuallyEq, FormalMultilinearSeries.radius. Missing: natural boundaries, Szegő's theorem, the Pólya-Carlson theorem.

equivalents.name: Not both 2- and 3-automatic; transcendental over F2(X) or over F3(X)
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff c is not both 2-automatic and 3-automatic (any multiplicatively independent pair of bases), iff C(X) is transcendental over F2(X) or over F3(X) (0/1 read in F2 and F3), iff S is not definable in both Büchi arithmetics (ℕ,+,V2) and (ℕ,+,V3), iff c is not k-automatic for some k >= 2.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: stated. Route: an EP c has a finite k-kernel for every k, hence is automatic (Eilenberg). Cobham 1969: k- and l-automatic with k, l multiplicatively independent implies EP. Christol 1979 and Christol-Kamae-Mendès France-Rauzy 1980: over F_p, p-automatic iff algebraic. Büchi-Bruyère and Cobham-Semenov give the definability form. Data: 2-kernel >= 262,143 and 3-kernel >= 265,720 elements.
equivalents.lean_statement:
def kernel (k : ℕ) (f : ℕ → Bool) : Set (ℕ → Bool) :=
  {g | ∃ e r, r < k ^ e ∧ g = fun n => f (k ^ e * n + r)}
def IsAutomatic (k : ℕ) (f : ℕ → Bool) : Prop := (kernel k f).Finite
theorem problem1_iff_not_two_three_automatic : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ (IsAutomatic 2 Rule30Prize.center ∧ IsAutomatic 3 Rule30Prize.center) := sorry
noncomputable def series (K : Type*) [Field K] : PowerSeries K :=
  PowerSeries.mk fun t => if Rule30Prize.center t then (1 : K) else 0
open scoped RatFunc in
theorem problem1_iff_transcendental_F2_or_F3 : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    Transcendental (RatFunc (ZMod 2)) ((series (ZMod 2) : PowerSeries (ZMod 2)) : LaurentSeries (ZMod 2)) ∨
    Transcendental (RatFunc (ZMod 3)) ((series (ZMod 3) : PowerSeries (ZMod 3)) : LaurentSeries (ZMod 3)) := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: DFA, Language, RatFunc, LaurentSeries, Transcendental, ZMod with the instances fact_prime_two and fact_prime_three. Missing: automatic sequences (formal-conjectures has AutomaticSequence.IsAutomatic via kernels), Christol's theorem, Cobham's theorem (no formalization found in any proof assistant; Krebs 2018 has a short proof), Büchi arithmetic.

equivalents.name: No fast one-tape (or sublog-space) decider for the unary language
equivalents.statement: Problem 1 holds iff no one-tape deterministic Turing machine decides {1^n : c(n) = 1} in time o(n log n), iff no DTM with a read-only input tape decides it in space o(log log n). So Problem 1 is exactly an effort lower bound for unary input; Problem 3 asks for one with binary input.
equivalents.proof_route: Status: sketch. Route: apply regular-languages together with the gap theorems: one-tape time o(n log n) gives only regular languages (Trakhtenbrot 1964, Hennie 1965, Hartmanis 1968), and so does space o(log log n) (Stearns-Hartmanis-Lewis 1965). Regular languages are decided in real time.
equivalents.difficulty: hard (classical theorem needed: Trakhtenbrot-Hartmanis and Stearns-Hartmanis-Lewis gap theorems, plus a machine model)
equivalents.lean_statement:
-- sketch: OneTapeDecidesInTime : Language Unit → (ℕ → ℕ) → Prop is not in Mathlib
def unaryLang : Language Unit := {l | Rule30Prize.center l.length = true}
theorem problem1_iff_no_fast_unary_decider : Rule30Prize.Problem1 ↔
    ¬ ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, (fun n => (f n : ℝ)) =o[Filter.atTop] (fun n => (n : ℝ) * Real.log n) ∧
      OneTapeDecidesInTime unaryLang f := sorry
equivalents.mathlib_support: Turing.TM0, Turing.TM1, Turing.TM2, Turing.TM2ComputableInTime (Mathlib/Computability/TuringMachine/Computable.lean); Asymptotics.IsLittleO. Missing: one-tape time-bounded acceptance, crossing sequences, and the gap theorems.

corrections: Section 8, item 10 is false as stated. The center trace is normal for μ-almost every configuration, but not for a comeager set. Normal sequences form a meager set in {0,1}^ℕ (classical; Oxtoby, Measure and Category; Šalát 1966). The width-1 trace map Tr₀ is continuous, surjective and open: by left-permutivity, the image of the cylinder fixing x[−n,n] is the cylinder fixing c(0..n). So the configurations with a normal center trace form a meager set. What is comeager is 'the center trace is disjunctive' (a dense G_δ pulled back through an open continuous surjection); comeager traces are not even simply normal. μ-a.e. normality is true because Tr₀ pushes Bernoulli(1/2) forward to Bernoulli(1/2): c(t) = x_{−t} ⊕ (function of cells used by no earlier c(s)). Own reasoning from standard facts.

Section 4, 'Strengthenings to avoid': three entries do not imply Problem 1, because every purely periodic sequence has them. They are 'c is uniformly recurrent', 'Ω(c) is minimal', and 'c is a Toeplitz sequence' (the Jacobs–Keane definition admits periodic sequences). A recurrent EP sequence is purely periodic, so each of these only reduces Problem 1 to 'c is not purely periodic', which is still open (the kernel gives P ≥ 16359 for T = 0). Fix them to 'uniformly recurrent and not purely periodic', 'Ω(c) minimal and infinite' and 'non-periodic Toeplitz'. As written they also contradict Section 6, which correctly calls recurrence independent of Problem 1. The other three items (MSO(ℕ,<,S) undecidable, orbit closure not sofic, defect bound with coefficient 2) are genuine strengthenings.

Section 4, 'Unbounded runs': the justification 'an EP c has bounded runs' is false for eventually constant c. The implication 'unbounded runs ⟹ Problem 1' needs the proved Rule30Prize.center_not_eventually_constant, and so does any proof of StmtStronger.UnboundedWhiteRuns → Problem1. Likewise, 'Disagreements of positive density: for every τ' must say τ ≥ 1.

[26] diagonal-array (summary table, §3.1 and JSON): 'each row j is purely periodic with period 2^j' holds only as 'a period dividing 2^j'.
  - The least periods are OEIS A094605: 1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16, 32, 32, 64, 64, 64, 64, 64, 64, 128, … (j = 0, 1, …). For example, the least period is 2, not 4, at j = 2, and it is 64 for j = 9…14. Simulation here confirmed j ≤ 10.
  - A short proof (own observation): diagArray j t = testBit (nksRow t) j (checked for j, t < 80), and nksRow t = f^t(1) with f(x) = x ⊕ (2x ∨ 4x).
  - f is a bijective T-function on ℤ₂: bit k of f(x) is x_k ⊕ (x_{k−1} ∨ x_{k−2}). So row j is the orbit of 1 under a permutation of ℤ/2^{j+1}. It is therefore purely periodic, and its cycle length starts at 1 mod 2 and at most doubles with each bit, so it divides 2^j.
  - The cycle lengths of 1 under f mod 2^{j+1}, computed here, reproduce A094605 exactly for j ≤ 15.
  - This explains the [CPY07] odometer remark and puts [25] and [26] one lemma apart.

[14](c) / center_dioph: DPRM is not needed. 'Hard (classical theorem needed)' and 'Missing: DPRM' overstate the gap.
  - Mathlib already has the hard step, Matiyasevich's exponentiation (Dioph.pow_dioph), together with Dioph.div_dioph, Dioph.mod_dioph, Dioph.sub_dioph and Dioph.dvd_dioph.
  - A direct exponential-Diophantine definition (own reasoning; standard Davis–Robinson–Matiyasevich coding): let w = 2n+4. Then c(n) = ⌊H/2^{nw+n}⌋ mod 2, where H is the unique number with H mod 2^w = 1, H < 2^{(n+1)w}, and ⌊H/2^w⌋ = Φ(H mod 2^{nw}), Φ(x) = x ⊕ (2x ∨ 4x). Rows a(t) < 2^{2t+1} never spill into the next block, so induction forces H = Σ a(t)·2^{tw}.
  - Bitwise operations are Diophantine through binomial coefficients. x ≼ y (bit mask) iff C(y,x) is odd (Lucas, Choose.choose_modEq_prod_range_choose). a ∧ b = 0 iff C(a+b,a) is odd (Kummer, Nat.Prime.emultiplicity_choose). C(n,k) = ⌊(u+1)^n/u^k⌋ mod u for u > 2^n.
  - Difficulty: elementary but long, several hundred lines.

[37] lz76: Lempel–Ziv's optimality theorem is not needed for the sInf ('fewest components') definition. Suppose a history with ≤ K components exists for infinitely many n. Pass to a subsequence on which the number of cut points is constant and each cut point is either constant or tends to ∞. The component starting at the last bounded cut point p has unbounded length, so it is eventually a copy from some source s < p, and some s recurs. Then c(x + p − s) = c(x) for all x ≥ s, so c is EP. Own reasoning. Difficulty drops to easy–moderate, and the argument even gives complexity → ∞.

[28] nlfsr: 'the same holds for the k-th order complexity for each fixed k' needs k ≥ 1. With k = 0 the feedback is constant and generates only eventually constant sequences, so every non-constant periodic sequence has infinite 0-th order complexity.

Section 6: 'The ANF degree of the t-step map is 2t − 1' is false at t = 1, because the local rule l ⊕ c ⊕ r ⊕ cr has degree 2. Computed here, the ANF degree of the center cell as a function of the 2t+1 initial cells is 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 for t = 1…7. State the claim as 'for t ≥ 2'.

Framing in §0 ('The common pattern') and the §2 layout ('Every file proves ∀ b, EP b ↔ X b'): not every equivalence specializes a general theorem about b. [6], [8], [21], [22], [25], [26] and [33] are identity transfers: another sequence is proved equal to c or ¬c, or to the unique solution of a causal system, using rule-30 lemmas. Seeds.lean and Symmetry.lean cannot have the ∀ b shape. Also in §2, [39] (Lagrange) is not a corollary of the binary-irrational hub; it needs its own continued-fraction periodicity hub (Euler–Lagrange).

References: [CN] conflates two works. arXiv:0903.1627 is J. Cassaigne, F. Nicolas, 'On the Morse–Hedlund complexity gap' (checked on arXiv). The book chapter is J. Cassaigne, F. Nicolas, 'Factor complexity', in V. Berthé, M. Rigo (eds.), Combinatorics, Automata and Number Theory, CUP 2010 (EMA 135), ch. 4. Cite them separately.

[KNO26] is arXiv:2609.20415, Karimov–Nieuwveld–Ouaknine, 'Rich Sequences and Decidability of Arithmetic Theories', 17 Sep 2026. Its abstract treats ⟨ℕ;+,P⟩ for linear recurrences, special functions and the totient. It does not confirm that an arbitrary disjunctive S suffices.
  - The claim 'S disjunctive ⟹ Th(ℕ,+,S) undecidable' is still sound, by an elementary argument (own reasoning). ∀x ranges over all windows S∩[x,x+k)−x, which by disjunctiveness realize every subset of [0,k). This interprets weak MSO over (ℕ,+).
  - Weak MSO over (ℕ,+) defines squaring, via the set {0, 1, 4, …, y²} whose consecutive differences grow by 2, and hence multiplication (cf. J. Robinson, Proc. AMS 9 (1958) 238–242).
  - Either label the claim as this argument or check the body of KNO26.

[Ner26a] is arXiv:2609.25077, Nersissian, 'Diagonal Periods and Newton Supports of Rules 30, 86 and 135'. Its abstract does not mention the 'LSD-first 2-DFAO needs ≥ 8191 states' bound, so treat that as unverified. The survey's own kernel data supersedes it anyway: the minimal LSD-first DFAO has as many states as the 2-kernel, so |2-kernel| ≥ 262,143 gives more (data). [Ner26b] is arXiv:2609.25078, 'Diagonal Bases and Diagonal Periods of Elementary Cellular Automata'. Its abstracts support unbounded diagonal periods and a lower bound of ⌊m/2⌋+1 for the period at depth m.

§8, item 3 overstates. Irrationality of specific constants has also been proved by Mahler's method (functional equations; automatic numbers), by lacunary or Liouville-type gap arguments, by Erdős's elementary method (Σ 1/(2^n−1), 1948), and by subspace-theorem criteria, which §8 item 4 itself cites. Suggested wording: known methods need arithmetic approximations or structure (functional equations, gaps, early repetitions) that x₂ is not known to have.

Kopra: cite the theorem numbers. Checked against arXiv:2202.13809; the arXiv title is 'A natural class of cellular automata containing fractional multiplication automata, Rule 30, and others'.
  - 'Number-like' means nonzero and left-finite (Def. 2.4).
  - Theorem 3.5: a rapidly left expansive CA of width w has no EP width-w trace from a number-like x. Rule 30 has width 2. The theorem generalizes Jen 1990, Prop. 3.
  - Theorem 4.5: frac(F^t x) = frac(x) for only finitely many t (the Dubickas analogue).
  - Theorem 4.7: (frac F^t x) has infinitely many limit points (the Pisot–Vijayaraghavan analogue).
  - Problem 4.8 is Problem 1.
  - [Kop21] is 'On the trace subshifts of fractional multiplication automata', TCS 851 (2021) 92–110, arXiv:2005.05112.
  Cite these numbers in §6 and §8 item 9.

additions.name: Linear independence of shifts; infinite Hankel rank; torsion-free in the K[X]-module of sequences
additions.proof_of_relation:
(⟸) If c is EP with (T, P), then σ^{T+P}c = σ^T c. So the shifts are not injective, hence not independent (LinearIndependent.injective). They span at most T+P dimensions, every Hankel block has rank ≤ T+P, and (X^{T+P} − X^T)·c_K = 0.
(⟹) A nontrivial relation Σ_{i≤d} a_i σ^i c_K = 0 with a_d ≠ 0 is a linear recurrence valid from n = 0. The window pigeonhole of [17] then makes c EP; this is R30Test.eventuallyPeriodic_of_recurrence in logic-computation/lean/LinRecTest.lean, valid over any field and using 0 ≠ 1 in K.
Rank form: if every leading block has rank ≤ r, the spaces V_n ⊆ K^{r+1} of relations among σ^0…σ^r on the window [0,n) form a decreasing chain of nonzero subspaces. The chain stabilizes at a nonzero space, which is a global relation.
This form therefore avoids Kronecker's determinant lemma, which only the 'H_n ≠ 0 infinitely often' form of [32] needs. Own reasoning, standard.
additions.lean: Mathlib has LinearIndependent and LinearIndependent.injective (LinearAlgebra/LinearIndependent/Defs.lean), Submodule.span, FiniteDimensional, Matrix.rank (LinearAlgebra/Matrix/Rank.lean), LinearRecurrence and LinearRecurrence.IsSolution (Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean), and Module.AEval (Algebra/Polynomial/Module/AEval.lean). Nothing essential is missing. problem1_iff_shifts_linearIndependent, problem1_iff_shift_span_not_finiteDimensional and problem1_iff_hankel_rank_unbounded typecheck in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30equiv/critique/Additions.lean.
additions.known_results: The algebra survey found H_m ≠ 0 over ℤ for 9 ≤ m < 45,000, checked modulo a large prime. So σ^0c … σ^{44998}c are already linearly independent over ℚ on a finite window (data). Kernel-checked: σ^0c … σ^{16358}c are pairwise distinct (Rule30FactorWindow).
sources: L. Kronecker, Monatsber. Königl. Preuss. Akad. Wiss. Berlin (1881) 535–600 (finite-rank Hankel matrices and rationality)
F. R. Gantmacher, The Theory of Matrices, vol. II, ch. XV
R. Lidl, H. Niederreiter, Finite Fields, 2nd ed., CUP 1997, ch. 8
Own reasoning for the determinant-free rank argument

additions.name: Skolem–Mahler–Lech zero-set form
additions.statement: Let S = {t : c(t) = 1}. Problem 1 holds iff S is not the zero set {t : u(t) = 0} of any linear recurrence sequence u over ℚ, or equivalently over any field of characteristic 0. The same equivalence holds over any finite field, where every linear recurrence sequence is EP.
additions.proof_of_relation:
(⟸) If c is EP, then u(t) = 1 − c_ℚ(t) is EP, so it satisfies u(t+T+P) = u(t+T), a linear recurrence, and its zero set is S.
(⟹) By Skolem–Mahler–Lech, the zero set of a linear recurrence sequence in characteristic 0 is a finite set plus finitely many full arithmetic progressions, hence EP. So c would be EP.
The finite-field version is elementary: the windows take finitely many values. Over infinite fields of characteristic p, zero sets can be non-EP (Derksen), so that version is strictly stronger; see the Derksen entry.
additions.lean: Mathlib has LinearRecurrence, LinearRecurrence.IsSolution and LinearRecurrence.mkSol (Algebra/LinearRecurrence.lean). It has no Skolem–Mahler–Lech: grep 'Skolem' finds only ModelTheory/Skolem.lean. The statement `∀ (E : LinearRecurrence ℚ) (u : ℕ → ℚ), E.IsSolution u → {t | u t = 0} ≠ {t | center t = true}` typechecks (critique/Additions.lean, problem1_iff_not_LRS_zero_set).
sources: T. Skolem (1934), Comptes Rendus 8e Congrès des Mathématiciens Scandinaves
K. Mahler, Proc. Akad. Wetensch. Amsterdam 38 (1935) 50–60
C. Lech, A note on recurring series, Ark. Mat. 2 (1953) 417–421
H. Derksen, A Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem in positive characteristic and finite automata, Invent. Math. 168 (2007) 175–224

additions.name: Durand's Cobham theorem for substitutions (generalizes [42])
additions.statement: For any two multiplicatively independent Perron numbers α and β (for example 2 and 3, or 2 and the golden ratio), Problem 1 holds iff c is not both α-substitutive and β-substitutive. Here α-substitutive means a letter-to-letter image of a fixed point of a substitution whose dominant eigenvalue is α.
additions.proof_of_relation: Durand (2011) proved that a sequence over a finite alphabet is both α-substitutive and β-substitutive iff it is ultimately periodic, for multiplicatively independent Perron numbers α and β. The abstract states 'if and only if'; checked on arXiv. So each such pair gives an equivalence. k-automatic sequences are k-substitutive, so the 2/3-automatic form of [42] (Cobham 1969) is a special case.
additions.lean: Mathlib has no substitutions, morphic words, Perron numbers, Cobham or Christol (grep for 'Cobham' or 'Christol' finds nothing). It has Real.goldenRatio. Stating this needs new definitions: a substitution as Fin m → List (Fin m), its fixed point, a coding, and the dominant eigenvalue.
additions.known_results: No data for non-integer Perron bases. The survey's kernel bounds (|2-kernel| ≥ 262,143 and |3-kernel| ≥ 265,720) cover only the integer case.
sources: F. Durand, Cobham's theorem for substitutions, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 13 (2011) 1799–1814, arXiv:1010.4009
A. Cobham, On the base-dependence of sets of numbers recognizable by finite automata, Math. Systems Theory 3 (1969) 186–192

additions.name: Mignosi–Restivo–Salemi golden-ratio local periodicity
additions.statement: Let φ be the golden ratio. Problem 1 holds iff infinitely many prefixes c(0)…c(n−1) have no suffix that is a repetition of exponent ≥ φ² ≈ 2.618, i.e. no suffix of length ℓ ≥ φ²·p that has period p.
additions.proof_of_relation:
Mignosi, Restivo and Salemi (1998) proved that an infinite word is ultimately periodic iff every sufficiently long prefix has a suffix that is an α²-power, with α the golden ratio. The constant is optimal, as the Fibonacci word shows.
The direction 'infinitely many prefixes without such a suffix ⟹ Problem 1' is easy (own reasoning): if c = u v^ω, every prefix of length ≥ |u| + 3|v| ends with a period-|v| suffix of exponent ≥ 3 > φ².
additions.lean: Mathlib has Real.goldenRatio (NumberTheory/Real/GoldenRatio.lean), List.HasPeriod and the Fine–Wilf lemma List.HasPeriod.gcd (Data/List/PeriodicityLemma.lean). The MRS theorem is missing. EndsWithGoldenPower and problem1_iff_infinitely_many_prefixes_without_golden_power typecheck (critique/Additions.lean).
additions.known_results: Computed here: 2054 of the first 3000 prefixes of c have no suffix of exponent ≥ φ², including lengths 2989, 2990, 2996, 2997 and 2998. This is what a random word does, and it is consistent with Problem 1. Shallit (2023) proves explicit versions for the Fibonacci word with Walnut.
sources: F. Mignosi, A. Restivo, S. Salemi, Periodicity and the golden ratio, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 204 (1998) 153–167
J. Shallit, Prefixes of the Fibonacci word, arXiv:2302.04640 (2023)

additions.name: Irrationality in a Pisot base (e.g. base 1+√2)
additions.statement: For every Pisot number β > 2, for example β = 1+√2 or 2+√3, Problem 1 holds iff x_β = Σ_t c(t)·β^{−(t+1)} ∉ ℚ(β). For β = 1+√2 this says there are no rationals a, b with x_β = a + b√2.
additions.proof_of_relation:
Because β > 2, the 0/1 digits form the greedy β-expansion: after a 0 digit the tail is < 1/β.
- If c is EP, x_β ∈ ℚ(β) by the geometric series.
- Conversely, Schmidt (1980) and Bertrand (1977) proved that for Pisot β every element of ℚ(β) ∩ [0,1) has an eventually periodic β-expansion.
- A self-contained route (own reasoning): β is an algebraic integer, so the tails x_t = β^t x_β − Σ_{s<t} c(s)β^{t−1−s} lie in (1/q)ℤ[β]. Each x_t lies in [0, 1/(β−1)], and its conjugates are bounded by |x̄_β| + 1/(1−|β̄|). Only finitely many lattice points satisfy these bounds, and c(t) = ⌊βx_t⌋, so the tails, and hence c, are EP.
For 1 < β < 2, such as the golden ratio, expansions are not unique and the equivalence fails, matching the catalog's caution. For a Salem number β > 2, x_β ∉ ℚ(β) still implies Problem 1, but the converse is open (Schmidt's conjecture).
additions.lean: Mathlib has Real.sqrt, Irrational, Zsqrtd and tsum_geometric_of_lt_one (Analysis/SpecificLimits/Basic.lean). It has no β-expansions and no Pisot numbers (grep 'Pisot': none). problem1_iff_not_mem_Q_sqrt_two typechecks (critique/Additions.lean). The quadratic case can use explicit a + b√2 coordinates and the bounded conjugate, with no number-field machinery.
sources: K. Schmidt, On periodic expansions of Pisot numbers and Salem numbers, Bull. London Math. Soc. 12 (1980) 269–278
A. Bertrand, Développements en base de Pisot et répartition modulo 1, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. A 285 (1977) 419–421
Own reasoning for the specialization to 0/1 digits with β > 2 and for the lattice proof

additions.name: Minkowski's question-mark function: ?⁻¹(x₂) is not a quadratic irrational
additions.statement: Let y = ?⁻¹(x₂), where ? is Minkowski's question-mark function. Then y = [0; 1, r_1, r_2, r_3, …], where r_k are the run lengths of c (OEIS A327983: 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, …), and y ≈ 0.734976078619449957611903590207. Problem 1 holds iff y is not a quadratic irrational.
additions.proof_of_relation:
? is an increasing homeomorphism of [0,1]. It maps ℚ onto the dyadic rationals and the quadratic irrationals onto the non-dyadic rationals (Minkowski 1904). Its formula is ?([0;a_1,a_2,…]) = 0.0^{a_1−1}1^{a_2}0^{a_3}…₂.
c is not eventually constant, so x₂ is not dyadic and y is irrational. Hence y is quadratic ⟺ x₂ ∈ ℚ ⟺ c is EP.
Equivalently, without ?: the Euler–Lagrange theorem plus 'run lengths EP ⟺ c EP', i.e. [29] and [39] combined.
additions.lean: Mathlib has no ? function (grep: none) and no Euler–Lagrange theorem. The statement typechecks through GenContFract.mk, Stream'.Seq.ofStream and Nat.nth run lengths (critique/Additions.lean: runLen, yMink, problem1_iff_minkowski_not_quadratic).
additions.known_results: Computed here: ?(y) computed from 400 partial quotients agrees with x₂ to 38 digits. The continued fraction of y is [0; 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, …].
sources: H. Minkowski, Zur Geometrie der Zahlen, Verhandlungen des III. Internationalen Mathematiker-Kongresses, Heidelberg 1904, 164–173
R. Salem, On some singular monotonic functions which are strictly increasing, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 53 (1943) 427–439
A. Denjoy, J. Math. Pures Appl. 17 (1938) 105–151
OEIS A327983

additions.name: Other expansions of x₂ that detect rationality: Engel, Sylvester, factorial base, Lüroth
additions.proof_of_relation:
These are classical facts about the expansions, then apply [1].
- A rational p/q has finite Engel and Sylvester expansions: the remainders keep denominator q and their numerators strictly decrease, since (a_k − 1)·p_k < q.
- Its factorial-base expansion stops by k = q, because q divides q!.
- Lüroth (1883): a number is rational iff its Lüroth expansion is finite or eventually periodic.
- An irrational number has infinite expansions in all four systems.
additions.lean: Mathlib has none of these expansions: grep 'Engel' finds only Order/Grade, and there is no Lüroth or Sylvester. The Engel form typechecks as problem1_iff_engel_infinite, using remainders engelRem (critique/Additions2.lean).
sources: J. Galambos, Representations of Real Numbers by Infinite Series, LNM 502, Springer 1976
P. Erdős, A. Rényi, P. Szüsz, On Engel's and Sylvester's series, Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest. Eötvös Sect. Math. 1 (1958) 7–32
J. Lüroth, Ueber eine eindeutige Entwickelung von Zahlen in eine unendliche Reihe, Math. Ann. 21 (1883) 411–423

additions.name: Long unbordered factors start arbitrarily late (Ehrenfeucht–Silberger / Duval)
additions.statement: Problem 1 holds iff for all n and L there is a factor c(i)…c(i+ℓ−1) with i ≥ n and ℓ ≥ L that is unbordered, i.e. no nonempty proper prefix of it equals a suffix. Equivalently, every tail of c has unbordered factors of unbounded length.
additions.proof_of_relation:
(⟸, easy) If a tail is purely periodic with period p, each of its factors of length > p has a border of length (length − p).
(⟹) If every factor of length ≥ L starting at ≥ n has a border, the tail σⁿc has no unbordered factor of length ≥ L. By the Duval-type finite-word theorem, the least period of w equals the maximal length μ(w) of its unbordered factors once |w| ≥ 3μ(w) (Harju–Nowotka 2007; the optimal bound 7μ/3 is due to Holub–Nowotka). So long prefixes of the tail have periods ≤ L. Some p ≤ L is a period of infinitely many prefixes, hence of all of them, and the tail is purely periodic.
The infinite-word corollary is own reasoning built on these theorems; Ehrenfeucht–Silberger (1979) started this line of work.
additions.lean: Mathlib has List.HasPeriod and Fine–Wilf (List.HasPeriod.gcd), but no borders and no Duval theorem. Bordered and problem1_iff_late_long_unbordered_factors typecheck (critique/Additions2.lean).
sources: A. Ehrenfeucht, D. M. Silberger, Periodicity and unbordered segments of words, Discrete Math. 26 (1979) 101–109
T. Harju, D. Nowotka, Periodicity and unbordered words: a proof of the extended Duval conjecture, J. ACM 54 (2007), arXiv:cs/0305039
Š. Holub, D. Nowotka, The Ehrenfeucht–Silberger problem, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 119 (2012) 668–682

additions.name: Automatic complexity (Shallit–Wang) of the prefixes tends to infinity
additions.statement: Let A(x) be the deterministic automatic complexity of a finite word x: the fewest states of a DFA that accepts x and no other word of length |x|. Problem 1 holds iff A(c(0)…c(n−1)) → ∞, or equivalently iff it is unbounded.
additions.proof_of_relation:
Own proof; I did not find this stated in Shallit–Wang 2001.
(⟸) If c = u v^ω, a lasso DFA with |u| + |v| states plus a dead state, whose accepting state is the one reached at time n, accepts exactly the length-n prefix among words of length n.
(⟹) Suppose A ≤ K for infinitely many n.
- There are finitely many DFAs on Fin K over {0,1}, so a single DFA M uniquely accepts the prefix for infinitely many n.
- Some state q is visited infinitely often by the run of M on c, at times t_0 < t_1 < ….
- Swapping two adjacent closed walks c[t_k, t_{k+1}) and c[t_{k+1}, t_{k+2}) at q yields another accepted word of the same length n. By uniqueness the two segments commute.
- By Lyndon–Schützenberger, all these segments are powers of one primitive word ρ, so c[t_0, ∞) = ρ^ω.
additions.lean: Mathlib has DFA, DFA.accepts, DFA.evalFrom and DFA.pumping_lemma (Computability/DFA.lean), plus List.HasPeriod and Fine–Wilf. It lacks automatic complexity and the commuting-words lemma xy = yx ⟹ common root, which is derivable from Fine–Wilf. UniquelyAccepts, AutComplexityLE and problem1_iff_automaticComplexity_tendsto_top typecheck (critique/Additions2.lean).
additions.known_results: Shallit–Wang: A(x) ≥ n/13 for almost all binary x of length n. Nothing has been computed for c.
sources: J. Shallit, M.-w. Wang, Automatic complexity of strings, J. Autom. Lang. Comb. 6 (2001) 537–554 (definition)
R. C. Lyndon, M. P. Schützenberger, The equation a^M = b^N c^P in a free group, Michigan Math. J. 9 (1962) 289–298 (commuting words)
Own proof of the equivalence

additions.name: The black times are not first-order definable in (ℕ, <) (weaker; true)
additions.statement: S = {t : c(t) = 1} is not first-order definable, with any parameters, in (ℕ, <) or in (ℕ, succ).

additions.name: The generating function is hypertranscendental (stronger)
additions.statement: C(z) = Σ c(t)z^t satisfies no algebraic differential equation P(z, C, C′, …, C^{(n)}) = 0 with P ≠ 0 over ℚ (equivalently, over ℂ).
additions.proof_of_relation:
If c is EP, C is rational and hence differentially algebraic (Q·C − R = 0). The implication is strict for 0/1 sequences: Σ z^{n²}, built on the non-EP set of squares, is a theta function and satisfies an algebraic differential equation (Jacobi 1848).
Context: Adamczewski–Dreyfus–Hardouin (2021) proved that a Mahler function is either rational or hypertranscendental. So if c were automatic and not EP, C would be hypertranscendental; in general neither 'not automatic' nor 'hypertranscendental' implies the other.
additions.lean: Mathlib has PowerSeries.derivative (RingTheory/PowerSeries/Derivative.lean) and MvPolynomial.aeval, but no differential-algebra API. The predicate Hypertranscendental typechecks (critique/Additions2.lean).
sources: B. Adamczewski, T. Dreyfus, C. Hardouin, Hypertranscendence and linear difference equations, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 34 (2021) 475–503
C. G. J. Jacobi, Über die Differentialgleichung, welcher die Reihen 1 ± 2q + 2q⁴ ± … Genüge leisten, J. reine angew. Math. 36 (1848) 97–112

additions.name: Not the zero set of a linear recurrence in characteristic p (stronger; Derksen)
additions.statement: S = {t : c(t) = 1} is not the zero set of any linear recurrence sequence over an infinite field of characteristic p, for example F_p(x).
additions.proof_of_relation:
If c is EP, S is the zero set of the EP, hence linear-recurrent, sequence 1 − c over any field, so the statement implies Problem 1.
Derksen (2007) proved that zero sets of linear recurrences in characteristic p are p-automatic, of a special 'p-normal' form. So 'c is not p-automatic' implies this statement, which therefore lies strictly between Problem 1 and non-p-automaticity.
It is strictly stronger than Problem 1: over F_p(x), u(n) = (x+1)^n − x^n − 1 has the non-EP zero set {p^k : k ≥ 0}.
additions.lean: Mathlib has LinearRecurrence and RatFunc (ZMod 2), but not Derksen's theorem. NotZeroSetCharTwo typechecks (critique/Additions2.lean).
sources: H. Derksen, A Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem in positive characteristic and finite automata, Invent. Math. 168 (2007) 175–224

additions.name: Right halves of the rows have infinitely many limit points (Kopra; related, proved)
additions.statement:
For the single seed δ:
- the right halves frac(F^t δ) = (cell(t,p))_{p≥0} ∈ {0,1}^ℕ have infinitely many limit points (Kopra, Theorem 4.7);
- frac(F^t δ) = frac(δ) for only finitely many t (Theorem 4.5).
Equivalently in terms of the dyadic reals y_t = Σ_{p≥0} cell(t,p)2^{−(p+1)}, for which c(t) = [y_t ≥ 1/2]. Problem 1 is the open question of whether the first-digit sequence of (y_t) is EP.
additions.proof_of_relation: Kopra 2023 proves these from Theorem 4.6: if (frac F^t x) had finitely many limit points, then for every w some width-w trace would be EP. That contradicts Theorem 3.5, which for rule 30 is Jen's two-column theorem. These are the rule-30 analogues of Pisot–Vijayaraghavan (Theorem 4.7) and of Dubickas (Theorem 4.5) for (p/q)^n mod 1. They are proved, but they neither imply nor follow from a solution of Problem 1.
additions.lean: The catalog's Rule30Jen.jen and Rule30Jen.not_adjacent already give the width-2 input (no two columns of the seed pattern are both EP). Theorem 4.6 is a finite counting argument over windows. Mathlib has no cellular automata. This could be a fully proved 'related' module.
additions.known_results: Proved (Kopra 2023). Wolfram (2019) plots y_t and asks about equidistribution of y_{Pk+r}.
sources: J. Kopra, Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 946 (2023) 113668; arXiv:2202.13809 (arXiv title: A natural class of cellular automata containing fractional multiplication automata, Rule 30, and others)
E. Jen, Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata, Physica D 45 (1990) 3–18

critic.overall:
The catalog is substantively correct.
- All 43 claimed equivalences hold by the routes given, and no direction is reversed.
- The spot-checked Lean statements say what they claim. About 50 cited Mathlib names were checked by grep and all exist.
- The headline numerics were reproduced independently: x₂, x₃, θ, the continued fraction of x₂, H_1–H_12, stripe seeds, nksRow and the right diagonals.
- The formal-conjectures text and Wolfram's degenerate formula were confirmed, the latter with Mathematica's c[5] = {1,1,0,1,1,1}.
- Three survey scratch-proof files were recompiled, and they are axiom-clean.

The real errors sit outside the equivalence list:
- (1) The 'comeager traces are normal' claim in §8.10 is false: normal traces are meager, and disjunctive ones are comeager.
- (2) Three 'strengthenings to avoid' (uniformly recurrent, Ω(c) minimal, Toeplitz) do not imply Problem 1, because periodic sequences satisfy them.
- (3) Some statements need small fixes: [26] should say 'period divides 2^j' (A094605), the ANF degree is 2t−1 only for t ≥ 2, k-th order complexity needs k ≥ 1, and unbounded runs needs the proved non-constancy.
- (4) Two difficulty claims are overstated. center_dioph needs no DPRM, since Mathlib's pow_dioph plus Lucas and Kummer suffice. LZ76 needs no Lempel–Ziv optimality theorem.
- (5) Reference issues: [CN] merges two works, and [KNO26] and [Ner26a] say less in their abstracts than is attributed to them.

For completeness, the main gaps are whole hubs, not single entries:
- A linear-relations hub: shift independence, Hankel rank and K[X]-torsion are easy, Kronecker-free and reuse LinRecTest; the Skolem–Mahler–Lech zero-set form also belongs here.
- Durand's Perron-number generalization of Cobham.
- Local-to-global periodicity of words: the Mignosi–Restivo–Salemi golden-ratio criterion, unbordered factors, and automatic complexity. For automatic complexity I give a short own proof that A(prefix) → ∞ ⟺ Problem 1.
- More expansions that detect rationality: Pisot bases β > 2 such as 1+√2, Engel, Sylvester and factorial-base expansions, and Minkowski's ?, where ?⁻¹(x₂) is the continued fraction of the run lengths.
- The proved bottom rung of the logic ladder: S is not FO(ℕ,<)-definable.
- Two stronger statements: hypertranscendence, and Derksen's characteristic-p zero sets.
- A proved 'related' theorem obtainable from the catalog's Jen theorem: Kopra's Theorem 4.7, that the right halves have infinitely many limit points.
- A T-function reading of [25]/[26]: f(x) = x ⊕ (2x ∨ 4x) is a bijection of ℤ₂, and its cycle lengths mod 2^{j+1} are exactly A094605. This gives a 3-line proof of diagonal periodicity and explains the odometer.

Suggested first targets to add:
- shift independence / Hankel rank (easy);
- Engel or factorial-base termination (easy);
- the Filter-form and List.HasPeriod bridges (trivial; good for upstreaming);
- automatic complexity (moderate);
- Pisot 1+√2 (moderate);
- Kopra's limit-point theorem (moderate, proved).
